Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 13

Middle and Inner Ear Disorders

Middle and inner ear disorders affect hearing, balance, and fall risk. ATI emphasizes assessment patterns, otoscopy and vestibular testing, vertigo medication safety, middle-ear surgery restrictions, and cochlear implant teaching.

TL;DR - Hearing Plus Balance Equals Fall Risk

Middle-ear problems often look like ear pain, fullness, conductive hearing loss, fever, bulging or inflamed tympanic membrane, and altered light reflex. Inner-ear problems often add vertigo, tinnitus, nausea/vomiting, nystagmus, altered balance, and sensorineural hearing changes.

Differentiate

  • Conductive hearing loss can result from otitis media, otosclerosis, or foreign body/impacted cerumen.
  • Sensorineural hearing loss involves cranial nerve VIII damage and can be associated with aging or ototoxic medication exposure.
  • BPPV is position-triggered vertigo; Meniere disease adds episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss.

Safety Moves

  • Use fall precautions, assistive devices, slow position changes, and a clutter-free environment for vertigo or balance limits.
  • Teach sedation precautions with meclizine, diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, scopolamine, or diazepam.
  • After middle-ear surgery, avoid air travel, straining/coughing, forceful nose blowing, water in the ear, and rapid movement until cleared.

Ear Disorder Care Map

Hearing Loss, Otitis Media, and Vertigo Patterns

Locate the problem
PatternExpected FindingsPriority Teaching
Otitis media / middle earEar pain or pressure, fever, headache, conductive hearing loss, red/bulging TM, altered light reflex, and purulent or bloody drainage if perforation occurs.Antibiotics, analgesics, heat, decongestants, or myringotomy/pressure-equalizing tube can be used as prescribed.
BPPVSudden vertigo with position change, related to disrupted canal debris.Move slowly, restrict head movement during episodes, and use short-course antivertigo medication when prescribed.
Meniere diseaseEpisodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss.Evenly space fluids, reduce sodium/MSG, avoid caffeine and alcohol, and use assistive devices for balance safety.
LabyrinthitisSudden severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, possible hearing loss, and tinnitus, often secondary to otitis media.Rest in a darkened environment; meclizine or dimenhydrinate can treat vertigo/nausea as prescribed.

Diagnostics and Medication Safety

Sedation watch
  • Audiometry checks hearing ability by frequency, pitch, and intensity.
  • Tympanogram measures tympanic membrane and middle-ear mobility and can help diagnose middle-ear disease.
  • Weber and Rinne tuning-fork tests help determine whether hearing loss is present.
  • Otoscopy should show a pearly gray intact TM, visible malleus, and normal light reflex; fluid or bubbles behind the TM are unexpected.
  • ENG and caloric testing assess vestibular function through eye-movement responses; the client is kept on bed rest and NPO until vertigo subsides after the procedure.
  • Monitor ototoxic medication exposure, including gentamicin, erythromycin, furosemide, ethacrynic acid, aspirin, ibuprofen, and cisplatin.
  • Meclizine, antihistamines, scopolamine, and diazepam can help vertigo/nausea but require sedation, urinary retention, fall, glaucoma, and older-adult safety monitoring.

Middle-Ear Surgery and Cochlear Implant Teaching

Protect the ear

After middle-ear surgery

  • Avoid air travel for 2 to 3 weeks.
  • Avoid straining/coughing and blow the nose gently with the mouth open for 2 to 3 weeks.
  • Keep the ear canal clean and dry; avoid washing hair or showering for several days to 1 week.
  • Expect temporary hearing loss from fluid or packing; report drainage from the ear canal.

Cochlear implant

  • Used for sensorineural hearing loss.
  • Includes microphone, speech processor, transmitter/receiver, and electrodes attached to the auditory nerve.
  • The unit is not turned on immediately after surgery; the external unit and processor programming happen later.
  • Teach infection prevention and MRI avoidance.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Cochlear Implant

ATI-supported ALS

A nurse is completing preoperative teaching for an adult client who will receive a cochlear implant. Complete the Therapeutic Procedure template by connecting description, indication, and nursing interventions.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
DescriptionA microphone picks up sound; a speech processor, transmitter, and receiver convert sound to electrical impulses; electrodes attach to the auditory nerve. The external transmitter connects by magnet to the receiver under the skin.
IndicationSensorineural hearing loss.
Nursing interventionsComplete pre- and postoperative teaching, provide outpatient surgical care, teach that the unit is not turned on immediately, teach that the external unit and speech processor are programmed later, prevent infection, and avoid MRI.

Application Exercises

1

Which otoscopic finding is unexpected?

  • A. Pearly gray tympanic membrane.
  • B. Malleus visible behind the tympanic membrane.
  • C. Soft cerumen in the external canal.
  • D. Fluid or bubbles behind the tympanic membrane.
D Fluid or bubbles behind the TM can indicate otitis media and are not expected.
A, B, C A pearly gray TM, visible malleus, and cerumen color variations can be expected findings.
2

Which findings are expected with severe otitis media? Select all that apply.

  • A. Enlarged adenoids.
  • B. Recent frequent colds.
  • C. Daily furosemide prescription.
  • D. Normal light reflex in the affected ear.
  • E. Ear pain relieved by meclizine.
A, B Enlarged adenoids and frequent colds are associated with middle-ear infection.
C, D, E Furosemide is ototoxic but does not cause middle-ear infection; the light reflex is altered or absent; meclizine treats inner-ear vertigo, not middle-ear pain.
3

Which actions can help control vertigo from benign paroxysmal positional vertigo? Select all that apply.

  • A. Reduce exposure to bright lighting.
  • B. Move the head slowly with position changes.
  • C. Avoid fruit high in potassium.
  • D. Plan evenly spaced daily fluid intake.
  • E. Avoid fluids containing caffeine.
A, B, D, E A dark quiet environment, slow movement, evenly spaced fluids, and caffeine avoidance can reduce vertigo triggers.
C ATI focuses on reducing sodium rather than potassium for vertigo-related fluid retention.
4

Which finding is expected with suspected Meniere disease?

  • A. Purulent lesion in the external ear canal.
  • B. Feeling of pressure in the ear.
  • C. Bulging, red bilateral tympanic membranes.
  • D. Unilateral hearing loss.
D Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss is expected with Meniere disease.
A, B, C External lesions and bulging red TMs are not Meniere findings; pressure fits otitis media more strongly.
5

Which statement indicates understanding after middle-ear surgery?

  • A. I should restrict rapid movements and avoid bending from the waist for several weeks.
  • B. I should wait until the day after surgery to wash my hair.
  • C. I will remove the dressing behind my ear in 7 days.
  • D. My hearing should be back to normal right after surgery.
A Rapid movement and bending from the waist should be avoided for several weeks after ear surgery.
B, C, D The ear must remain dry for several days to 1 week, middle-ear surgery is through the TM, and temporary decreased hearing is expected from packing or drainage.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 14

Head Injury

Head injury care is a neurologic emergency. ATI priorities are cervical spine protection, oxygenation, early neurologic deterioration recognition, ICP reduction, seizure/safety precautions, and family support.

TL;DR - Stabilize C-Spine, Protect Oxygen, Watch ICP

Assume cervical spine injury with head trauma until cleared. Respiratory status is the priority assessment, changes in level of consciousness are the earliest sign of neurologic decline, and ICP rises with hypercarbia, suctioning, coughing, Valsalva, neck/hip flexion, low HOB, and stimulation.

Injury Patterns

  • Concussion changes neurologic function without identified brain damage and usually resolves within 72 hr.
  • Contusion bruises the brain and involves unconsciousness with stupor or confusion.
  • Diffuse axonal injury causes widespread injury and coma after severe trauma; hemorrhage can occur epidural, subdural, or intracerebral.

Emergency Cues

  • Test bloody drainage for a halo sign if CSF leak from nose or ears is suspected.
  • Increased ICP findings include severe headache, nausea/vomiting, declining LOC, restlessness, nonreactive pupils, abnormal breathing, posturing, Cushing triad, and seizures.
  • Brain herniation signs include fixed dilated pupils, deteriorating LOC, Cheyne-Stokes respirations, hemodynamic instability, and abnormal posturing.

Head Injury Care Map

Assessment Priorities and Diagnostics

ABC + GCS
  • Maintain cervical spine stability until imaging clears the neck.
  • Assess respiratory status first because brain tissue has minimal reserve when oxygen is deprived.
  • Use the Glasgow Coma Scale and level-of-consciousness trends to detect early neurologic deterioration.
  • Assess pupils, cranial nerve function, bilateral sensory/motor responses, seizure activity, and evidence of CSF leakage.
  • Diagnostics can include cervical spine films, CT/MRI of head or neck, labs for oxygenation/electrolytes/osmolality/glucose/toxicology, and cerebral perfusion calculation when ICP monitoring is in place.

Increased ICP: Prevent the Rise

Reduce stimulation

Raises ICP

  • Hypercarbia, suctioning, coughing, extreme neck or hip flexion/extension, HOB below 30 degrees, restrictive clothing, and Valsalva.
  • Overhydration, noisy environments, frequent stimulation, and uncontrolled pain/restlessness can worsen risk.
  • Opioids can obscure neurologic assessment and depress respirations if the client is not mechanically ventilated.

Lowers ICP risk

  • Elevate HOB at least 30 degrees and keep head/body midline and neutral.
  • Maintain airway, give oxygen as indicated, limit noise/visitors, and use stool softeners to avoid Valsalva.
  • Monitor fluids, electrolytes, osmolality, strict intake/output, daily weight, and signs of DI or SIADH.

Medications, Craniotomy, and Complications

Rapid response
  • Mannitol treats cerebral edema by drawing fluid from brain tissue into the blood; monitor urine output, renal status, electrolytes, osmolality, hypovolemia, and hyponatremia.
  • Barbiturate coma can decrease cellular metabolic demand but requires mechanical ventilation, cardiac/hemodynamic monitoring, and ICP monitoring.
  • Phenytoin can prevent or treat seizures; monitor therapeutic blood levels and interactions.
  • Craniotomy can remove nonviable tissue, evacuate epidural/subdural hematomas, reduce ICP, or remove tumors.
  • Brain herniation, hematoma/hemorrhage, pulmonary edema, DI, and SIADH are major complications requiring close neurologic and physiologic monitoring.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Head Injury

ATI-supported ALS

A nurse is reviewing the plan of care for a client who has a head injury. Complete the System Disorder template by naming diagnostic priorities, nursing care, and client teaching.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
Priority assessmentRespiratory status, because the brain depends on oxygen and neurologic damage can begin quickly when oxygenation is inadequate.
Earliest deterioration cueChanges in level of consciousness.
Nursing careElevate HOB at least 30 degrees, maintain airway, keep oxygen saturation greater than 92%, maintain cervical spine stability until cleared, report CSF drainage, provide a calm environment, prevent immobility complications, monitor fluids/electrolytes/osmolality, avoid overhydration, maintain seizure precautions, and explain actions to the client/family.
Client educationAvoid coughing and forceful nose blowing because these can increase ICP.

Application Exercises

1

An unresponsive client arrives after a head-on crash with spontaneous respirations and a bleeding forehead laceration. What is the priority action?

  • A. Keep the neck stabilized.
  • B. Insert a nasogastric tube.
  • C. Monitor pulse and blood pressure frequently.
  • D. Establish IV access and begin fluid replacement.
A Cervical spine injury must be assumed and the neck kept immobile until injury is ruled out.
B, C, D These can matter, but spinal cord protection is the immediate priority in this scenario.
2

After surgical evacuation of a subdural hematoma, which assessment is the priority?

  • A. Glasgow Coma Scale.
  • B. Cranial nerve function.
  • C. Oxygen saturation.
  • D. Pupillary response.
C Oxygen saturation is priority by ABCs because brain tissue is quickly damaged by poor oxygenation.
A, B, D These are important neurologic assessments, but oxygenation comes first.
3

Which actions decrease the risk of raising ICP? Select all that apply.

  • A. Suction the endotracheal tube frequently.
  • B. Decrease noise in the room.
  • C. Elevate the client's head on two pillows.
  • D. Administer a stool softener.
  • E. Keep the client well hydrated.
B, D Reducing noise/stimulation and preventing Valsalva with stool softeners help prevent ICP increases.
A, C, E Frequent suctioning raises ICP, pillows can hyperflex the neck, and overhydration can worsen ICP risk.
4

Which assessment findings indicate increased ICP? Select all that apply.

  • A. Headache.
  • B. Dilated pupils.
  • C. Tachycardia.
  • D. Decorticate posturing.
  • E. Hypotension.
A, B, D Headache, dilated pupils, and abnormal posturing are findings associated with increased ICP.
C, E Bradycardia and hypertension, not tachycardia and hypotension, are the classic late pattern.
5

A client with increased ICP has a new prescription for mannitol. Which adverse effect should the nurse monitor?

  • A. Hyperglycemia.
  • B. Hyponatremia.
  • C. Hypervolemia.
  • D. Oliguria.
B Mannitol is a powerful osmotic diuretic and can cause electrolyte imbalance such as hyponatremia.
A, C, D Hyperglycemia is not expected; hypovolemia and polyuria, not hypervolemia and oliguria, are monitored with mannitol.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 15

Stroke

Stroke care moves quickly: identify whether the event is ischemic or hemorrhagic, protect oxygenation and cerebral perfusion, screen swallowing before intake, and build safety around communication, vision, neglect, and mobility changes.

TL;DR - Type, Time, Swallow, Side

First priority is rapid recognition and imaging so treatment matches the stroke type. Ischemic stroke can qualify for thrombolytic therapy only within the ordered time window and only after bleeding is ruled out. After stabilization, protect from aspiration, injury, immobility complications, and frustration from language or perception changes.

Classify Fast

  • Hemorrhagic stroke involves vessel rupture and rising intracranial pressure risk from bleeding.
  • Thrombotic ischemic stroke often evolves as a clot forms on plaque.
  • Embolic ischemic stroke can begin suddenly when material from another site blocks cerebral flow.

Protect Function

  • Keep oxygen saturation above the ordered goal and monitor neurologic status closely.
  • Screen gag and swallowing before oral intake; keep suction available when feeding begins.
  • Teach scanning, positioning, and affected-side safety for hemianopsia or unilateral neglect.

Stroke Care Map

Stroke Type, Side, and TIA Warning

Localization

Patterns

  • Transient ischemic attack can present with brief visual changes, dizziness, slurred speech, or extremity weakness and can warn of an impending stroke.
  • Left-hemisphere stroke commonly affects language, reading, writing, calculation, recognition, and the right side of the body.
  • Right-hemisphere stroke commonly affects visual-spatial awareness, depth perception, impulse control, judgment, and the left side of the body.

Risk Reduction

  • Control hypertension, blood glucose, lipids, weight, tobacco exposure, and activity level.
  • Recognize high-risk conditions such as atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, hypercoagulability, aneurysm, and arteriovenous malformation.
  • Use prescribed antithrombotic therapy or carotid intervention when indicated for prevention.

Rapid Diagnostics and Acute Priorities

ED window
  • Noncontrast CT is the rapid first-line test to help distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke and determine thrombolytic eligibility.
  • MRI, MRA, cerebral angiography, and lumbar puncture can help evaluate ischemia, edema, aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation, perfusion, or blood in cerebrospinal fluid when ordered.
  • Monitor vital signs, temperature, oxygenation, cardiac rhythm, glucose, and level of consciousness because fever, hypoxia, dysrhythmias, hyperglycemia, and increased ICP worsen risk.
  • Position with HOB about 30 degrees, head midline, and neck neutral; avoid flexion or extension that can impair venous drainage.
  • Alteplase or other thrombolytic therapy is time-sensitive for eligible ischemic stroke and is contraindicated if hemorrhage or major bleeding risk is present.

Dysphagia, Neglect, and Rehab Safety

Aspiration + injury prevention

Swallow and Communication

  • Assess comprehension with simple commands and verify yes/no accuracy before relying on responses.
  • Use slow, clear speech, one-step instructions, picture boards, and extra response time for aphasia.
  • Keep the client NPO until swallowing safety is evaluated when dysphagia is suspected.
  • Use prescribed food texture and fluid thickness, feed on the unaffected side, and keep the head/neck slightly flexed forward when swallowing.

Mobility and Vision

  • Protect the affected arm and shoulder; support the limb in bed, wheelchair, and during ambulation to reduce subluxation risk.
  • Perform active ROM on the unaffected side and passive ROM on the affected side; elevate swollen extremities and move edema toward the body as taught.
  • Teach scanning toward the affected visual field for homonymous hemianopsia.
  • For unilateral neglect, teach dressing the affected side first and checking the affected limb for injury.

Active Learning Scenario

Nursing Skill - Dysphagia After Stroke

ATI-supported ALS

A nurse is caring for a client who has dysphagia after a stroke. Complete the Nursing Skill template by identifying safety actions before and during oral intake.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
AssessmentAssess gag and swallowing readiness; if gag is present, a small sip of water can help identify choking or poor fluid control.
CollaborationRequest speech-language pathology swallowing evaluation when the client has difficulty handling food or fluids.
Nursing actionsKeep the client NPO until evaluated if dysphagia is suspected; use prescribed diet consistency, observe closely for choking, keep suction available, and have the nurse perform the initial feeding.
TeachingExplain recommended food texture and fluid thickness; teach upright positioning with the head flexed forward during swallowing.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings should the nurse expect after a right-hemisphere stroke? Select all that apply.

  • A. Poor impulse control.
  • B. Left-sided weakness.
  • C. Impaired depth perception.
  • D. Expressive aphasia.
  • E. Limited awareness of deficits.
A, B, C, E Right-sided brain injury commonly affects impulse control, visual-spatial awareness, perception of deficits, and the left side of the body.
D Aphasia is more strongly associated with left-hemisphere involvement.
2

A client has left homonymous hemianopsia after a stroke. Which setup supports safe eating?

  • A. Teach the client to scan only toward the right side.
  • B. Place the meal tray and bedside table where the client can see them on the right.
  • C. Use the clock method to identify the food positions.
  • D. Position the wheelchair on the client's left side for transfer.
B With loss of the left visual field, placing needed items in the intact right field supports immediate safety while scanning is reinforced.
A, C, D The client should learn to scan toward the lost field, the clock method does not correct visual field loss, and transfers should favor the stronger side.
3

Which actions belong in a dysphagia safety plan? Select all that apply.

  • A. Keep suction equipment available.
  • B. Provide thickened liquids if prescribed.
  • C. Place food on the unaffected side of the mouth.
  • D. Delegate the first post-stroke feeding to assistive personnel.
  • E. Have the client swallow with the neck slightly flexed forward.
A, B, C, E Suction readiness, prescribed consistency, unaffected-side placement, and forward neck flexion reduce aspiration risk.
D The nurse should perform the initial feeding because aspiration and choking risk require skilled assessment.
4

Which communication strategies are appropriate for global aphasia? Select all that apply.

  • A. Speak slowly and clearly.
  • B. Offer picture cards or a communication board.
  • C. Raise the volume for each instruction.
  • D. Finish the client's sentences to save energy.
  • E. Use one-step directions.
A, B, E Slow clear speech, visual communication tools, and one-step directions support understanding and expression.
C, D Loud speech can feel patronizing when hearing is not the problem, and completing sentences can increase frustration.
5

Which finding is most consistent with a left-hemisphere stroke?

  • A. Impulsive behavior.
  • B. Poor safety judgment.
  • C. Inability to recognize familiar objects.
  • D. Loss of depth perception.
C Agnosia can occur with left-hemisphere involvement.
A, B, D Impulsivity, poor judgment, and depth perception problems are more typical of right-hemisphere injury.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 16

Spinal Cord Injury

Spinal cord injury care protects the cord first, then prevents secondary injury from hypoxia, hypotension, shock, immobility, bladder/bowel complications, skin breakdown, and autonomic dysreflexia.

TL;DR - Immobilize, Breathe, Perfuse, Decompress Triggers

In acute SCI, prevent further cord damage by minimizing movement and supporting oxygenation/perfusion. C4 or higher threatens spontaneous ventilation. Later care focuses on bowel/bladder routines, skin protection, gradual mobility, spasticity management, and rapid response to autonomic dysreflexia.

Level Predicts Loss

  • Cervical injury can cause quadriplegia and respiratory compromise.
  • Injury below T1 can cause paraplegia; upper thoracic lesions can also impair trunk stability.
  • Complete injury causes loss of voluntary movement and sensation below the lesion; incomplete injury causes variable loss.

Shock and Dysreflexia

  • Spinal shock causes temporary flaccidity, absent reflexes, and autonomic loss below the injury.
  • Neurogenic shock produces hypotension, bradycardia, dependent edema, and temperature dysregulation.
  • Autonomic dysreflexia is an emergency: sit upright, find the trigger, and treat severe hypertension.

Spinal Cord Injury Care Map

Assessment, Imaging, and Respiratory Priority

ABC + cord level
  • Assess motor function, sensation, reflexes, bowel/bladder control, pain, respiratory depth, and blood pressure response to position changes.
  • Use light touch, sharp/dull discrimination, and hot/cold discrimination to map sensory loss below the lesion.
  • CT, MRI, and x-rays help identify cord injury extent, fractures, blood, or bone fragments.
  • Respiratory status is the first priority because high cervical or upper thoracic lesions can impair involuntary or voluntary breathing.
  • Provide oxygen, suction, intubation or ventilation support as needed; assist coughing with abdominal pressure and teach incentive spirometry when appropriate.

Shock, Immobilization, and Mobility

Prevent secondary injury

Perfusion and Tone

  • Monitor for neurogenic shock within the first 24 hr and for several days to weeks: hypotension, bradycardia, edema, and poor temperature regulation.
  • Support ordered mean arterial pressure goals and treat adverse findings with prescribed fluids, vasopressors, or atropine.
  • Upper motor neuron injuries can become spastic after neurogenic shock resolves; lower motor neuron injuries often remain flaccid.
  • Use anticoagulation prophylaxis and assess for VTE findings because immobility and venous pooling increase risk.

Stabilization

  • Maintain alignment and immobilization until traction or surgery stabilizes the spine.
  • For halo fixation or cervical tongs, keep weights hanging freely, monitor skin and pin sites, and never use the halo device to turn or move the client.
  • After anterior cervical fusion, watch for airway compromise from swelling or bleeding and assess for tracheal deviation.
  • Transfer gradually to prevent postural hypotension, using a reclining wheelchair and lowering the angle if dizziness occurs.

Bowel, Bladder, Skin, and Autonomic Dysreflexia

Long-term safety
  • Turn at least every 2 hr in bed and every 1 hr in a wheelchair; use pressure-relief surfaces because the client might not feel prolonged pressure.
  • Spastic bladder after upper motor neuron injury can be managed with male condom catheter options or indwelling catheterization for female clients when urine release is unpredictable.
  • Flaccid bladder after lower motor neuron injury can require intermittent catheterization or manual bladder expression.
  • Maintain a bowel schedule with stool softeners or bulk-forming laxatives; use suppository or digital stimulation only as ordered and cautiously because vagal response can cause bradycardia or syncope.
  • Autonomic dysreflexia can cause severe hypertension, headache, sweating, pallor below the lesion, flushing above the lesion, blurred vision, bradycardia, nausea, and nasal stuffiness.
  • For dysreflexia, sit the client upright, notify the provider, check for bladder distention or catheter obstruction, remove fecal impaction as ordered, loosen tight clothing, control drafts, assess for injury or infection, monitor vital signs, and give prescribed antihypertensives.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Spinal Cord Injury

ATI-supported ALS

Template PartStudy Fill-In
Sensory findingsDecreased ability to feel light touch, distinguish sharp from dull, or distinguish hot from cold below the level of injury.
Motor/reflex findingsAbsent deep tendon reflexes and flaccid muscles can occur, especially during spinal shock.
Respiratory findingsShallow respirations or respiratory compromise can occur with high cervical involvement.
Perfusion/autonomic findingsHypotension that worsens upright, dependent edema, temperature dysregulation, and neurogenic shock findings can occur after spinal trauma.

Application Exercises

1

A client had a T12 spinal cord injury 1 week ago and has no lower-limb, bowel, or bladder control. Which priority should guide the plan of care?

  • A. Prevent additional spinal cord damage.
  • B. Prevent lower-extremity contractures.
  • C. Prevent skin breakdown in areas without sensation.
  • D. Prevent postural hypotension during wheelchair transfer.
A During the acute phase, minimizing movement until stabilization and supporting oxygenation help prevent further cord injury.
B, C, D ROM, turning, and gradual transfer are important, but they do not outrank protection from further cord damage.
2

A client with SCI reports a sudden severe headache and is diaphoretic. Blood pressure is 220/110 mm Hg and apical pulse is 54/min. What should the nurse do first?

  • A. Inspect the skin for irritation.
  • B. Raise the client to an upright position.
  • C. Check whether the urinary catheter is obstructed.
  • D. Give the prescribed antihypertensive medication.
B These findings indicate autonomic dysreflexia; sitting upright is the first action to help lower blood pressure.
A, C, D Finding the trigger and treating hypertension matter, but the immediate first step is upright positioning.
3

A client has a C4 spinal cord injury. Which complication is the priority risk?

  • A. Neurogenic shock.
  • B. Paralytic ileus.
  • C. Stress ulcer.
  • D. Respiratory compromise.
D C4 involvement can impair phrenic nerve function, so airway and ventilation are the priority by ABCs.
A, B, C These are important SCI complications, but breathing takes priority.
4

A client experienced a cervical spine injury 24 hr ago. Which prescription should the nurse question?

  • A. Anticoagulant.
  • B. Plasma expander.
  • C. H2-receptor antagonist.
  • D. Muscle relaxant.
D Muscle spasms are not expected until after spinal shock resolves, so a muscle relaxant early after injury needs clarification.
A, B, C VTE prophylaxis, hypotension support, and stress-ulcer prevention can be appropriate early SCI care.
5

Three months after a cervical SCI, which bladder management option is expected for a male client with a spastic bladder?

  • A. Condom catheter.
  • B. Intermittent urinary catheterization.
  • C. Crede method.
  • D. Indwelling urinary catheter.
A Upper motor neuron injuries can produce spastic bladder, and a condom catheter is a noninvasive option for male clients.
B, C, D Intermittent catheterization and Crede method fit flaccid bladder management; an indwelling catheter is more invasive.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 17

Respiratory Diagnostic Procedures

Respiratory diagnostics help answer three urgent questions: how well oxygen and carbon dioxide are moving, whether the airway can be visualized or sampled safely, and whether pleural fluid or air is compressing lung tissue.

TL;DR - Test the Air, Guard the Airway

PFTs measure lung function, ABGs measure oxygenation and acid-base status, bronchoscopy requires NPO and postprocedure gag-return safety, and thoracentesis removes or samples pleural fluid or air while the nurse watches for pneumothorax, bleeding, infection, and respiratory decline.

Before the Test

  • For PFTs, avoid smoking for 6 to 8 hr before testing and follow facility directions for holding inhalers.
  • For ABGs, verify radial and ulnar circulation with Allen's test when radial puncture is planned.
  • For bronchoscopy or thoracentesis, verify consent and procedure-specific preparation.

After the Test

  • After ABG puncture, hold pressure long enough to stop bleeding and monitor circulation at the site.
  • After bronchoscopy, do not resume oral intake until gag reflex and swallowing are safe.
  • After thoracentesis, monitor breath sounds, oxygenation, dressing drainage, and postprocedure chest x-ray results.

Respiratory Diagnostic Care Map

PFTs and ABGs: Function, Oxygenation, Acid-Base

Measurement

PFTs

  • Used to evaluate lung volumes, capacities, diffusion, gas exchange, flow rates, airway resistance, and ventilation distribution.
  • Helpful for dyspnea evaluation, lung disease identification, and preoperative respiratory risk screening.
  • Teach the client not to smoke 6 to 8 hr before testing and to follow instructions about holding inhalers before the test.

ABGs

  • Measure pH, PaO2, PaCO2, HCO3, and SaO2 to evaluate oxygenation and acid-base balance.
  • Before radial arterial puncture, perform Allen's test to confirm collateral circulation.
  • Collect in a heparinized syringe, send the specimen promptly, hold pressure at least 5 min after puncture, and hold at least 20 min if the client receives anticoagulants.
  • Monitor for bleeding, swelling, pulse loss, color change, temperature change, hematoma, arterial occlusion, or air embolism findings.

Bronchoscopy: Visualize, Biopsy, Clear

Airway safety
  • Bronchoscopy visualizes the larynx, trachea, and bronchi; it can identify abnormalities, obtain biopsy or cultures, remove secretions or foreign bodies, and treat selected airway problems.
  • Preprocedure priorities include consent, allergy and anticoagulant review, denture removal, NPO status for aspiration prevention, and ordered premedications.
  • During the procedure, monitor vital signs, respiratory pattern, and oxygenation; older adult clients with respiratory insufficiency are at increased sedation risk.
  • Afterward, monitor respirations, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, heart rate, level of consciousness, cough/gag return, swallowing ability, fever, cough, hemoptysis, hypoxemia, aspiration, and laryngospasm.
  • Expected mild findings can include a sore throat, dry cough, mild fever for less than 24 hr, and small blood-tinged sputum; bronchospasm or significant hemoptysis is not expected.

Thoracentesis: Pleural Fluid or Air Removal

Stillness + follow-up
  • Thoracentesis punctures the chest wall and pleural space to obtain specimens, instill medication, or remove pleural fluid or air.
  • Use imaging or assessment findings to locate the effusion; position the client upright with arms and shoulders supported and feet stable.
  • Teach the client to remain still and avoid coughing or talking unless instructed because movement increases needle injury risk.
  • During the procedure, use strict surgical asepsis, monitor vital signs, skin color, and oxygenation, measure fluid removed, and send specimens promptly.
  • Fluid removal is limited to 1 L at a time to reduce re-expansion pulmonary edema risk.
  • Afterward, apply and assess the dressing, monitor respiratory status hourly for the first several hours, auscultate for reduced breath sounds, encourage deep breathing, and obtain the postprocedure chest x-ray.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Thoracentesis

ATI-supported ALS

A nurse is assessing a client following thoracentesis. Complete the Therapeutic Procedure template by naming postprocedure nursing actions.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
Site careApply a dressing over the puncture site and assess it for bleeding or drainage.
Respiratory monitoringMonitor vital signs and respiratory status, including respiratory rate and rhythm, breath sounds, and oxygenation, hourly for the first several hours.
Focused lung assessmentAuscultate for reduced breath sounds on the side of the thoracentesis.
Expansion supportEncourage deep breathing to help re-expand the lung.

Application Exercises

1

A client is scheduled for thoracentesis. Which preprocedure action should the nurse take?

  • A. Position the client upright, leaning over the bedside table.
  • B. Explain the procedure in detail as the provider would.
  • C. Obtain arterial blood gases.
  • D. Administer benzocaine spray.
A Upright positioning over the table widens the intercostal space for pleural access.
B, C, D The provider explains the procedure; ABGs are not automatically indicated; benzocaine spray fits bronchoscopy preparation.
2

Which teaching should the nurse include before pulmonary function tests?

  • A. Do not use inhalers for 6 hr after the test.
  • B. Do not smoke tobacco for 6 to 8 hr before the test.
  • C. Bear down and hold the breath during the test.
  • D. Expect an Allen's test as part of the test.
B Smoking should be avoided for 6 to 8 hr before PFTs to support accurate results.
A, C, D Inhalers might be held before, not after, testing; Valsalva and Allen's test relate to ABG sampling, not PFTs.
3

Which post-bronchoscopy finding should the nurse report immediately?

  • A. Blood-tinged sputum.
  • B. Dry, nonproductive cough.
  • C. Sore throat.
  • D. Bronchospasms.
D Bronchospasm can threaten airway patency and requires immediate provider notification.
A, B, C Small blood-tinged sputum, dry cough, and sore throat can be expected after bronchoscopy.
4

Which supplies should be available for thoracentesis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Oxygen equipment.
  • B. Incentive spirometer.
  • C. Pulse oximeter.
  • D. Sterile dressing.
  • E. Suture removal kit.
A, C, D Oxygen, pulse oximetry, and sterile dressing supplies support monitoring and postpuncture care.
B, E Incentive spirometry is more specific to postoperative pulmonary expansion, and suture removal is not part of thoracentesis setup.
5

After thoracentesis, which findings indicate possible complications? Select all that apply.

  • A. Dyspnea.
  • B. Localized bloody drainage contained on the dressing.
  • C. Fever.
  • D. Hypotension.
  • E. Pain at the puncture site.
A, C, D Dyspnea can signal pneumothorax or reaccumulated fluid, fever can indicate infection, and hypotension can indicate intrathoracic bleeding.
B, E Localized contained bloody drainage and puncture-site pain can be expected findings after the procedure.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 18

Chest Tube Insertion and Monitoring

Chest tube care keeps negative pressure working so air, blood, fluid, or pus can leave the pleural space and the lung can re-expand. The nurse protects the water seal, drainage path, insertion site, and emergency supplies.

TL;DR - Keep It Low, Upright, Sealed

Keep the drainage system upright and below chest level, maintain the prescribed water seal and suction, watch tidaling and bubbling patterns, never clamp/strip/milk unless specifically prescribed, and keep sterile water, enclosed hemostats, and an occlusive dressing at the bedside.

Expected System

  • First chamber collects drainage.
  • Second chamber is the water seal that lets air out and prevents air from entering.
  • Third chamber controls suction, either wet or dry depending on the system.

Red Flags

  • Continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber suggests an air leak.
  • No tidaling can mean lung re-expansion or system obstruction.
  • SaO2 below 90%, visible chest tube eyelets, unexpected drainage change, or complications require immediate provider notification.

Chest Tube Care Map

Drainage System Function

Three chambers

What It Does

  • Chest tubes drain fluid, blood, or air; restore negative pressure; support lung expansion; and reestablish normal intrapleural pressure.
  • Indications include pneumothorax, hemothorax, postoperative chest drainage, pleural effusion, and pulmonary empyema.
  • Air tubes are placed toward the apex; fluid drainage tubes are placed closer to the lung base.

What to Watch

  • Keep the system below chest level and upright, including during ambulation.
  • Maintain the water seal level and prescribed wet or dry suction setting.
  • Expect tidaling in the water seal chamber; continuous bubbling belongs in the suction chamber, not the water seal chamber.
  • With mediastinal tubes after open heart surgery, bubbling and tidaling are not expected, though pulsations can be seen.

Preprocedure Through Postprocedure Priorities

Setup + monitoring
  • Before insertion, verify consent, assess anesthetic allergies, position the client as ordered, prepare the drainage system, give prescribed pain/sedation medications, and prep the insertion site.
  • During insertion, assist with dressing and drainage-system setup, keep tubing straight from bed to system, and place the drainage system below chest level.
  • After insertion, assess vital signs, breath sounds, SaO2, color, and respiratory effort at least every 4 hr and more often if unstable.
  • Encourage coughing and deep breathing every 2 hr, position in semi- to high-Fowler's, and administer prescribed pain medication.
  • Document drainage amount and color hourly for the first 24 hr, then at least every 8 hr; report excessive drainage, cloudy drainage, red drainage, stopped early drainage, or drainage above the ordered amount.
  • Keep two enclosed hemostats, sterile water, and an occlusive dressing at the bedside.

Air Leaks, Dislodgement, Tension Pneumothorax, and Removal

Emergency readiness
  • Continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber indicates an air leak; check connections, notify the provider, and use a padded clamp only if prescribed and only briefly to locate the leak.
  • If tubing separates, have the client exhale and cough; if the drainage system is compromised, place the chest tube end in sterile water to create a temporary seal.
  • If the chest tube is accidentally removed, apply dry sterile gauze to the site first, then secure as directed and assess respiratory status.
  • Suspect tension pneumothorax with tracheal deviation, absent unilateral breath sounds, distended neck veins, respiratory distress, chest asymmetry, or cyanosis; notify the provider or rapid response team immediately.
  • Before removal, give pain medication 30 min prior; during removal, coach Valsalva or breath-holding as directed, then apply an airtight sterile petroleum gauze dressing and monitor for recurrence or infection.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Chest Tube Placement

ATI-supported ALS

A nurse is caring for a client scheduled for chest tube placement. Complete the Therapeutic Procedure template by naming preprocedure nursing actions.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
Consent and teachingVerify signed consent and reinforce that breathing should improve after the tube is in place.
Safety assessmentAssess for allergies to local anesthetics.
Client preparationAssist into the ordered position, often supine or semi-Fowler's, and administer prescribed pain and sedation medications.
Equipment and sitePrepare the chest drainage system according to facility protocol, fill the water seal chamber, and prep the insertion site with the approved antiseptic.

Application Exercises

1

Which items should be available in the room after chest tube placement? Select all that apply.

  • A. Oxygen.
  • B. Sterile water.
  • C. Enclosed hemostat clamps.
  • D. Indwelling urinary catheter.
  • E. Occlusive dressing.
A, B, C, E Oxygen, sterile water, enclosed hemostats, and an occlusive dressing support respiratory distress response, temporary water seal, air leak checks, and dislodgement care.
D A urinary catheter is not indicated solely because a client has a chest tube.
2

The chest tube is accidentally removed. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Obtain a chest x-ray.
  • B. Apply sterile gauze to the insertion site.
  • C. Place tape around the insertion site.
  • D. Assess respiratory status.
B By ABC priority, covering the site with sterile gauze is the first action to allow air escape and reduce tension pneumothorax risk.
A, C, D Chest x-ray, securing the dressing, and respiratory assessment matter, but the site must be covered first.
3

Which findings are expected with a functioning chest tube drainage system? Select all that apply.

  • A. Continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber.
  • B. Gentle constant bubbling in the suction control chamber.
  • C. Rise and fall of water in the water seal chamber with respirations.
  • D. Exposed sutures without dressing.
  • E. Drainage system upright at chest level.
B, C Gentle bubbling in the suction chamber and tidaling in the water seal chamber can indicate expected system function.
A, D, E Water-seal bubbling suggests an air leak, sutures should be covered, and the drainage system should be upright below chest level.
4

Which action should the nurse take when assisting with chest tube removal?

  • A. Position the client prone with arms at the sides.
  • B. Complete a surgical checklist.
  • C. Tell the client removal causes minimal discomfort.
  • D. Place an occlusive dressing over the site after removal.
D An occlusive dressing is applied after removal and the site is monitored for drainage.
A, B, C Position depends on insertion site, bedside removal does not require a surgical checklist, and removal can be painful.
5

Which interventions belong in the plan of care after chest tube insertion? Select all that apply.

  • A. Encourage coughing and deep breathing.
  • B. Check for continuous bubbling in the suction chamber.
  • C. Strip drainage tubing every 4 hr.
  • D. Clamp the tube once daily.
  • E. Obtain a chest x-ray.
A, B, E Coughing/deep breathing promotes lung expansion, suction bubbling verifies suction, and chest x-ray verifies placement.
C, D Stripping/milking and clamping are not routine and should occur only when prescribed because they can harm lung tissue or cause tension pneumothorax.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 19

Respiratory Management and Mechanical Ventilation

Respiratory support starts with the least oxygen needed to correct hypoxemia, then escalates to positive-pressure support or mechanical ventilation when the client cannot maintain a patent airway, oxygenation, or ventilation.

TL;DR - Lowest Oxygen, Secure Airway, Respect Alarms

Choose the oxygen device that matches the client's needed FiO2, titrate to the prescribed saturation, prevent oxygen-related complications, verify every artificial airway, and treat ventilator alarms as client-safety signals until the cause is found.

Oxygen Device Logic

  • Nasal cannula is easy to tolerate but delivers variable oxygen and can dry nares.
  • Simple masks need at least 5 L/min to reduce CO2 rebreathing risk.
  • Venturi masks deliver the most precise FiO2 and are useful when exact oxygen control matters.

Ventilator Priorities

  • Document tube placement, use two staff for repositioning, and keep a manual resuscitation bag at the bedside.
  • Never silence or ignore ventilator alarms without assessing the client and system.
  • Watch weaning for tachypnea, desaturation, dysrhythmias, anxiety, diaphoresis, and declining tidal volume.

Respiratory Support Care Map

Oxygen Delivery Devices: Match Device to Need

FiO2 selection

Low-flow systems

  • Nasal cannula is safe, comfortable, and allows eating and talking, but FiO2 varies with flow and breathing pattern.
  • Assess nares, fit prongs correctly, use water-soluble gel for dryness, and add humidification for higher flows per facility practice.
  • Simple face masks cover the nose and mouth; keep flow at least 5 L/min to help flush CO2 from the mask.
  • Partial rebreather masks require the reservoir bag to stay inflated during inspiration.
  • Nonrebreather masks deliver very high oxygen concentrations; keep the bag partly inflated and check the valve and flaps frequently.

High-flow and humidified systems

  • Venturi masks deliver precise oxygen concentrations through adapters and are well suited for clients who need exact FiO2 control.
  • Check the ordered adapter/flow, keep tubing free of kinks, and assess skin under the mask.
  • Aerosol masks, face tents, tracheostomy collars, and T-pieces provide high humidity and require frequent equipment checks.
  • For humidified devices, drain condensation, keep water in the humidification canister, verify mist during inspiration and expiration, and avoid pulling on the airway.

Oxygen Therapy: Titrate, Monitor, Prevent Harm

Safety

Oxygenation assessment

  • Early hypoxemia can show as tachypnea, tachycardia, restlessness, pallor, elevated blood pressure, accessory muscle use, nasal flaring, tracheal tugging, or adventitious sounds.
  • Late hypoxemia can progress to confusion, stupor, cyanosis, bradypnea, bradycardia, hypotension, and dysrhythmias.
  • Use semi-Fowler's or Fowler's position, monitor respiratory rate, effort, lung sounds, SaO2, and ABGs, and titrate oxygen to the prescribed saturation.

Complication prevention

  • Use the lowest oxygen level that corrects hypoxemia and monitor for oxygen toxicity when high concentrations or prolonged therapy are needed.
  • In clients with COPD and chronic hypercarbia, monitor level of consciousness, respiratory pattern, and SaO2 for oxygen-induced hypoventilation.
  • Post oxygen-in-use signs, keep flammable materials away, use cotton gowns when indicated, and ensure electrical equipment is grounded.
  • Promote oral care, turning, coughing, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, suctioning, rest, nutrition, hydration, and skin protection.

Positive-Pressure Support and Mechanical Ventilation

Airway support

Escalation path

  • CPAP keeps airways open throughout the respiratory cycle and improves gas exchange during spontaneous breathing.
  • BiPAP delivers a higher inspiratory pressure and a lower expiratory pressure, often for clients with COPD who need ventilatory assistance.
  • Endotracheal intubation provides emergency airway management; confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide and chest x-ray, then auscultate bilateral breath sounds and watch chest movement.
  • Keep resuscitation equipment, including a manual bag and face mask, at the bedside.

Ventilator care

  • Mechanical ventilation supports gas exchange, decreases work of breathing, and can be delivered through an ET or tracheostomy tube.
  • Document tube placement in centimeters at the teeth or lips, use two staff members when repositioning or resecuring, and support tubing to prevent displacement.
  • Suction oral and tracheal secretions to maintain patency, assess respiratory status every 1 to 2 hr, and monitor/document ventilator settings hourly.
  • Low-pressure alarms suggest disconnection, cuff leak, or displacement; high-pressure alarms suggest secretions, biting, kinks, coughing, pulmonary edema, bronchospasm, or pneumothorax.
  • Assess cuff pressure at least every 8 hr and monitor for signs of air leak, inadequate oxygenation, or accidental extubation risk.

Modes, Adjuncts, Weaning, and Complications

Ventilator judgment

Modes and adjuncts

  • Assist-control delivers preset rate and tidal volume and can require sedation if the client hyperventilates.
  • SIMV delivers synchronized machine breaths while allowing spontaneous breaths; it can be used for weaning but can increase work of breathing.
  • PEEP improves oxygenation by keeping alveoli open at end expiration and helping prevent atelectasis.
  • PSV decreases the work of spontaneous breathing by delivering preset pressure during inspiration; CPAP supplies positive pressure during spontaneous breathing.

Weaning and complications

  • Weaning intolerance includes respirations greater than 30/min or less than 8/min, blood pressure or heart rate changes more than 20%, SaO2 less than 90%, dysrhythmias, decreasing tidal volume, labored breathing, diaphoresis, anxiety, or decreased level of consciousness.
  • After extubation, monitor for ineffective cough, dyspnea, stridor, airway obstruction, and respiratory distress; assess SpO2 and vital signs every 5 min initially.
  • Mechanical ventilation can cause barotrauma, volutrauma, fluid retention, oxygen toxicity, decreased venous return, aspiration, and stress ulcers.
  • Keep the head of bed elevated 30 degrees for clients receiving enteral feedings unless contraindicated, and monitor residuals per protocol.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Mechanical Ventilation

ATI-supported ALS

Scenario: A nurse is planning care for a client who is receiving mechanical ventilation through an endotracheal tube.

Maintain the airway

  • Assess tube position and placement, and document placement in centimeters at the teeth or lips.
  • Use two staff members when repositioning or resecuring the tube.
  • Use caution during movement and apply protective barriers according to policy when self-extubation risk is present.

Prevent loss of ventilation

  • Suction oral and tracheal secretions to maintain tube patency.
  • Support ventilator tubing to prevent mucosal erosion or tube displacement.
  • Keep a manual resuscitation bag with a face mask at the bedside for ventilator malfunction or accidental extubation.

Application Exercises

1

A nurse is caring for a client receiving mechanical ventilation in pressure support ventilation mode. Which statement shows correct understanding of PSV?

  • A. "It keeps alveoli open and prevents atelectasis at end expiration."
  • B. "It delivers preset pressure during spontaneous ventilation."
  • C. "It guarantees a minimum minute ventilation."
  • D. "It delivers a preset rate and tidal volume."
B PSV supports spontaneous breaths with preset pressure to decrease the work of breathing.
A, C, D PEEP keeps alveoli open, PSV does not guarantee minimum minute ventilation, and assist-control delivers preset rate and tidal volume.
2

Which findings are early manifestations of hypoxemia? Select all that apply.

  • A. Confusion.
  • B. Pale skin.
  • C. Bradycardia.
  • D. Hypotension.
  • E. Elevated blood pressure.
B, E Pallor and elevated blood pressure can appear early as oxygenation worsens.
A, C, D Confusion, bradycardia, and hypotension are later, more ominous findings.
3

A client is mechanically ventilated through an endotracheal tube. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Apply a vest restraint if the client attempts self-extubation.
  • B. Monitor ventilator settings every 8 hr.
  • C. Document tube placement in centimeters at the angle of the jaw.
  • D. Assess breath sounds at least every 4 hr.
D Ongoing respiratory assessment includes auscultating breath sounds and monitoring for unequal or diminished sounds.
A, B, C Use soft wrist restraints if prescribed/policy-supported, monitor ventilator settings much more frequently, and document ET placement at the teeth or lips.
4

Which oxygen device should the nurse use when a client with dyspnea needs a precise oxygen concentration?

  • A. Nonrebreather mask.
  • B. Venturi mask.
  • C. Nasal cannula.
  • D. Simple face mask.
B A Venturi mask uses adapters to deliver a precise oxygen concentration.
A, C, D Nonrebreather masks, nasal cannulas, and simple masks deliver less precise oxygen concentrations.
5

Which ventilator modes or supports can increase the client's work of breathing? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assist-control.
  • B. Synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation.
  • C. Continuous positive airway pressure.
  • D. Pressure support ventilation.
  • E. Independent lung ventilation.
B, C, D SIMV, CPAP, and PSV require the client to generate force for spontaneous breaths.
A, E Assist-control takes over more of the work of breathing, and independent lung ventilation is used for unilateral lung disease.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 20

Acute Respiratory Disorders

Acute respiratory disorders range from rhinitis and sinusitis to influenza and pneumonia, but the nursing priority stays steady: maintain airway patency, promote oxygenation, reduce transmission, and catch deterioration early.

TL;DR - Airway First, Infection Control Always

For acute respiratory disorders, prioritize airway clearance, oxygenation, hydration, rest, hand hygiene, cough etiquette, immunization, and cultures before antibiotics when pneumonia is suspected.

Upper Airway

  • Rhinitis causes rhinorrhea, congestion, sneezing, pruritus, watery eyes, sore throat, inflamed mucosa, and low-grade fever.
  • Sinusitis causes congestion, headache, facial pressure worse when leaning forward, cough, purulent or bloody drainage, and orbital/facial tenderness.
  • Decongestants can cause rebound congestion if used longer than 3 to 4 days.

Influenza and Pneumonia

  • Influenza prevention leans on yearly vaccination, hand hygiene, cough etiquette, and avoiding close contact during outbreaks.
  • Pneumonia in older adults can present vaguely, with confusion from hypoxia as a common manifestation.
  • For pneumonia, oxygen comes first when saturation is low, then sputum culture before antibiotics when possible.

Acute Respiratory Disorder Care Map

Risk, Rhinitis, and Sinusitis

Upper airway

Prevention and risk

  • Use hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, vaccination, allergen reduction, and smoking cessation to reduce acute respiratory disorders.
  • Risk rises with very young or older age, lack of current influenza or pneumococcal immunization, tobacco smoke, substance use, chronic lung disease, immunocompromise, aspiration risk, immobility, impaired secretion clearance, and mechanical ventilation.
  • Rhinitis can be infectious or allergic and often overlaps with asthma or other allergy patterns.

Rhinitis and sinusitis care

  • For rhinitis, encourage 8 to 10 hr of rest, at least 2,000 mL/day of fluid if not contraindicated, humidification or steam, tissue disposal, and cough etiquette.
  • Antihistamines, leukotriene inhibitors, mast cell stabilizers, decongestants, intranasal glucocorticoids, antipyretics, and antibiotics can be used depending on cause and symptoms.
  • For sinusitis, encourage steam, sinus irrigation, saline sprays, hot wet packs, fluids, rest, and correct nasal spray or irrigation technique.
  • Report severe headache, nuchal rigidity, or high fever because meningitis or encephalitis can occur if pathogens spread.

Influenza: Contagious Window and Prevention

Viral illness

Recognize

  • Seasonal influenza is highly contagious and commonly occurs in fall and winter.
  • Adults can transmit influenza from 24 hr before symptoms begin until about 5 days after onset.
  • Expected findings include severe headache, muscle aches, chills, fatigue, weakness, fever, and cough; severe diarrhea, cough, and hypoxia are emphasized for avian influenza patterns.

Act

  • Use droplet and contact precautions for hospitalized clients with pandemic influenza.
  • Monitor respiratory status, hydration, intake, and output; provide saline gargles and fluids as prescribed.
  • Begin prescribed antiviral therapy within 24 to 48 hr of symptom onset.
  • Teach annual influenza vaccination, hand hygiene, cough etiquette, increased fluids/rest if symptoms occur, and avoiding close contact or crowds during outbreaks.

Pneumonia: Assess, Culture, Oxygenate, Treat

Lower airway

Assessment and diagnostics

  • Pneumonia fills alveoli with inflammatory fluid or exudate and can be triggered by infection or aspiration.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia is common and can follow influenza; health care-associated pneumonia has higher mortality and can be more antibiotic-resistant.
  • Expected findings include fever, chills, flushed face, diaphoresis, dyspnea, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, sputum, crackles, wheezes, cough, dull percussion, and low oxygen saturation.
  • Older adults can have vague findings; confusion from hypoxia can be the most common manifestation.
  • Obtain sputum culture before antibiotics when possible, and monitor CBC, ABGs, blood culture, electrolytes, chest x-ray, and pulse oximetry.

Nursing care and complications

  • Position in high-Fowler's unless contraindicated, encourage coughing or suctioning, administer oxygen, breathing treatments, and medications, and monitor skin under oxygen devices.
  • Encourage incentive spirometry, rest periods, nutrition, and 2 to 3 L/day of fluids if not contraindicated to thin secretions and support healing.
  • Give antibiotics after cultures are obtained; monitor stool frequency and kidney function, especially in older adults receiving penicillins or cephalosporins.
  • Monitor bronchodilator and steroid effects, including albuterol tremor/tachycardia, ipratropium dry mouth or palpitations, theophylline toxicity, hyperglycemia, fluid retention, and poor wound healing.
  • Watch for atelectasis, bacteremia/sepsis, and ARDS when hypoxemia persists despite oxygen therapy.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Rhinitis

ATI-supported ALS

Scenario: A nurse in a clinic is discussing health promotion and disease management with a client who has rhinitis.

Risk factors and findings

  • Risk factors include recent viral, bacterial, or influenza exposure; lack of current immunizations; allergens or environmental contaminants; tobacco smoke; substance use; foreign body; and immobility.
  • Expected findings include rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, purulent nasal drainage, sneezing, pruritus of the nose/throat/ears, watery eyes, sore dry throat, inflamed nasal mucosa, and low-grade fever.

Teaching and medications

  • Teach rest, increased fluids if not contraindicated, humidification or steamy air, tissue disposal, and cough etiquette.
  • Medication examples include brompheniramine/pseudoephedrine, cromolyn sodium, phenylephrine, and antipyretics as appropriate.

Application Exercises

1

Which clients are at increased risk for pneumonia? Select all that apply.

  • A. A client who has dysphagia.
  • B. A client who has AIDS.
  • C. A client vaccinated for pneumococcus and influenza 6 months ago.
  • D. A postoperative client who received local anesthesia.
  • E. A client with a closed head injury receiving mechanical ventilation.
  • F. A client who has myasthenia gravis.
A, B, E, F Dysphagia, immunocompromise, mechanical ventilation, and impaired secretion clearance or muscle weakness increase pneumonia risk.
C, D Recent vaccination lowers risk, and local anesthesia is not the same risk pattern as general anesthesia, immobility, or ventilation.
2

A client awakens disoriented and reports chills and pleuritic chest pain. Which action is the nurse's priority?

  • A. Obtain baseline vital signs and oxygen saturation.
  • B. Obtain a sputum culture.
  • C. Obtain a complete history.
  • D. Provide a pneumococcal vaccine.
A The first priority is assessment, including oxygenation, to determine immediate respiratory risk.
B, C, D Culture, history, and vaccination can matter, but the nurse first assesses current status and oxygenation.
3

A client with pneumonia has RR 30/min, HR 100/min, and SaO2 91% on room air. In what order should the nurse act?

  • A. Administer antibiotics.
  • B. Administer oxygen therapy.
  • C. Obtain a sputum culture.
  • D. Teach yearly influenza vaccination.
B, C, A, D Use ABCs first: oxygenate, obtain sputum culture before antibiotics, administer antibiotics, then provide prevention teaching.
Why not antibiotics first? A culture should be collected before antibiotics when possible, but oxygenation is the immediate priority.
4

Which assessment technique helps identify sinusitis manifestations?

  • A. Percussion of posterior lung lobes.
  • B. Auscultation of the trachea.
  • C. Inspection of the conjunctiva.
  • D. Palpation of the orbital areas.
D Sinusitis can cause tenderness over the orbital, frontal, and facial areas.
A, B, C These techniques fit other assessments, not the focused sinus tenderness check.
5

Which statement shows correct influenza teaching?

  • A. "I should wash my hands after blowing my nose to prevent spreading the virus."
  • B. "I should avoid drinking fluids if symptoms develop."
  • C. "I need a flu shot every 2 years."
  • D. "I should cover my mouth with my hand when I sneeze."
A Hand hygiene reduces transmission of influenza viruses.
B, C, D Fluids should increase if tolerated, influenza vaccination is yearly, and sneezing into the elbow/shoulder or tissue avoids contaminating hands.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 21

Asthma

Asthma is intermittent, reversible airway obstruction driven by inflammation, hyperresponsiveness, bronchoconstriction, mucosal edema, and mucus production. The nurse's job is to read airflow decline early and match rescue versus prevention therapy.

TL;DR - Rescue Fast, Prevent Daily, Escalate Early

Asthma worsens when wheezing, retractions, tachycardia, low SaO2, or rising PaCO2 appear. Use short-acting beta2 agonists for rapid relief, anti-inflammatory therapy for prevention, peak flow zones for self-management, and prepare for intubation if respiratory failure or status asthmaticus develops.

Trigger Control

  • Promote smoking cessation, infection prevention, influenza/pneumonia vaccines, and protective masks or ventilation in dusty or particle-heavy environments.
  • Teach avoidance of cold air shifts, humidity changes, pollutants, strong odors, seasonal/perennial allergens, stress, aspirin/NSAIDs, beta-blockers, cholinergics, detergents, cleaners, sinusitis/postnasal drip, and viral infections when relevant.
  • Exercise is part of therapy, but some clients need premedication before activity.

Red Flags

  • Early ABGs can show low PaO2 with low PaCO2 from hyperventilation; later high PaCO2 signals fatigue and worsening ventilation.
  • Status asthmaticus is life-threatening and can be unresponsive to usual treatment.
  • For severe obstruction, prepare for emergency intubation and give prescribed IV fluids, oxygen, bronchodilators, epinephrine, and systemic steroids.

Asthma Care Map

Assess Severity and Identify Triggers

Airflow obstruction

Classification and risk

  • Asthma is classified by symptom frequency: mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, or severe persistent.
  • Risk factors include family history, smoking, secondhand smoke, environmental allergies, chemical irritants or dust, GERD, and age-related loss of pulmonary reserve.
  • Older adults have decreased pulmonary reserve, more infection susceptibility, and reduced beta-adrenergic receptor sensitivity, which can blunt response to beta agonists.

Expected and declining findings

  • Expected asthma manifestations include dyspnea, chest tightness, anxiety, coughing, wheezing, mucus production, accessory muscle use, prolonged exhalation, low SaO2, and increased chest diameter.
  • Ask about onset, duration, triggers, medication changes, relief medications, other medications, and self-care used during current and prior exacerbations.
  • Wheezing, sternal retractions, tachycardia, worsening oxygenation, and increased work of breathing show declining status.

Diagnostics and Acute Nursing Care

Priority response

Tests

  • ABGs can show hypoxemia, hypocarbia early in an attack, and hypercarbia later in an attack.
  • Sputum culture can identify infection when bacteria are present.
  • PFTs are the most accurate test for diagnosing asthma and severity; FEV1 can drop below expected values, and improvement after bronchodilator therapy supports asthma diagnosis.
  • Chest x-ray can show structural changes over time.

Acute care

  • Position in high-Fowler's to maximize ventilation.
  • Administer prescribed oxygen and medications, initiate/maintain IV access, and monitor heart rhythm, respiratory effort, symmetry, SaO2, and lung sounds.
  • Stay calm and reassuring; anxiety can worsen air hunger.
  • Provide rest periods and safe walking paths for older adults with dyspnea.
  • Encourage prompt treatment of infections and appropriate immunizations.

Medication Logic: Rescue Versus Prevention

Pharmacology

Bronchodilators

  • Short-acting beta2 agonists, such as albuterol, provide rapid relief for acute manifestations and can prevent exercise-induced asthma.
  • Anticholinergics, such as ipratropium, support bronchodilation and decrease secretions; monitor dry mouth and heart rate.
  • Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range and is used only when other treatments are ineffective; monitor levels and toxicity signs such as tachycardia, nausea, and diarrhea.
  • Long-acting beta2 agonists, such as salmeterol, are for prevention, not rescue at attack onset.

Anti-inflammatory agents

  • Corticosteroids, leukotriene antagonists, mast cell stabilizers, and monoclonal antibodies decrease airway inflammation and are used for prophylaxis.
  • Monitor for decreased immune function, poor wound healing, hyperglycemia, fluid retention, weight gain, mouth/throat lesions, and anaphylaxis with omalizumab.
  • Teach prednisone with food, hydration, black/tarry stool reporting, hand and mouth care, infection avoidance, and no abrupt discontinuation.
  • If separate inhaled bronchodilator and anti-inflammatory agents are both prescribed at the same time, give the bronchodilator first to improve absorption of the anti-inflammatory medication.

Complications: Respiratory Failure and Status Asthmaticus

Escalation

Respiratory failure

  • Persistent hypoxemia from asthma can progress to respiratory failure.
  • Monitor oxygenation and acid-base balance closely.
  • Prepare for intubation and mechanical ventilation when ventilation or oxygenation cannot be maintained.

Status asthmaticus

  • Status asthmaticus is a life-threatening airway obstruction episode that can be unresponsive to common treatment.
  • Findings include extreme wheezing, labored breathing, accessory muscle use, distended neck veins, and risk for cardiac or respiratory arrest.
  • Prepare for emergency intubation and administer prescribed IV fluids, oxygen, bronchodilators, epinephrine, and systemic steroids.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Prednisone for Asthma

ATI-supported ALS

Scenario: A nurse is caring for a client who has asthma and a prescription for prednisone.

Nursing interventions

  • Monitor for decreased immune function and delayed wound healing.
  • Monitor blood glucose for hyperglycemia.
  • Observe for fluid retention and weight gain.
  • Inspect the mouth and throat for aphthous lesions.

Client teaching

  • Take prednisone with food to reduce GI distress.
  • Report black, tarry stools.
  • Maintain hydration, hand hygiene, and mouth care.
  • Do not stop glucocorticoids suddenly without provider guidance.

Application Exercises

1

A client is having an acute asthma attack. Which findings indicate declining respiratory status? Select all that apply.

  • A. SaO2 95%.
  • B. Wheezing.
  • C. Retraction of sternal muscles.
  • D. Pink mucous membranes.
  • E. Tachycardia.
B, C, E Wheezing, sternal retractions, and tachycardia indicate airway narrowing, increased work of breathing, and decreased oxygenation.
A, D SaO2 95% and pink mucous membranes are expected findings, not signs of decline.
2

A client with asthma has SaO2 91%, audible wheezes, and accessory muscle use. Which class of medication should the nurse expect to administer?

  • A. Antibiotic.
  • B. Beta-blocker.
  • C. Antiviral.
  • D. Beta2 agonist.
D A beta2 agonist rapidly dilates bronchioles to relieve wheezing and open the airway.
A, B, C Antibiotics treat bacterial infection, antivirals treat viral infection, and beta-blockers can worsen bronchospasm risk.
3

Which statement by a client taking prednisone for asthma shows correct teaching?

  • A. "I will decrease my fluid intake while taking this medication."
  • B. "I will expect to have black, tarry stools."
  • C. "I will take my medication with meals."
  • D. "I will monitor for weight loss while taking this medication."
C Prednisone should be taken with food to reduce GI distress.
A, B, D Fluids are encouraged if not contraindicated, black/tarry stools should be reported, and fluid retention/weight gain can occur.
4

Which factor should the nurse identify as an asthma risk factor?

  • A. Sex.
  • B. Environmental allergies.
  • C. Alcohol use.
  • D. History of diabetes.
B Environmental allergies are associated with asthma and can coexist with allergic rhinitis or skin manifestations.
A, C, D Sex, alcohol use, and diabetes history are not listed asthma risk factors in this ATI source section.
5

Which client statement shows correct understanding of a bronchodilator?

  • A. "This medication can decrease my immune response."
  • B. "I take this medication to prevent asthma attacks."
  • C. "I need to take this medication with food."
  • D. "This medication has a slow onset to treat my symptoms."
B Bronchodilators can prevent attacks and rapidly relieve bronchospasm depending on the agent.
A, C, D Decreased immune response and food-with-dose teaching fit anti-inflammatory agents; bronchodilators have a fast onset for acute manifestations.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type
