Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 52

Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease asks you to compare ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, and diverticulitis, then protect nutrition, hydration, electrolytes, infection risk, and perforation/peritonitis safety.

TL;DR · IBD and Diverticulitis

Ulcerative colitis usually starts in the rectum/rectosigmoid colon with bloody mucus/pus stools and LLQ cramping. Crohn's often affects the distal ileum, can involve all bowel layers, and causes fistulas, malabsorption, and RLQ cramping. Diverticulitis is infected/inflamed diverticula and can perforate.

Compare patterns

  • Ulcerative colitis can involve mucosa/submucosa, produce 15 to 20 liquid stools/day, and increase colon cancer risk.
  • Crohn's can affect mouth to anus, creates sporadic full-thickness lesions, and commonly causes fistulas.
  • Diverticulitis causes acute LLQ pain, fever, chills, tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, distention, and occult blood risk.

Priority care

  • Monitor I&O, weight, dehydration, potassium and other electrolytes, albumin, Hgb/Hct, WBC, ESR/CRP, and stool blood.
  • Teach small frequent high-protein, high-calorie, low-fiber meals during active disease, no caffeine/alcohol, vitamin/iron supplementation, and emergency care for obstruction or perforation cues.
  • Peritonitis is life-threatening: boardlike abdomen, rebound tenderness, fever, tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, and older-adult confusion need rapid escalation.

Core Concepts

Disease Map

ATI source-authored

Acute inflammatory disorders

  • Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, often from obstruction by a fecalith; adolescents and young adults are at increased risk.
  • Peritonitis is inflammation/infection of the peritoneum after puncture, GI rupture, or peritoneal dialysis infection.
  • Gastroenteritis is stomach and small-intestine inflammation triggered by bacterial or viral infection; vomiting and watery stools increase fluid/electrolyte and nutrition risk.

Chronic inflammatory disorders

  • Ulcerative colitis produces edema/inflammation primarily in the rectum and rectosigmoid colon and can extend through the colon in severe cases.
  • Crohn's disease produces inflammation and ulceration often at the distal ileum, can involve the entire GI tract, and can affect all bowel layers.
  • Diverticulitis is inflammation/infection caused when bacteria, food, or fecal matter becomes trapped in diverticula.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Pattern recognition

Expected findings

  • Ulcerative colitis: LLQ cramping, anorexia, weight loss, fever, 15 to 20 liquid stools/day, mucus/blood/pus in stool, rectal bleeding, distention, tenderness, and high-pitched bowel sounds.
  • Crohn's disease: RLQ cramping, anorexia, weight loss, fever, loose stools with mucus or pus, steatorrhea, distention, tenderness, and high-pitched bowel sounds.
  • Diverticulitis: acute LLQ abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, chills, tachycardia, and abdominal distention.
  • UC, Crohn's, and diverticulitis can have decreased Hgb/Hct, increased ESR/WBC, positive occult blood, and fluid/electrolyte changes.

Diagnostics

  • Magnetic resonance enterography can be used for IBD; the client remains NPO beforehand and might drink contrast.
  • Ulcerative colitis can be diagnosed by sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy; CT or MRI can identify abscesses.
  • Crohn's diagnostics include endoscopy, capsule endoscopy, proctosigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy/sigmoidoscopy, ultrasound, x-ray, and CT scan for bowel thickening.
  • Barium enema can help distinguish ulcerative colitis and show diverticulosis, but it is contraindicated with diverticulitis due to perforation risk.

Care and Medication Safety

Inflammation control

Nursing care

  • Teach the usual course of the disease, medication therapy, vitamins, food-trigger identification, and colonoscopy monitoring because colon cancer risk increases.
  • Monitor potassium and other electrolytes, I&O, dehydration, weight, and stool count.
  • During active UC/Crohn's, teach high-protein, high-calorie, low-fiber intake, small frequent meals, caffeine/alcohol avoidance, multivitamin with iron, protein supplements, and weekly weights.
  • Severe diverticulitis can require hospitalization, NPO status, NG suction, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, and opioid analgesics.

Medication map

  • Sulfasalazine reduces intestinal mucosal inflammation; monitor CBC, kidney and hepatic function, and teach full water intake, sun avoidance, folic acid, and reporting sore throat/rash/bruising/fever.
  • Mesalamine, balsalazide, and olsalazine are nonsulfonamide 5-ASA options; monitor kidney toxicity and report headache or GI problems.
  • Corticosteroids induce remission but are not long-term therapy; taper slowly, monitor BP/electrolytes/glucose, and report infection or fluid retention.
  • Immunosuppressants and immunomodulators increase infection/bleeding risk; monitor CBC, liver enzymes, coagulation studies, pancreatitis, neutropenia, and possible TB reactivation.
  • Antidiarrheals reduce stool frequency but can precipitate toxic megacolon; monitor fever, hypotension, distention, and decreased bowel sounds.

Procedures and Complications

Escalation cues
  • Surgery is considered when medical therapy fails or complications occur, such as bowel perforation or colon cancer.
  • Ulcerative colitis surgery can include colectomy with or without ileostomy; Crohn's procedures can include stricturoplasty or fistula repair; diverticulitis can require colon resection with or without colostomy.
  • When a stoma is planned, collaborate with an enterostomal therapy nurse; after ileostomy, output can reach 1,000 mL/day, so fluid-volume deficit prevention matters.
  • Peritonitis cues include rigid boardlike abdomen, abdominal distention, nausea/vomiting, rebound tenderness, tachycardia, fever, and older-adult confusion.
  • Complications include bleeding, fluid/electrolyte imbalance, peritonitis, abscess/fistula formation, and toxic megacolon.
  • Toxic megacolon requires NG suction, IV fluids/electrolytes, antibiotics/corticosteroids as prescribed, and surgery preparation if no improvement occurs within 72 hr.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Diverticulitis

ATI-supported ALS

Pathophysiology and findings

  • Diverticulitis is inflammation and infection of bowel mucosa when bacteria or fecal material becomes trapped in diverticula.
  • Risk factors include older age and male sex.
  • Expected findings can include decreased hemoglobin/hematocrit and stool positive for occult blood.
  • Diagnostics can include abdominal x-ray, CT scan, colonoscopy, and sigmoidoscopy when clinically appropriate.

Diet teaching

  • Use clear liquids until manifestations subside.
  • Advance to low-fiber foods once solid foods are tolerated.
  • Slowly advance to a high-fiber diet after inflammation resolves.
  • Avoid seeds or indigestible material such as nuts, popcorn, and seeds; avoid alcohol and limit fat intake.

Application Exercises

1

Which blood laboratory results should increase during an acute Crohn's exacerbation? Select all that apply.

  • A. Hematocrit.
  • B. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
  • C. WBC count.
  • D. Folic acid.
  • E. Albumin.
B, C ESR and WBC increase with inflammation and active disease.
A, D, E Hematocrit can decrease with chronic blood loss, and folic acid/albumin can decrease with malabsorption.
2

A client taking prednisone for IBD reports several findings. Which is the priority?

  • A. Difficulty sleeping.
  • B. Glucose in the urine.
  • C. Elevated body temperature.
  • D. Weight gain over 6 months.
C Prednisone can cause immunosuppression, so fever or other infection cues are the priority.
A, B, D Insomnia, hyperglycemia, and fluid-related weight gain can occur, but infection risk is the immediate priority.
3

Which sulfasalazine teaching should the nurse include?

  • A. Take it 2 hr after eating.
  • B. Stop it if skin or urine turns yellow-orange.
  • C. Notify the provider for a sore throat.
  • D. Expect black stools.
C Sore throat can signal infection or blood dyscrasia and should be reported.
A, B, D Take after meals with water; yellow-orange discoloration can be harmless; black stools can indicate GI bleeding and are not expected.
4

Which discharge instruction fits Crohn's disease nutrition teaching?

  • A. Decrease calorie-dense foods.
  • B. Use canned protein supplements.
  • C. Increase high-fiber foods during exacerbation.
  • D. Eat high-residue foods.
B High-protein supplements can support nutrition when Crohn's causes malabsorption and weight loss.
A, C, D High-calorie/high-protein and low-fiber/low-residue intake is recommended during active inflammation.
5

Which statement shows understanding of ulcerative colitis teaching?

  • A. "I will limit fiber in my diet during active symptoms."
  • B. "I will restrict fluids with meals."
  • C. "I will switch from coffee to black tea."
  • D. "I will choose cold foods when my stomach is upset."
A Low-fiber foods can reduce bowel stimulation during active ulcerative colitis.
B, C, D Fluid restriction with meals is dumping-syndrome teaching, caffeine can worsen diarrhea/cramping, and cold foods can increase motility.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 53

Cholecystitis and Cholelithiasis

Gallbladder disease is about blocked bile flow: recognize biliary colic, obstructed duct findings, atypical older-adult presentations, and post-procedure drainage or bile-leak red flags.

TL;DR · Biliary Obstruction

Cholecystitis is gallbladder-wall inflammation, usually from gallstones obstructing the cystic or common bile duct. Think RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder, pain after high-fat foods, nausea/vomiting, fever, and obstructed-bile cues such as jaundice, dark urine, clay stools, steatorrhea, and pruritus.

Recognize

  • Risk is higher with female sex, estrogen therapy or some oral contraceptives, obesity/high cholesterol, older age, type 2 diabetes, Crohn's disease, rapid weight loss, and some ancestry patterns.
  • Murphy's sign is pain with deep inspiration during right subcostal palpation; Blumberg's sign is rebound tenderness.
  • Older adults might have no pain or fever; delirium or localized tenderness can be the first clue.

Act

  • Use labs and imaging to separate inflammation, duct obstruction, liver involvement, and pancreatic involvement.
  • Manage pain with prescribed analgesics; bile acids can dissolve cholesterol stones gradually but are not acute pain relief.
  • After cholecystectomy, monitor drainage, bile-leak findings, bile peritonitis, infection, and return of stool color.

Core Concepts

Disease Map

ATI source-authored

Pathophysiology

  • Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder wall, most often when gallstones obstruct bile flow from the gallbladder toward the duodenum.
  • Cholelithiasis means stones are present in the gallbladder; stones form when bile or cholesterol precipitates.
  • Obstruction can back up bile, inflame the gallbladder, obstruct the pancreatic duct, cause pancreatitis, or progress to rupture and secondary peritonitis.

Prevention and risk

  • Health promotion includes a low-fat diet with HDL-supporting foods, regular exercise, and no smoking.
  • Common risk factors include female sex, estrogen exposure, obesity, high cholesterol, genetics, older age, type 2 diabetes, Crohn's disease, low-calorie liquid protein diets, and rapid weight loss.
  • Older adults can present atypically, so mental-status change or localized tenderness deserves attention even without classic pain or fever.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Obstruction cues

Expected findings

  • Classic pain is sharp RUQ pain that can radiate to the right shoulder.
  • Biliary colic after high-fat foods can cause intense pain, tachycardia, pallor, diaphoresis, nausea, and vomiting.
  • Other findings include Murphy's sign, rebound tenderness, dyspepsia, belching, flatulence, and fever.
  • Chronic or obstructed bile flow can cause jaundice, icterus, clay-colored stools, steatorrhea, dark urine, and pruritus.

Testing logic

  • WBC elevation supports inflammation.
  • Direct, indirect, and total bilirubin can rise when a bile duct is obstructed.
  • Amylase and lipase can rise with pancreatic involvement; AST, LDH, and ALP can rise with liver dysfunction or common bile duct obstruction.
  • Ultrasound visualizes gallstones and common bile duct dilation; CT or x-ray can show calcified stones or an enlarged gallbladder.
  • HIDA evaluates biliary patency; ERCP can visualize the duct and remove stones with sphincterotomy; MRCP helps determine cause with MRI plus contrast.

Medications and Procedures

Pain and stone removal
  • Prescribed opioids such as morphine or hydromorphone are preferred for acute biliary pain; ketorolac can be used for mild to moderate pain, with GI bleeding monitoring.
  • Bile acids such as chenodiol or ursodiol gradually dissolve cholesterol-based stones. Use caution with liver disorders or varices, report abdominal pain/diarrhea/vomiting, and expect therapy to be limited to about 2 years with ultrasound monitoring during the first year.
  • Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy can break small cholesterol stones in selected nonsurgical candidates; teach that repeated treatments and procedural pain from spasms or stone movement can occur.
  • Cholecystectomy can be laparoscopic, minimally invasive through a natural orifice, or open. Laparoscopic discharge is often within 24 hr; open surgery can require a longer stay.
  • Open procedures can include a Jackson-Pratt drain or T-tube. Monitor amount, color, skin condition, bile leakage, infection, stool color, and food response.
  • If a T-tube is present, report absent drainage with nausea and pain, clamp before and after meals if prescribed, and monitor for bile peritonitis: pain, fever, and jaundice.

Postoperative Teaching and Complications

Safety priorities

Postoperative teaching

  • After laparoscopic surgery, ambulate frequently to decrease free-air pain under the right clavicle, shoulder, or scapula.
  • Report pain, vomiting, or abdominal distention because these can indicate a bile leak.
  • For an open approach, resume activity gradually, avoid heavy lifting for 4 to 6 weeks, shower instead of bathing until tubes are removed, and report sudden drainage increase, foul odor, pain, fever, or jaundice.
  • Diet teaching includes low-fat foods, reduced dairy, avoiding fried foods/chocolate/nuts/gravies and gas-forming foods, small frequent meals, weight reduction if indicated, and prescribed fat-soluble vitamins or bile salts.

Complications

  • Bile duct obstruction can lead to ischemia, gangrene, rupture, abscess, or peritonitis with rigid boardlike abdomen and guarding.
  • Bile peritonitis is rare but dangerous; pain, fever, and jaundice require immediate reporting.
  • Postcholecystectomy syndrome means pain or nausea resembling prior gallbladder disease continues or returns and might require further diagnostic workup.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Gallbladder Disease

ATI-supported ALS

Risk factors

  • Female sex, estrogen therapy, and some oral contraceptives.
  • Obesity, high-fat or low-calorie liquid protein diets, and rapid weight loss.
  • Genetic predisposition, age over 60, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and Native American or Mexican American ethnicity.

Findings and prevention

  • Expected findings include RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder, pain with right subcostal palpation, high-fat meal pain with nausea/vomiting, dyspepsia, belching, flatulence, fever, jaundice, clay stools, steatorrhea, dark urine, and pruritus.
  • Prevention teaching includes regular exercise, tobacco cessation, and a low-fat diet with HDL-supporting foods such as seafood, nuts, and olive oil.

Application Exercises

1

Which discharge instructions should the nurse include after laparoscopic cholecystectomy? Select all that apply.

  • A. Resume the prescribed diet after discharge.
  • B. Clean puncture sites with mild soap and water.
  • C. Remove adhesive strips after 24 hr.
  • D. Report nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
  • E. Avoid showering for 1 week.
A, B, D Diet can usually resume as directed, puncture sites are cleansed gently, and nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain can signal a complication.
C, E Adhesive strips should fall off naturally, and bathing/showering instructions depend on the approach and provider directions.
2

Which history finding is a risk factor for cholecystitis?

  • A. Obesity.
  • B. Male sex.
  • C. Low triglyceride level.
  • D. Slow weight gain over 10 years.
A Obesity and impaired fat metabolism increase risk for gallbladder disease.
B, C, D Female sex, increased cholesterol/triglyceride patterns, and rapid weight loss are stronger ATI-supported risks.
3

Which teaching belongs in preoperative preparation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy?

  • A. "You might feel shoulder pain after surgery."
  • B. "A Jackson-Pratt drain is expected with every laparoscopic case."
  • C. "Walking should be limited for 1 to 2 weeks."
  • D. "The scope is passed through the rectum for this approach."
A Free air after laparoscopic surgery can cause shoulder, clavicle, or scapular pain, and ambulation helps.
B, C, D Drains are more associated with open or complicated cases, ambulation is encouraged, and rectal entry refers to selected NOTES procedures.
4

Which teaching should be included for chenodiol?

  • A. It relieves acute biliary pain within minutes.
  • B. It gradually dissolves cholesterol gallstones.
  • C. It requires thyroid testing every 6 months.
  • D. It is first-line therapy for clients with liver disorders and varices.
B Bile acid therapy gradually dissolves cholesterol-based gallstones and can be limited to long-term monitored therapy.
A, C, D Acute biliary pain requires analgesics, ultrasound monitoring is used, and liver conditions or varices require caution.
5

Which laboratory result supports suspected cholelithiasis with duct obstruction?

  • A. Direct bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL.
  • B. WBC 9,000/mm3.
  • C. Amylase within the expected range.
  • D. Alkaline phosphatase below the expected range.
A Bilirubin can increase when a bile duct is obstructed.
B, C, D WBC can rise with inflammation, amylase can rise with pancreatic involvement, and ALP can rise with common bile duct obstruction.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 54

Pancreatitis

Pancreatitis is premature activation of digestive enzymes that injure the pancreas; priority care rests the pancreas, protects volume/electrolytes, controls pain, and catches necrosis or organ failure early.

TL;DR · Pancreatic Autodigestion

Acute pancreatitis presents with severe constant knifelike or boring epigastric/LUQ pain that can radiate to the back, left flank, or left shoulder. Pain worsens lying down and improves somewhat with fetal position or sitting upright and leaning forward.

Recognize

  • Major risks include biliary tract disease, alcohol use disorder, ERCP complications, GI surgery, metabolic disturbances, kidney failure/transplant, trauma, penetrating ulcer, medication toxicity, viral infections, and smoking.
  • Findings can include nausea/vomiting, weight loss, jaundice, decreased bowel sounds, ascites, hyperglycemia cues, flank ecchymosis, periumbilical discoloration, and hypocalcemia tetany.
  • High amylase and lipase support pancreatic cell injury; high glucose reflects decreased insulin production.

Act

  • Rest the pancreas: NPO until pain-free, antiemetics, NG decompression if severe vomiting or ileus, and nutrition support for severe disease.
  • Use comfort positioning, prescribed analgesics, glucose monitoring/insulin, hydration monitoring, IV fluids, and electrolyte replacement.
  • Escalate for hypovolemia, infection or pseudocyst/abscess, diabetes, lung complications, DIC, and multi-system organ failure.

Core Concepts

Pathophysiology and Assessment

ATI source-authored

Disease map

  • Pancreatitis is autodigestion of the pancreas after digestive enzymes activate too early, before reaching the intestines.
  • Inflammation can obstruct ducts, increase pressure, rupture ducts, and release enzymes into pancreatic tissue, causing inflammation, necrosis, and hemorrhage.
  • Acute disease ranges from mild inflammation to necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis. Chronic disease is progressive inflammation and fibrosis and can be calcifying, obstructive, autoimmune, idiopathic, or hereditary.

Assessment pattern

  • Pain is sudden, severe, boring, and epigastric; it can radiate to the back, left flank, or left shoulder.
  • Pain worsens when lying down and improves somewhat in fetal position or sitting upright and bending forward.
  • Expected findings include nausea, vomiting, weight loss, jaundice, absent or decreased bowel sounds, warm moist skin, fruity breath, ascites, and tetany.
  • Flank ecchymosis and bluish-gray periumbilical discoloration are concerning bruising patterns from enzyme-related tissue injury.

Labs, Imaging, and Nursing Care

Rest the pancreas

Diagnostics

  • Blood amylase rises early and can remain elevated for several days; prolonged elevation can suggest abscess or pseudocyst.
  • Blood lipase rises more slowly and remains elevated longer than amylase; urine amylase can remain elevated after serum levels.
  • WBC and ESR can rise; platelets, calcium, and magnesium can fall; liver enzymes and bilirubin can rise with biliary dysfunction; glucose can rise from reduced insulin production.
  • CT scan with contrast is a reliable diagnostic test for acute pancreatitis.

Nursing care

  • Keep the client NPO until pain-free; severe disease can require enteral or parenteral nutrition.
  • Resume bland, high-protein, low-fat foods with no stimulants such as caffeine; use small frequent meals.
  • Administer antiemetics, use NG decompression for severe vomiting or paralytic ileus, and reinforce no alcohol, no smoking, and stress limitation.
  • Position for comfort, administer prescribed analgesics, monitor glucose/insulin need, track hydration with orthostatic BP, I&O, and labs, and replace IV fluids/electrolytes as prescribed.

Medications and Procedures

Pain, acid, enzymes
  • Morphine or hydromorphone can be prescribed for acute pain; ketorolac can be used for mild to moderate pain. Meperidine is discouraged because seizure risk is a concern, especially in older adults.
  • Imipenem can be indicated for acute necrotizing pancreatitis; monitor for infection and seizures.
  • Cimetidine reduces gastric acid secretion; teach separation from antacids by 1 hr. Omeprazole also reduces acid; monitor magnesium.
  • Pancrelipase helps digest fats and proteins with meals and snacks. Teach a full glass of water, no chewing, mouth rinsing/lip wiping to prevent irritation, and sprinkling capsule contents only on nonprotein foods if needed.
  • Procedures can include ERCP for gallstone-related sphincter opening, cholecystectomy for cholecystitis/gallstones, sphincterotomy, endoscopic necrosectomy or NOTES for necrotic tissue, and pancreaticojejunostomy to reroute pancreatic drainage.
  • Interprofessional care can include dietary referral, home health for nutrition/wound care/ADLs, and substance-use support when alcohol use disorder contributes.

Complications

Escalation cues

Fluid and infection

  • Hypovolemia can occur from third spacing and can progress to shock; monitor electrolytes, hypotension, tachycardia, and replace fluids/electrolytes as prescribed.
  • Pancreatic pseudocyst or abscess can occur when fluid leaks from a damaged duct; watch for fever, epigastric mass, nausea, vomiting, and jaundice.
  • If drainage is present, maintain the sump tube and protect surrounding skin from corrosive enzymes.

Systemic complications

  • Destruction of pancreatic beta cells can cause type 1 diabetes mellitus, requiring glucose monitoring, insulin, and long-term diabetes teaching.
  • Left lung effusion and atelectasis can precipitate pneumonia, especially in older adults; monitor hypoxia and provide ventilatory support as needed.
  • Necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis can trigger DIC and multi-system organ failure; monitor coagulation, bleeding, respiratory distress, jaundice, oliguria, and other organ-failure cues.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Pancreatitis

ATI-supported ALS

Classic presentation and labs

  • Classic presentation is severe constant knifelike pain in the LUQ or midepigastric area that can radiate to the back.
  • Expected labs include increased blood amylase and lipase, increased urine amylase, increased WBC, decreased calcium and magnesium, increased liver enzymes/bilirubin with biliary dysfunction, and increased glucose.

Nursing care

  • Maintain NPO status until pain-free, and provide prescribed parenteral or jejunal nutrition when needed.
  • Maintain NG decompression for severe vomiting or paralytic ileus.
  • Restart with bland high-protein, low-fat foods without caffeine; plan small frequent meals.
  • Administer antiemetics, limit stress, provide pain management, and reinforce no alcohol or smoking.

Application Exercises

1

Which laboratory finding should the nurse expect with acute pancreatitis?

  • A. Decreased blood lipase.
  • B. Decreased blood amylase.
  • C. Increased blood calcium.
  • D. Increased blood glucose.
D Pancreatic injury can decrease insulin production, causing increased glucose.
A, B, C Lipase and amylase increase with pancreatic cell injury; calcium can decrease due to fat necrosis.
2

Which action should the nurse take when administering pancrelipase?

  • A. Offer a full glass of water after administration.
  • B. Have the client chew the medication before swallowing.
  • C. Give it 30 min before meals only.
  • D. Sprinkle capsule contents on peanut butter.
A Pancrelipase teaching includes drinking a full glass of water after taking the medication.
B, C, D Do not chew it; take it with every meal and snack; if sprinkling contents, use nonprotein foods rather than peanut butter.
3

Which pain description is most consistent with pancreatitis?

  • A. RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder.
  • B. Pain relieved by defecation.
  • C. Epigastric pain radiating to the left shoulder.
  • D. Pain that improves when lying flat.
C Pancreatitis can cause severe boring epigastric pain radiating to the back, left flank, or left shoulder.
A, B, D RUQ to right shoulder fits gallbladder disease; relief with defecation fits IBS patterns; pancreatitis is worse lying down.
4

Which assessment finding is a manifestation of pancreatitis?

  • A. Gray-blue discoloration around the umbilicus.
  • B. Hyperactive bowel sounds.
  • C. Generalized cyanosis.
  • D. Wheezing in the lower lung fields.
A Bluish-gray periumbilical discoloration can occur with pancreatitis.
B, C, D Bowel sounds are more often decreased/absent; jaundice and diminished breath sounds/dyspnea are more expected than cyanosis or wheezing.
5

Which nutrition statements show correct pancreatitis teaching? Select all that apply.

  • A. "I will eat small frequent meals."
  • B. "I will choose bland, easy-to-digest foods."
  • C. "I will use skim milk when cooking."
  • D. "I will drink regular cola with meals."
  • E. "I will avoid alcohol."
A, B, C, E Small frequent bland low-fat meals and no alcohol support pancreatic rest and prevent recurrence.
D Regular cola contains caffeine; stimulant-free intake is recommended.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 55

Hepatitis and Cirrhosis

Liver disorders ask you to connect transmission and inflammation with declining liver function: impaired detoxification, bleeding risk, ascites, varices, encephalopathy, and transplant complications.

TL;DR · Liver Inflammation to Failure

Hepatitis inflames liver cells; cirrhosis permanently scars the liver after chronic injury. Watch the pattern: jaundice/dark urine/clay stools in hepatitis, then cirrhosis findings such as ascites, varices, bleeding, low albumin, prolonged PT/INR, high ammonia, asterixis, and fetor hepaticus.

Hepatitis priorities

  • HAV and HEV are fecal-oral; HBV and HCV are bloodborne; HDV occurs with HBV coinfection.
  • Use vaccines, infection control, safe injection practice, hand hygiene, and travel food/water precautions to prevent transmission.
  • ALT/AST and bilirubin rise with hepatitis; disease-specific antibodies or viral tests identify the type.

Cirrhosis priorities

  • Monitor respiratory effort, skin integrity, fluid volume excess, neurologic changes, nutrition, GI bleeding, and pain.
  • Use diuretics, beta blockers, lactulose, and nonabsorbable antibiotics as prescribed; give other liver-metabolized medications sparingly.
  • Escalate encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, transplant rejection, infection, clotting problems, hepatic complications, and acute kidney injury.

Core Concepts

Hepatitis Map

ATI source-authored

Transmission and risk

  • Hepatitis is liver-cell inflammation from viral, toxic, medication, chemical, alcohol, or secondary viral causes; it can be acute or chronic.
  • HAV and HEV spread by fecal-oral exposure, including contaminated food or water and contact with infected stool.
  • HBV spreads through blood and sexual or perinatal exposure; HCV spreads through blood, contaminated needles/equipment, organ or blood-product exposure, and sexual contact.
  • HDV occurs as coinfection with HBV and shares blood/sexual exposure risks.

Prevention

  • Follow vaccination recommendations and CDC infection-control precautions.
  • Use safe injection practices: aseptic preparation, sterile single-use needles/syringes, single-dose vials when possible, and needleless systems or safety caps.
  • Use proper hand hygiene before food preparation/eating and after toileting or diaper care.
  • When traveling in underdeveloped areas, drink purified water and avoid shared utensils and linens.

Hepatitis Assessment and Care

Transmission control

Findings and labs

  • Expected findings include exposure history, fatigue, decreased appetite with nausea, abdominal pain, joint pain, fever, vomiting, dark urine, clay-colored stools, and jaundice.
  • ALT, AST, bilirubin, and sometimes ALP rise with hepatitis.
  • Anti-HAV identifies hepatitis A; HBsAg identifies infectious hepatitis B; anti-HCV, EIA, and HCV RNA PCR support hepatitis C diagnosis.
  • Anti-HDV and anti-HEV support hepatitis D and E identification.

Care and medications

  • Most clients receive home care unless acutely ill; use indicated precautions and teach home transmission prevention.
  • After nausea and anorexia improve, provide high-carbohydrate, high-calorie, moderate-fat, moderate-protein nutrition with small frequent meals.
  • Promote hepatic rest: give only necessary medications, avoid alcohol, and limit activity.
  • HAV postexposure protection can include immunization or immunoglobulin for selected clients. Acute HBV and HEV receive supportive care; chronic HBV uses antivirals; HCV treatment can use combination antiviral therapy.

Cirrhosis Map

Scarring and portal pressure

Pathophysiology and risks

  • Cirrhosis is extensive permanent scarring after necrotic injury or chronic inflammation; fibrotic tissue replaces functioning liver tissue.
  • Scarring and nodules can obstruct bile channels and normal hepatic blood flow, causing jaundice and portal-pressure complications.
  • Types include postnecrotic cirrhosis, Laennec's cirrhosis from chronic alcohol use disorder, and biliary cirrhosis from chronic obstruction or autoimmune disease.
  • Risk factors include alcohol use disorder, chronic HBV/HCV/HDV, autoimmune hepatitis, fatty liver disease, medications/substances/toxins/infections, chronic biliary obstruction, and severe right-sided heart failure.

Expected findings

  • General findings include fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain/distention, severe pruritus, and confusion or difficulty thinking.
  • Neurologic signs include cognitive change, altered sleep-wake pattern, personality or mood changes, asterixis, and fetor hepaticus.
  • Portal and bleeding findings include varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, splenomegaly with thrombocytopenia, ascites, dependent edema, petechiae, ecchymoses, nosebleeds, hematemesis, and melena.
  • Skin findings include jaundice, icterus, palmar erythema, and spider angiomas.

Cirrhosis Labs, Diagnostics, and Care

Function loss

Testing logic

  • Liver enzymes can be elevated early; ALT and AST can normalize when damaged liver cells can no longer mount an inflammatory response. ALP increases with intrahepatic biliary obstruction.
  • Bilirubin rises because the liver cannot excrete it. Total protein and albumin decrease from reduced hepatic synthesis.
  • RBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelets decrease; PT/INR prolongs due to decreased prothrombin synthesis.
  • Ammonia rises when the liver cannot convert ammonia to urea; creatinine can rise when advanced liver disease impairs kidney function.
  • Ultrasound, x-ray, CT, MRI, liver biopsy, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy help identify ascites, organ enlargement, obstruction, masses, disease progression, and varices.

Nursing care

  • Monitor oxygen saturation and respiratory distress; elevate the head of bed or use a chair position to ease breathing when ascites or plasma volume excess impairs effort.
  • Protect skin from pressure and scratching; cold-water washing and lotion can reduce pruritus discomfort.
  • Track strict I&O, daily weights, ascites, peripheral edema, abdominal girth over the largest area, vital signs, pain, GI bleeding, and neurologic deterioration.
  • Nutrition commonly includes high-carbohydrate, high-protein, moderate-fat, low-sodium intake with thiamine, folate, multivitamins, and small frequent meals; protein restriction can be needed with encephalopathy.

Procedures and Complications

Escalation cues
  • Paracentesis relieves ascites. Before the procedure, explain, witness consent, obtain vital signs and weight, and have the client void; afterward, monitor vital signs, bed rest, fluid amount/color, lab specimen, puncture site drainage, and weight.
  • Varices can be banded or sclerosed endoscopically; banding lowers hemorrhage risk. Severe portal hypertension/ascites can require TIPS or surgical shunting.
  • Liver transplantation requires multidisciplinary care and transplant eligibility; severe cardiac/respiratory disease, metastatic malignant liver cancer, or active alcohol/substance use disorder can exclude candidacy.
  • After transplant, monitor acute graft rejection: tachycardia, fever, RUQ pain, changed bile color or more jaundice, and increased ALT/AST. Also monitor infection, clotting problems, hepatic complications, and acute kidney injury.
  • Hepatic encephalopathy occurs when ammonia and other toxins reach the brain. Give lactulose as prescribed, monitor potassium because diarrhea can cause hypokalemia, assess LOC/orientation, and report asterixis or fetor hepaticus.
  • Esophageal varices are fragile collateral vessels from portal hypertension. Monitor bleeding, hemoglobin, and vital signs; assist with lavage, balloon tamponade, transfusion, ligation/sclerotherapy, or shunting as prescribed.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Liver Biopsy

ATI-supported ALS

Description and nursing actions

  • A liver biopsy collects a liver tissue sample for diagnostic testing using a needle inserted between the right lower ribs into the liver.
  • Preprocedure: explain the procedure, witness informed consent, verify fasting since midnight, and administer prescribed medication.
  • Intraprocedure: position supine with RUQ exposed, support relaxation, have the client exhale and hold during needle insertion, resume breathing after removal, and apply pressure.
  • Postprocedure: position right side-lying for several hours, monitor vital signs, assess abdominal pain, and check the puncture site for bleeding.

Potential complications

  • Bleeding.
  • Bile peritonitis.
  • Pneumothorax.

Application Exercises

1

Which plan-of-care action fits a client who has hepatitis B with ascites?

  • A. Initiate contact precautions.
  • B. Weigh the client weekly.
  • C. Measure abdominal girth at the base of the ribcage.
  • D. Provide a high-calorie, high-carbohydrate diet.
D Hepatitis nutrition emphasizes high-calorie, high-carbohydrate intake after nausea and anorexia improve.
A, B, C HBV is bloodborne and standard precautions are generally used; fluid status needs daily weights and abdominal girth measured over the largest part of the abdomen.
2

Which laboratory finding supports a new diagnosis of hepatitis C?

  • A. Presence of immunoglobulin G antibodies.
  • B. Positive enzyme immunoassay test.
  • C. AST 35 units/L.
  • D. ALT 15 units/L.
B An EIA can detect antigens or antibodies associated with hepatitis C infection.
A, C, D IgG fits hepatitis A history, and AST/ALT are expected to be elevated rather than within reference range.
3

Which findings indicate hepatic encephalopathy in advanced cirrhosis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Change in orientation.
  • B. Asterixis.
  • C. Ascites.
  • D. Fetor hepaticus.
  • E. Anorexia.
A, B, D Orientation changes, asterixis, and fruity/musty breath odor indicate worsening encephalopathy.
C, E Ascites and anorexia occur with liver dysfunction but are not the specific encephalopathy indicators in this item.
4

Which medications can the nurse expect for a client who has cirrhosis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Diuretic.
  • B. Beta-blocking agent.
  • C. Opioid analgesic.
  • D. Lactulose.
  • E. Sedative.
A, B, D Diuretics reduce excess fluid, beta blockers help prevent variceal bleeding, and lactulose promotes ammonia excretion.
C, E Opioids and sedatives are liver-metabolized and used sparingly or avoided when possible in cirrhosis.
5

Which home-care teaching should be included for hepatitis B? Select all that apply.

  • A. Limit physical activity.
  • B. Avoid alcohol.
  • C. Take acetaminophen for comfort.
  • D. Wear a mask in public places.
  • E. Eat small frequent meals.
A, B, E Activity limitation, alcohol avoidance, and small frequent meals support hepatic rest and nutrition.
C, D Acetaminophen is metabolized in the liver and should be avoided unless specifically approved; masks do not prevent bloodborne HBV transmission.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 56

Renal Diagnostic Procedures

Renal diagnostics hinge on kidney function, contrast safety, infection monitoring, bleeding risk, and protecting clients whose renal reserve is already limited.

TL;DR · Contrast, Catheters, and Kidney Function

Creatinine is the kidney-specific red flag, BUN can rise from kidney disease and other stressors, and urinalysis points toward infection or metabolic problems. For procedures, separate noncontrast tests from contrast studies, then watch for kidney injury, bleeding, infection, and urinary obstruction.

Lab logic

  • Blood creatinine rises with kidney disease; at least substantial kidney function loss can be present before it elevates.
  • BUN reflects urea nitrogen from protein breakdown and can rise with dehydration, infection, chemotherapy, steroid therapy, damaged tissue reabsorption, or kidney disease.
  • Urinalysis can detect glucose, ketones, protein, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, sediment, RBCs, and other clues; culture and sensitivity identifies the organism and antibiotic options.

Procedure safety

  • Contrast procedures increase acute kidney injury risk, especially for older adults, dehydration, prior renal insufficiency, and nephrotoxic medication use.
  • Kidney biopsy requires coagulation review and postprocedure monitoring for hemorrhage, hematuria, dressing changes, Hgb/Hct, and pain.
  • Cystoscopy and retrograde studies require infection/bleeding monitoring, urine-output checks, pink-tinged urine teaching, and catheter irrigation if clots reduce output.

Core Concepts

Renal Laboratory Map

ATI source-authored

Blood and urine tests

  • Blood creatinine comes from protein and muscle breakdown; kidney disease is the condition that raises it.
  • BUN comes from protein breakdown in the liver and renal excretion of urea nitrogen; liver failure can lower BUN even when kidney failure is also present.
  • Urinalysis evaluates urine color, clarity, concentration/dilution, specific gravity, pH, drug metabolites, glucose, ketones, protein, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, sediment, and RBCs.
  • A 24-hr urine collection can measure creatinine, urea nitrogen, electrolytes, catecholamines, and proteins; 24-hr creatinine clearance estimates GFR.

Collection teaching

  • Use an early-morning specimen when a more concentrated urinalysis sample is needed.
  • For a 24-hr urine collection, discard the first voided specimen and record that time as the collection start.
  • Refrigerate the collection or keep it on ice.
  • If leukocyte esterase and nitrites are positive, obtain a clean-catch urine specimen for culture and sensitivity.

Imaging and Contrast Safety

Risk reduction
  • KUB x-ray visualizes kidneys, ureters, and bladder and can detect calculi, strictures, calcium deposits, or obstructions; no contrast is used.
  • CT gives three-dimensional renal/urinary images and can use iodine-based contrast; contrast can cause acute kidney injury.
  • MRI requires the client to lie still and is not used when metal implants can be affected by the magnet.
  • Ultrasound images kidney size, ureters, bladder, masses, cysts, calculi, and lower urinary tract obstruction and is an alternative to excretory urography.
  • Excretory urography uses iodine contrast to detect obstruction, masses, and kidney size; before it, encourage fluids the day before, bowel cleanse, NPO after midnight, assess iodine/seafood/egg/milk/chocolate allergy and asthma, check BUN/creatinine, and withhold metformin for 24 hr.
  • After excretory urography, give IV or oral fluids to flush contrast, check BUN/creatinine before restarting metformin, and monitor for contrast-related kidney injury.

Instrumentation and Biopsy

Bleeding and infection

Catheter-based studies

  • VCUG uses catheter-instilled contrast to image the bladder/ureters and determine whether urine refluxes into the ureters; contrast does not reach blood or kidneys and is not nephrotoxic.
  • After VCUG, monitor for infection, encourage fluids to dilute urine and reduce burning, and report urine output below 30 mL/hr when pelvic or urethral trauma is suspected.
  • Cystoscopy/cystourethroscopy evaluates bladder-wall abnormalities or ureter/urethral occlusion; preprocedure care includes NPO after midnight and bowel preparation as prescribed.
  • After cystoscopy, monitor vital signs and urine output, document urine color, encourage oral fluids, and irrigate with 0.9% sodium chloride if clots or decreased/absent urine output occur.

Biopsy and renal scan

  • Kidney biopsy removes tissue for cytology/histology; preprocedure care includes coagulation review and NPO status, and postprocedure care includes vital signs, dressing/urine assessment, Hgb/Hct review, and analgesia.
  • Hemorrhage is the priority kidney biopsy complication.
  • Renal scan evaluates renal blood flow and estimates GFR after IV radioactive material; if captopril is used, monitor blood pressure and orthostatic hypotension.
  • Increase fluids after renal scan if hypotension occurs and to promote radioisotope excretion; the radioisotope is not nephrotoxic.

Gerontological Considerations

Lower reserve
  • Kidney size, function, blood-flow adaptability, and GFR decrease with aging.
  • Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and heart failure can further affect GFR.
  • Older adults are more vulnerable to kidney injury from contrast media and medications due to decreased kidney size, blood flow, and GFR.
  • Tubular changes can cause urgency and nocturnal polyuria; short urethra and weak urinary sphincter can increase incontinence and UTI risk in women, and enlarged prostate can cause retention and infection in men.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Cystoscopy with Retrograde Pyelogram

ATI-supported ALS

Description and indications

  • Cystoscopy is instrumentation into the urinary tract to inspect the bladder wall.
  • Retrograde pyelogram injects media into the ureters to inspect the ureters and kidney pelvis.
  • Cystoscopy can identify bladder-wall cysts, tumors, or stones.
  • Retrograde pyelogram can identify ureter or renal pelvis obstruction and structural disorders such as strictures, stones, or masses.

Nursing interventions

  • Preprocedure: keep the client NPO after midnight and administer a laxative the night before if prescribed.
  • Postprocedure: monitor vital signs, encourage oral fluids to reduce burning, and document urine color.
  • If a urinary catheter is present, irrigate with 0.9% sodium chloride for active bleeding, clots, or decreased/absent urine output.

Application Exercises

1

Which teaching should the nurse include for an x-ray of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder?

  • A. "You will receive contrast dye."
  • B. "An enema is required before the procedure."
  • C. "You will lie prone during the procedure."
  • D. "The procedure can determine whether you have a kidney stone."
D A KUB can identify renal calculi, strictures, calcium deposits, and urinary obstructions.
A, B, C KUB does not use contrast, does not require bowel prep for this ATI item, and is performed supine.
2

Which kidney biopsy complication creates the greatest risk?

  • A. Infection.
  • B. Hemorrhage.
  • C. Hematuria.
  • D. Pain.
B Hemorrhage is the priority risk after kidney biopsy because clotting at the puncture site can fail.
A, C, D Infection, hematuria, and pain can occur, but hemorrhage is the greatest risk.
3

Which actions belong before excretory urography for a client with type 2 diabetes mellitus? Select all that apply.

  • A. Identify seafood allergy.
  • B. Withhold metformin for 24 hr.
  • C. Administer an enema as prescribed.
  • D. Obtain a blood coagulation profile.
  • E. Assess for asthma.
A, B, C, E Contrast allergy risk, metformin-related lactic acidosis risk, bowel cleansing, and asthma risk should be addressed.
D Coagulation studies are a priority before kidney biopsy, not excretory urography.
4

A client received captopril during a renal scan. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Assess for hypertension.
  • B. Restrict fluid intake.
  • C. Monitor for orthostatic hypotension.
  • D. Encourage early ambulation.
C Captopril can cause orthostatic hypotension during or after a renal scan.
A, B, D Monitor for hypotension, increase fluids if needed, and protect from falls.
5

Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Repeat the test early tomorrow.
  • B. Start a 24-hr urine collection for creatinine clearance.
  • C. Obtain a clean-catch urine specimen for culture and sensitivity.
  • D. Insert an indwelling catheter for specimen collection.
C Culture and sensitivity identifies the organism and antibiotic most likely to treat the UTI.
A, B, D Repeating the urinalysis will not change the result, creatinine clearance assesses kidney function, and catheterization is reserved for clients who cannot empty the bladder.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 57

Hemodialysis and Peritoneal Dialysis

Dialysis sustains life by removing fluid, electrolytes, and waste, but it does not restore kidney function or replace hormonal kidney roles. Safety depends on access protection, fluid shifts, infection prevention, and complication recognition.

TL;DR · Hemodynamics vs Peritoneal Filtering

Hemodialysis moves blood through a dialyzer and needs vascular access; peritoneal dialysis instills hypertonic dialysate into the abdomen and uses the peritoneum as the membrane. Hemodialysis priorities are access patency, bleeding, hypotension, and disequilibrium. Peritoneal priorities are asepsis, cloudy outflow, glucose absorption, protein loss, and inflow/outflow problems.

Hemodialysis

  • Indications include renal insufficiency, AKI, CKD, medication or illicit drug toxicity, persistent hyperkalemia, and diuretic-resistant hypervolemia.
  • Before dialysis, assess access bruit/thrill, distal circulation, labs, vital signs, weight, and medications to hold.
  • After dialysis, compare weights, check labs/vitals, assess bleeding/infection, and monitor hypovolemia and disequilibrium syndrome.

Peritoneal dialysis

  • Use surgical asepsis, warm dialysate without a microwave, monitor inflow/outflow, and keep the outflow bag below the abdomen.
  • Clear light-yellow outflow is expected; cloudy or opaque effluent is the earliest peritonitis cue.
  • Monitor blood glucose, protein loss, access leakage/infection, respiratory distress, abdominal pain, and poor dialysate flow.

Core Concepts

Dialysis Map

ATI source-authored

Functions

  • Dialysis removes excess fluid and electrolytes, restores acid-base balance, eliminates waste products, and supports internal homeostasis through osmosis, diffusion, and ultrafiltration.
  • Dialysis can sustain life in AKI or CKD but does not replace kidney hormonal function.
  • Client presentations can include fluid volume changes, electrolyte or pH imbalance, nitrogenous waste buildup, fluid overload, neurologic changes, bleeding, and uremia.

Compare modalities

  • Hemodialysis shunts blood from the body through a dialyzer and back to circulation and requires vascular access.
  • Peritoneal dialysis instills hypertonic dialysate into the peritoneal cavity, allows dwell time, then drains fluid containing waste products.
  • Peritoneal dialysis requires an intact peritoneal membrane and is often used for older adults or clients who cannot tolerate anticoagulation, have difficult vascular access, chronic infections, instability, or chronic disease burdens.

Hemodialysis Care

Access and fluid shifts

Before and during

  • Check informed consent, use temporary access until a long-term device is available, and assess AV fistula or graft bruit, thrill, distal pulses, and circulation.
  • Avoid blood pressure, injections, venipuncture, or IV catheters on the access arm; elevate the extremity after AV fistula creation to reduce swelling.
  • Assess vital signs, BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, hematocrit, and weight; discuss which dialyzable or blood-pressure-lowering medications to hold until after dialysis.
  • During dialysis, monitor for circuit clotting, air in tubing, dialysate temperature issues, ultrafiltration regulation, hypotension, cramping, vomiting, access-site bleeding, contamination, and coagulation status.

After and teaching

  • Compare pre- and postprocedure weights to estimate fluid removed; 1 L fluid equals about 1 kg or 2.2 lb.
  • Monitor vitals, BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, hematocrit, bleeding, infection, hypovolemia, muscle cramps, headache, and disequilibrium findings.
  • Avoid invasive procedures for several hours after dialysis because anticoagulation increases bleeding risk.
  • Teach access protection: report bleeding longer than 30 min, absent thrill/bruit, or infection cues; avoid heavy lifting, constriction, sleeping on the access arm, and venipuncture or BP on that arm.
  • Diet teaching includes folate replacement, high-folate foods, increased protein compared with predialysis restriction, and continued sodium, potassium, and phosphorus limits as prescribed.

Hemodialysis Complications

Unexpected responses
  • Access clotting or infection: use surgical asepsis during cannulation, avoid compression, avoid BP/venipuncture on the access arm, assess thrill/bruit, inspect redness/swelling/drainage, and monitor fever.
  • Disequilibrium syndrome occurs when BUN and circulating volume drop too quickly, causing cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure; watch for nausea, vomiting, LOC change, seizures, and agitation.
  • For disequilibrium risk, use a slow exchange rate for older adults or first-time hemodialysis and administer prescribed anticonvulsants or barbiturates if needed.
  • Hypotension can result from antihypertensives and rapid fluid removal; replace volume carefully, slow the exchange rate, lower the head of bed, and discontinue dialysis for severe unresponsive hypotension.
  • Anemia can worsen from blood loss and folate removal; erythropoietin, Hgb/RBC monitoring, hypotension/tachycardia monitoring, and transfusion can be used as prescribed.
  • Frequent blood access raises HIV and hepatitis B/C transmission risk; use sterile equipment, skin antisepsis, and standard precautions.

Peritoneal Dialysis Care

Asepsis and outflow

Before and during

  • Assess dry weight, vital signs, electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, and glucose; determine whether the client can self-perform dialysis and maintain sterile technique.
  • Monitor initial hospital dialysis vital signs frequently and monitor blood glucose because dialysate contains glucose.
  • Record inflow compared with outflow; expected outflow is clear, light yellow, and equal to or greater than inflow.
  • Warm dialysate before instillation, but do not use a microwave; follow prescribed infusion, dwell, and outflow timing.
  • Maintain surgical asepsis at the catheter site and when accessing the catheter; keep the outflow bag below the abdomen and reposition for poor flow.

Teaching and complications

  • Teach that fullness can occur during dwell and initial infusion discomfort can happen.
  • CAPD occurs daily with exchanges across the day; CCPD and APD use nighttime cycling patterns with prescribed dwell timing.
  • Monitor for infection: fever, bloody/cloudy/frothy dialysate, drainage, redness, swelling, or cloudy opaque effluent.
  • Watch respiratory distress, abdominal pain, insufficient outflow, discolored outflow, wet access-site dressing, catheter leakage, and exit-site infection.
  • Support home access care, careful adherence, medication/supplement use, local support resources, and body-image concerns from bloating.

Peritoneal Dialysis Complications

Flow and metabolic safety
  • Peritonitis: maintain surgical asepsis, monitor fever, pain, purulent drainage, redness, swelling, and cloudy or discolored drained dialysate, and teach strict sterile exchange technique.
  • Access-site infection can result from dialysate leakage and can progress to peritonitis; assess wetness, leakage, tugging, twisting, redness, swelling, drainage, and fever.
  • Protein loss occurs when dialysis removes protein along with fluid and waste; increase dietary protein over predialysis restrictions and monitor albumin.
  • Hyperglycemia can occur because glucose is absorbed from hypertonic dialysate; monitor glucose, administer insulin as prescribed, and follow the provider's diet plan.
  • Hyperlipidemia can occur with long-term therapy and contribute to hypertension; administer antilipemic medications and antihypertensives as prescribed.
  • Poor inflow or outflow can be caused by tubing obstruction/twisting, constipation, positioning, fibrin clot, or catheter displacement; reposition, check clamps/kinks, milk tubing for fibrin clots as prescribed, and prevent constipation.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Peritoneal Dialysis

ATI-supported ALS

Description and complications

  • Peritoneal dialysis instills hypertonic dialysate into the peritoneal cavity, allows prescribed dwell time, and drains fluid containing waste products.
  • Potential complications include peritonitis, protein loss, hyperglycemia, and poor dialysate inflow or outflow.

Nursing actions

  • Peritonitis: maintain surgical asepsis and monitor outflow color, pain, and fever.
  • Protein loss: increase dietary protein and monitor albumin.
  • Hyperglycemia: monitor blood glucose and administer insulin as prescribed.
  • Poor flow: reposition, milk tubing for fibrin clots if prescribed, check for kinks or closed clamps, and prevent constipation with diet and stool softeners.

Application Exercises

1

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client beginning hemodialysis?

  • A. Hemodialysis restores kidney function.
  • B. Hemodialysis replaces hormonal kidney function.
  • C. Hemodialysis allows an unrestricted diet.
  • D. Hemodialysis returns balance to blood electrolytes.
D Hemodialysis removes excess electrolytes, fluid, and waste and helps restore acid-base balance.
A, B, C Dialysis sustains life but does not restore kidney function, replace hormonal function, or remove renal diet restrictions.
2

Which actions should the nurse take before initiating hemodialysis for acute kidney injury? Select all that apply.

  • A. Review current medications.
  • B. Assess the AV fistula for bruit.
  • C. Measure the client's weight.
  • D. Check blood electrolytes.
  • E. Use the access site for venipuncture.
A, B, C, D Medication review, access patency, baseline weight, and electrolyte assessment are preprocedure priorities.
E Never use the access site area for venipuncture because compression can damage or collapse vascular access.
3

Which interventions should be included after hemodialysis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Check BUN and blood creatinine.
  • B. Administer medications withheld before dialysis as appropriate.
  • C. Observe for hypovolemia.
  • D. Assess the access site for bleeding.
  • E. Measure blood pressure on the arm with AV access.
A, B, C, D Postdialysis care includes lab review, medication timing, hypovolemia monitoring, and bleeding assessment because heparin is used.
E Blood pressure is never measured on the access extremity because compression can harm the fistula or graft.
4

A client develops disequilibrium syndrome after hemodialysis. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Administer an opioid medication.
  • B. Monitor for hypertension.
  • C. Assess level of consciousness.
  • D. Increase the dialysis exchange rate.
C Disequilibrium can increase intracranial pressure, so decreased level of consciousness is a priority assessment.
A, B, D Opioids can worsen status, hypotension is more expected, and the dialysis exchange rate should be decreased rather than increased.
5

Which actions should be included for peritoneal dialysis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Monitor blood glucose levels.
  • B. Report cloudy dialysate return.
  • C. Warm dialysate in a microwave oven.
  • D. Assess for shortness of breath.
  • E. Check the access-site dressing for wetness.
  • F. Maintain medical asepsis when accessing the catheter site.
A, B, D, E Dialysate contains glucose, cloudy outflow suggests infection, respiratory distress can mean intolerance of dialysate volume, and wet dressings suggest leakage.
C, F Do not microwave dialysate, and use surgical rather than medical asepsis for catheter access.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 58

Kidney Transplant

Kidney transplant improves quality of life for eligible clients with end-stage kidney disease, but success depends on donor matching, lifelong immunosuppression, infection prevention, urine-output surveillance, and rapid rejection recognition.

TL;DR · Graft Perfusion and Rejection Watch

After kidney transplant, urine output is the pulse of the graft. Report urine output below 30 mL/hr, abrupt output decrease, fever, hypertension, transplant-site pain, bloody drainage, oliguria/anuria, fluid retention, or infection cues immediately.

Before transplant

  • Donor matching includes ABO compatibility and histocompatibility, including human leukocytic antigen and minor antigens.
  • Living related donors with matching tissue type have the greatest graft-survival chance.
  • Risk rises with very young or older age, advanced cardiac disease, active cancer, chemical dependency, chronic infection, coagulopathy, morbid obesity, diabetes, chronic pulmonary disease, and untreated GI disease.

After transplant

  • Monitor vital signs, hourly I&O, urine appearance, daily urinalysis, daily weight, electrolytes, infection, rejection, bleeding, and fluid balance.
  • Replace hourly urine output with IV fluids as prescribed and maintain catheter drainage/CBI to protect the graft from clot obstruction.
  • Teach strict medication adherence, infection reporting, grapefruit avoidance with cyclosporine, activity progression, and avoiding contact sports.

Core Concepts

End-Stage Kidney Disease and Candidacy

ATI source-authored

ESKD indicators

  • Indications include anuria, proteinuria, marked azotemia, severe electrolyte imbalance such as hyperkalemia or hypernatremia, fluid-volume excess with heart failure or pulmonary edema, and uremic lung.
  • Expected findings can include anorexia, fatigue, numbness/tingling, shortness of breath, dry itchy skin, metallic taste, muscle cramping, decreased attention span, seizures, tremor, heart failure, edema, dyspnea, distended neck veins, anemia, vomiting, hypertension, dysrhythmias, pallor, bruising, halitosis, and diminished or dark urine.
  • Labs can show proteinuria, hematuria, elevated BUN/creatinine, decreased GFR, decreased Hgb/Hct, elevated potassium/phosphorus, sodium changes, and metabolic acidosis.

Matching and risk

  • Donors can be living, non-heart-beating, or cadaver donors; donor kidneys must be adequately perfused to remain viable.
  • Recipient and donor tissue matching includes ABO compatibility and histocompatibility testing.
  • Risks that increase transplant surgery, immunosuppression, or rejection complications include age younger than 2 or older than 70, advanced untreatable cardiac disease, active cancer, chemical dependency, chronic infections such as HIV or hepatitis B/C, coagulopathies, immune disorders, morbid obesity, diabetes mellitus, chronic pulmonary disease, and untreated peptic ulcer disease.

Preprocedure Priorities

Readiness and immunosuppression
  • Dialysis is usually performed within 24 hr of surgery.
  • Preoperative labs include blood chemistry, CBC/differential, bleeding times, urine culture, blood type, and crossmatch.
  • Prescribed preoperative medications can include prophylactic antibiotics and immunosuppression.
  • Corticosteroids decrease the inflammatory immune response; cyclosporine and azathioprine prevent donor-kidney rejection; mTOR inhibitors interrupt T-cell signaling; everolimus helps prevent B- and T-cell activation; basiliximab or daclizumab bind T cells to decrease activation.
  • Teaching includes mental/emotional preparation, transplant-team roles, lifelong immunosuppression adherence, smoking cessation, and blood pressure/glucose control.

Postprocedure Monitoring

Protect the graft

Early monitoring

  • Assess vital signs frequently at first, then per protocol, and keep blood pressure within prescribed parameters.
  • Assess I&O at least hourly; urine output should stay above 30 mL/hr.
  • Report oliguria below 30 mL/hr and abrupt urine-output decrease because these can indicate rejection, tissue injury, renal artery thrombosis, or urinary obstruction.
  • Assess urine appearance and odor hourly; urine can be pink/bloody at first and gradually clear over days to weeks.
  • Monitor daily urinalysis, daily weight, fluid/electrolyte imbalance, infection, rejection cues, and surgical dressing bleeding.

Fluid, catheter, and medication care

  • Administer IV fluids as prescribed, often replacing hourly urine output; transition to oral fluids when bowel function returns and fluids are tolerated.
  • Maintain the large indwelling urinary catheter to dependent bedside drainage and use continuous bladder irrigation as prescribed to prevent clot obstruction that could injure the graft.
  • Remove the urinary catheter as soon as possible to reduce infection risk.
  • Oliguria can require prescribed diuretics or dialysis until kidney function is satisfactory; excessive diuresis can cause hypovolemia, hypotension, and reduced graft blood flow.
  • Administer immunosuppressive medications, antibiotics, stool softeners, and follow-up/counseling referrals as prescribed.

Client Teaching

Lifelong safety
  • Report infection findings such as fever, incisional drainage, redness, fatigue, discomfort, or mental-status change.
  • Adhere to immunosuppressive therapy and other prescribed medications.
  • When taking prednisone, avoid concentrated sugars or carbohydrates as prescribed for glycemic control.
  • Magnesium supplements can be needed because cyclosporine can reduce magnesium levels.
  • Avoid grapefruit with cyclosporine because it can raise cyclosporine blood levels.
  • Avoid contact sports that could injure the transplanted kidney and increase activity as tolerated.

Complications

Report rapidly

Rejection and ischemia

  • Hyperacute rejection occurs within 48 hr and is not reversible; fever, hypertension, and transplant-site pain require immediate treatment, often donor-kidney removal.
  • Acute rejection occurs from 1 week to 2 years and can cause oliguria, anuria, low-grade fever, hypertension, tenderness over the transplanted kidney, lethargy, azotemia, and fluid retention; treatment uses increased immunosuppression.
  • Chronic rejection develops gradually over months to years with returning azotemia, fluid retention, electrolyte imbalance, and fatigue; conservative monitoring continues until dialysis is required.
  • Ischemia can occur when transplanting is delayed after harvesting; monitor urine output, creatinine, and BUN, report output below 30 mL/hr, assist with dialysis, and prepare for biopsy to distinguish ischemia from rejection.

Vascular and infection risks

  • Renal artery stenosis can occur from surgical anastomosis scarring; report hypertension, bruit over the anastomosis, oliguria, and elevated BUN/creatinine.
  • Thrombosis can form in a major graft vessel; sudden urine-output decrease requires emergency escalation and possible transplant nephrectomy.
  • Infection is a major first-year morbidity and mortality cause, and immunosuppression can make early signs subtle.
  • Prioritize infection control with frequent hand hygiene, avoiding crowds or communicable illness exposure, possible mask use in public when indicated, and rapid reporting of localized or systemic infection.

Active Learning Scenario

Nursing Skill - Post-Transplant Urinary Catheter Care

ATI-supported ALS

Indications and complications

  • Indications include hourly urine-output monitoring and monitoring urine color/clots.
  • Potential complications include oliguria, infection from the indwelling urinary catheter, and blood clot formation.

Nursing interventions

  • Regulate IV fluids according to urinary output as prescribed.
  • Keep the drainage bag lower than the client for gravity drainage.
  • Remove the indwelling catheter within a few days after the procedure when prescribed.
  • Implement continuous bladder irrigation as prescribed to remove clots that could obstruct drainage and damage the donor kidney.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings should the nurse expect with end-stage kidney disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Anuria.
  • B. Marked azotemia.
  • C. Crackles in the lungs.
  • D. Increased calcium level.
  • E. Proteinuria.
A, B, C, E ESKD can cause anuria, elevated BUN/creatinine, pulmonary edema with crackles, and proteinuria.
D Calcium tends to decrease as phosphate rises in end-stage kidney disease.
2

Which postoperative actions should the nurse include after kidney transplant? Select all that apply.

  • A. Obtain daily weights.
  • B. Assess dressings for bloody drainage.
  • C. Replace hourly urine output with IV fluids as prescribed.
  • D. Expect oliguria during the first 4 hr.
  • E. Monitor blood electrolytes.
A, B, C, E Daily weights, dressing checks, urine-output replacement, and electrolyte monitoring protect fluid status and graft function.
D Oliguria can indicate ischemia, acute kidney injury, rejection, or hypovolemia and should be reported.
3

Which cyclosporine teaching should the nurse include after kidney transplant?

  • A. Decrease protein-rich foods.
  • B. Take the medication with grapefruit juice.
  • C. Report a sore throat to the provider.
  • D. Expect skin to turn yellow.
C Cyclosporine causes immunosuppression, so infection cues such as sore throat should be reported.
A, B, D Protein supports healing, grapefruit raises cyclosporine levels, and jaundice should be reported as possible hepatotoxicity rather than expected.
4

Which findings increase kidney transplantation surgery risk? Select all that apply.

  • A. Age older than 70 years.
  • B. BMI of 41.
  • C. Insulin-requiring diabetes mellitus.
  • D. Past history of lymphoma.
  • E. Blood pressure averaging 120/70 mm Hg.
A, B, C, D Older age, morbid obesity, diabetes, and cancer history increase risk from surgery, lifelong immunosuppression, or rejection.
E This blood pressure is within expected range and is not the increased-risk finding in this item.
5

Which rejection teaching should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

  • A. Hyperacute rejection can require immediate donor-kidney removal.
  • B. Dialysis is the primary treatment for hyperacute rejection.
  • C. Fever can occur with acute rejection.
  • D. Fluid retention can occur with acute rejection.
  • E. Increased immunosuppression treats chronic rejection.
A, C, D Hyperacute rejection can require immediate graft removal; fever and fluid retention can occur with acute rejection.
B, E Dialysis is conservative support for chronic failure progression, and increased immunosuppression treats acute rejection rather than chronic rejection.
