Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 59

Polycystic Kidney Disease, Acute Kidney Injury, and Chronic Kidney Disease

Kidney failure questions usually turn on time course, perfusion, obstruction, nephrotoxins, fluid balance, potassium, and whether the client needs urgent stabilization, dialysis planning, or long-term disease management.

TL;DR · Perfusion, Potassium, and Progression

For AKI, identify the cause and protect perfusion fast. For CKD, trend GFR, BUN/creatinine, potassium, phosphorus, anemia, fluid overload, and uremia. For PKD, blood pressure control and infection/stone surveillance are the priority cues.

AKI test logic

  • Prerenal AKI points to low perfusion from hypovolemia, shock, low cardiac output, sepsis, renal vascular obstruction, or medication effects.
  • Intrarenal AKI points to direct nephron damage from ischemia, trauma, nephrotoxins, transfusion reaction, infection, vasculitis, or glomerulonephritis.
  • Postrenal AKI points to obstruction such as stones, tumors, bladder atony, prostate enlargement, urethral stricture, or spinal cord disorder.

CKD/PKD test logic

  • CKD is progressive and irreversible; stage 4 means severe GFR reduction, and stage 5 means kidney failure/end-stage kidney disease.
  • CKD safety centers on renal diet, fluid restriction when prescribed, nephrotoxin avoidance, dialysis/transplant planning, anemia treatment, and potassium/phosphate control.
  • PKD is hereditary; watch for hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, hematuria/cloudy urine, stones, constipation, cyst infection or rupture, and progressive kidney failure.

Core Concepts

Acute Kidney Injury

ATI source-authored

Phases and classes

  • AKI is abrupt renal-function loss after kidney blood flow or kidney tissue is compromised.
  • Phases move from onset, to oliguria, to diuresis, to recovery; recovery can take months.
  • Severity is staged by creatinine rise and urine-output decline; severe AKI includes marked creatinine elevation or very low urine output for many hours.
  • Expected findings are often waste buildup and output changes, but cardiovascular, respiratory, neurologic, integumentary, and renal findings can all appear.

Findings and diagnostics

  • Assess for hypertension, fluid overload, edema, dysrhythmias from hyperkalemia, crackles, decreased oxygenation, shortness of breath, hematuria, lethargy, twitching, seizures, dry skin, and dry mucous membranes.
  • Trend BUN, creatinine, urine specific gravity, electrolytes, hematocrit, urinalysis sediment, and ABGs for metabolic acidosis.
  • Imaging can include KUB, ultrasound, CT without contrast, MRI, or nuclear medicine studies when obstruction, perfusion, or anatomy must be evaluated.
  • Kidney biopsy can be used when the AKI cause remains unclear or immune disease/reversibility must be evaluated.

Nursing care

  • Correct the underlying cause, monitor hemodynamics, and track strict intake/output, daily weights, edema, heart failure cues, pulmonary edema cues, fever, infection, urine particles or blood, and ECG changes.
  • Avoid or reduce nephrotoxic medications when possible and use contrast cautiously; report flank pain, nausea, vomiting, urine-stream changes, or difficulty starting urine.
  • Restrict fluids and electrolytes such as potassium, phosphate, sodium, or magnesium when prescribed, and individualize protein support to the client's phase and catabolic state.
  • Prepare for continuous renal replacement therapy, hemodialysis, or peritoneal dialysis when kidney function and complications require renal support.

Medication logic

  • IV fluids can restore kidney perfusion or replace losses during the diuretic phase when prescribed.
  • Diuretics can be prescribed to promote urine formation and fluid removal when appropriate.
  • Sodium polystyrene sulfonate, sorbitol, insulin/dextrose, calcium, or sodium bicarbonate can be used for potassium or severe acid-base problems as prescribed.
  • Phosphate-binding agents can be used when phosphate rises.

Chronic Kidney Disease

Progressive and irreversible

Risk and staging

  • CKD can remain quiet until physiologic stress or advancing nephron loss makes manifestations visible.
  • Older adults are at higher risk because functioning nephrons and GFR decline with age; dehydration risk rises with bed rest, confusion, poor thirst, or poor water access.
  • Risk factors include AKI, diabetes mellitus, chronic glomerulonephritis, nephrotoxic medications or chemicals, hypertension, autoimmune disease, PKD, renal artery stenosis, and recurrent severe infections.
  • Stage 1 has minimal damage with expected-range GFR; stage 3 is moderate GFR decrease; stage 4 is severe GFR decrease; stage 5 is kidney failure/end-stage kidney disease.

Expected findings

  • Assess for nausea, fatigue, lethargy, leg movements, depression, hiccups, reduced attention, slurred speech, tremors, ataxia, seizures, coma, and uremic breath.
  • Fluid overload can cause jugular distention, sacral/ocular/peripheral edema, hypertension, heart failure, crackles, pleural friction rub, frothy pink sputum, and dysrhythmias from hyperkalemia.
  • Anemia, bruising, GI bleeding, mouth/throat ulcers, vomiting, fragile bones, protein/blood/particles in urine, pruritus, yellow skin cast, and uremic frost can occur.
  • Labs can show hematuria, proteinuria, low specific gravity, rising creatinine/BUN, low sodium/calcium, high potassium/phosphorus/magnesium, and low hemoglobin/hematocrit from reduced erythropoietin.

Daily care

  • Monitor urinary pattern, blood pressure, weight, vascular access or peritoneal dialysis sites, medication/herb history, skin integrity, activity tolerance, and injury risk.
  • Control protein intake based on CKD stage and dialysis plan; restrict sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, and fluids when prescribed.
  • Teach daily weight and blood pressure tracking, renal diet adherence, prescribed fluid limits, dialysis instructions, rest periods, skin-breakdown reporting, and avoidance of magnesium-containing antacids.
  • Dialysis and kidney transplantation can sustain life but are not cures for CKD.

Medication cautions

  • Avoid nephrotoxic antimicrobials, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and IV contrast unless the provider determines they are necessary.
  • Digoxin doses can need reduction because CKD slows excretion; monitor digoxin and potassium levels and toxicity cues.
  • Sodium polystyrene increases potassium elimination but adds sodium, so monitor for fluid retention and hypertension.
  • Epoetin alfa and iron support anemia management; calcium carbonate binds dietary phosphate and can cause constipation.
  • Loop diuretics can remove excess fluid, but avoid giving them to clients with end-stage kidney disease unless specifically prescribed.

Polycystic Kidney Disease

Hereditary cyst disorder

Assessment

  • PKD is hereditary and causes multiple fluid-filled renal cysts that replace healthy kidney tissue.
  • The autosomal dominant form is most common and usually becomes clinically apparent in adulthood; the recessive form is present at birth.
  • Expected findings include family history, anxiety or guilt, abdominal/flank pain, headaches, hypertension from renal ischemia, enlarged abdominal girth, constipation, hematuria/cloudy urine, stones, hyponatremia, nocturia, and progressive kidney failure.
  • Dull pain can suggest kidney enlargement or cyst infection; sharp pain can suggest ruptured cyst or renal lithiasis.
  • Testing can include urinalysis, BUN/creatinine/creatinine clearance trends, ultrasound, CT, or MRI.

Care priorities

  • Blood pressure control is the priority nursing focus; teach the client and family to measure and record blood pressure and daily weights.
  • Use prescribed pain medication and nonpharmacologic strategies; use NSAIDs cautiously in kidney disease.
  • Prevent infection by administering prescribed antibiotics and monitoring creatinine and urine output for nephrotoxicity.
  • Support bowel regularity with allowed fluids, fiber, ambulation, bowel assessment, and stool softeners as prescribed.
  • Teach daily blood pressure and weight monitoring, low-sodium diet adherence, elevated temperature reporting, and reporting urine or bowel-pattern changes.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - CKD Medication Safety

ATI-supported ALS

Medication purpose

  • Digoxin increases myocardial contractility and supports cardiac output.
  • Sodium polystyrene promotes potassium elimination.
  • Calcium carbonate binds phosphate in food to reduce phosphate absorption.
  • Furosemide promotes diuresis of excess fluid when kidney function and provider direction support its use.

Nursing interventions

  • With digoxin, monitor digoxin level, potassium level, and toxicity cues such as nausea, vomiting, anorexia, or visual changes.
  • With sodium polystyrene, monitor for hypokalemia and restrict sodium intake as prescribed.
  • With furosemide, monitor intake/output and blood pressure, and avoid use in end-stage kidney disease unless specifically prescribed.
  • Across CKD medication administration, screen for nephrotoxic agents and anticipate renal-dose adjustments.

Application Exercises

1

A client has prerenal AKI after abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, urine output of 60 mL over 2 hr, and blood pressure of 92/58 mm Hg. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?

  • A. Prepare for CT with contrast.
  • B. Administer nitroprusside.
  • C. Prepare for a prescribed fluid challenge.
  • D. Place the client flat in Trendelenburg.
C Low blood pressure and low urine output after a perfusion insult support hypovolemia/prerenal AKI, so a prescribed fluid challenge can restore kidney perfusion.
A, B, D Contrast can worsen AKI, nitroprusside is not appropriate for hypotension, and positioning should support venous return without an unsafe flat Trendelenburg default.
2

Which interventions fit a client who has postrenal AKI from metastatic cancer and a creatinine of 5 mg/dL? Select all that apply.

  • A. Provide protein support as prescribed for the catabolic state.
  • B. Assess urine for blood, stones, or particles.
  • C. Monitor for intermittent anuria.
  • D. Weigh the client once each week.
  • E. Use NSAIDs for pain control.
A, B, C AKI can require protein support, obstruction surveillance, and monitoring for intermittent anuria.
D, E Daily weight is needed for fluid retention, and NSAIDs are nephrotoxic.
3

Which actions should the nurse include for a client who has stage 4 CKD? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assess for jugular venous distention.
  • B. Provide frequent mouth rinses.
  • C. Auscultate for a pleural friction rub.
  • D. Encourage a high-sodium diet.
  • E. Monitor for dysrhythmias.
A, B, C, E Stage 4 CKD can cause fluid overload, uremic breath/mouth discomfort, respiratory findings from fluid and acid-base imbalance, and dysrhythmias from hyperkalemia.
D Sodium is commonly restricted rather than increased.
4

Which lab finding best matches stage 4 CKD?

  • A. BUN 15 mg/dL.
  • B. GFR 20 mL/min.
  • C. Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL.
  • D. Potassium 5.0 mEq/L.
B Stage 4 CKD is severe kidney damage with severe GFR reduction, roughly 15 to 29 mL/min.
A, C, D BUN and creatinine are expected to rise substantially, and potassium is typically above the expected range when hyperkalemia develops.
5

Which findings should the nurse expect with prerenal AKI? Select all that apply.

  • A. Reduced BUN.
  • B. Elevated cardiac enzymes.
  • C. Reduced urine output.
  • D. Elevated blood creatinine.
  • E. Elevated blood calcium.
C, D Prerenal AKI commonly reduces urine output and raises creatinine as perfusion falls and waste products accumulate.
A, B, E BUN is expected to rise, cardiac enzymes point to cardiac tissue injury, and calcium is more likely to be reduced in this context.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 60

Infections of the Renal and Urinary System

Renal infection questions are priority questions: protect kidney tissue, prevent ascending infection and sepsis, treat the organism with the full antibiotic course, and watch high-risk clients for atypical or systemic findings.

TL;DR · Treat Infection Before It Ascends

For UTI, antibiotics are the priority because untreated infection can progress to pyelonephritis, urosepsis, septic shock, CKD, and death. For pyelonephritis, track fever, flank/CVA pain, urine output, cultures, BUN/creatinine, and sepsis cues. For glomerulonephritis, watch fluid overload, hypertension, cola-colored urine, proteinuria, and falling GFR.

UTI logic

  • Lower UTI includes cystitis, urethritis, and prostatitis; upper UTI includes pyelonephritis.
  • Common findings include urgency, frequency, dysuria, bladder discomfort, incomplete emptying, hematuria, pyuria, cloudy/foul urine, fever, vomiting, nocturia, and small voids.
  • Older adults can present with confusion, incontinence, appetite loss, nocturia/dysuria, or urosepsis findings instead of classic symptoms.

Kidney involvement logic

  • Pyelonephritis often starts as lower-tract bacteria ascending into the kidney pelvis and can scar renal tissue after repeated infections.
  • Chronic pyelonephritis can lead to CKD, hypertension, and septic shock if infection enters the bloodstream.
  • Glomerulonephritis is immune-mediated glomerular injury that can follow infection or systemic disease and can progress to ESKD.

Core Concepts

Urinary Tract Infection

ATI source-authored

Risk factors and findings

  • Risk rises with alkaline urine, indwelling urinary catheters, stool incontinence, bladder distention, urinary stasis/anomalies/calculi/residual urine, diabetes mellitus, and possible genetic factors.
  • Female risk factors include short urethra, urethra-to-rectum proximity, decreased estrogen with aging, intercourse, feminine hygiene products, spermicides, pregnancy, poorly fitted diaphragm, synthetic underwear, wet bathing suits, baths/hot tubs, and vaginal flora changes.
  • Older adult risks include incomplete bladder emptying from prostate problems, bladder prolapse, neurogenic bladder, poor perineal hygiene, hypoestrogenism, fewer functioning nephrons, and decreased fluid intake.
  • Expected findings include lower back or suprapubic discomfort, bladder tenderness, nausea, urgency/frequency, dysuria, bladder cramping/spasms, incomplete emptying, retention, perineal itching, hematuria, pyuria, fever, vomiting, nocturia, urethral discharge, and cloudy or foul-smelling urine.

Diagnostics and treatment

  • Urinalysis/culture can show bacteria, sediment, WBCs, RBCs, leukocyte esterase, and nitrites; collect clean-catch or catheterized specimens correctly.
  • If urosepsis is suspected, monitor WBC/differential for elevation and left shift.
  • STI testing can be needed because chlamydia, gonorrhea, herpes simplex, trichomoniasis, and candida can mimic UTI manifestations.
  • Complicated cases can require cystoscopy, cystourethroscopy, CT for pyelonephritis, ultrasonography, or transrectal ultrasound for male prostate/bladder conditions.
  • Administer prescribed antibiotics promptly; phenazopyridine can relieve bladder discomfort but does not treat infection.

Priority nursing care

  • Administer antibiotics as prescribed; this is the priority intervention when active infection threatens renal injury and sepsis.
  • Consult the provider about fluid restrictions before encouraging extra fluids.
  • Avoid indwelling urinary catheters when possible to reduce infection risk.
  • Pregnant clients need rapid and effective treatment to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm labor.
  • Warm sitz baths can support comfort but do not replace antimicrobial treatment.

Client teaching

  • Take the full prescribed antibiotic course even when symptoms improve; take medication with food when directed and report watery diarrhea.
  • Fluoroquinolones and sulfonamides can increase sun sensitivity; take them with a full glass of water and increase fluids when allowed.
  • Phenazopyridine can turn urine orange and should be taken with food.
  • Drink about 2 L/day when not restricted, empty the bladder every 3 to 4 hr and with urgency, urinate before/after intercourse, bathe daily, and wipe front to back.
  • Avoid bubble baths, perfumed feminine products, wet bathing suits, pantyhose with slacks, tight clothing, and synthetic underwear that traps moisture.

Pyelonephritis

Ascending kidney infection

Acute vs chronic

  • Pyelonephritis is infection/inflammation of the kidney pelvis, calyces, and medulla; organisms usually ascend from the lower urinary tract.
  • Acute pyelonephritis is an active bacterial infection that can cause interstitial inflammation, tubular cell necrosis, abscess formation, and temporary kidney-function change.
  • Chronic pyelonephritis results from repeated infections, progressive inflammation, scarring, calyx thickening, fibrosis, and permanent renal tissue damage.
  • Risk factors include older age with prostate problems, chronic stones, spinal cord injury with reflux, pregnancy, congenital malformations, bladder tumors, chronic illness, alkaline urine, incomplete emptying, and older-adult thermoregulation changes.

Findings and testing

  • Assess for chills, colicky abdominal pain, nausea, malaise, fatigue, burning/urgency/frequency, costovertebral angle tenderness, flank/back pain, nocturia, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, vomiting, and bacteremia.
  • Chronic pyelonephritis can impair urine concentration and sodium conservation.
  • Labs include urinalysis/culture, WBC/differential, blood cultures when systemic infection is suspected, serum creatinine, BUN, C-reactive protein, and ESR.
  • Imaging can include KUB, ultrasound, gallium scan, and IV pyelogram to evaluate calculi, obstruction, infection, inflammation, or structural/vascular problems.

Nursing care and medications

  • Monitor nutrition, intake/output, fluid/electrolyte balance, temperature, and pain onset, quality, duration, and severity.
  • Increase fluid intake to about 2 L/day when not contraindicated, give antipyretics and analgesics as prescribed, support hygiene and rest/activity balance, and provide emotional support.
  • Mild to moderate pyelonephritis can be treated at home with prescribed oral anti-infectives; severe pyelonephritis can require hospitalization and IV antibiotics for initial stabilization.
  • For surgical care, assess dressings/incision, teach infection monitoring, and support nutrition and fluid intake.

Procedures and complications

  • Procedures can include pyelolithotomy for a large infected obstructing stone, nephrectomy when infection cannot be cleared, or ureteroplasty to repair/revise the ureter and preserve kidney function.
  • Teach clients to maintain nutrition, drink about 2 L/day unless restricted, report acute pain or fever, express fears, rest as needed, and follow up as directed.
  • Complications include septic shock from bloodstream spread, CKD from inflammation/fibrosis/scarring and filtration damage, and hypertension from fluid/sodium retention.

Glomerulonephritis

Immune-mediated glomerular injury

Assessment cues

  • Glomerulonephritis can begin in the kidneys or follow another health disorder such as lupus or diabetic nephropathy.
  • Acute glomerulonephritis often follows infection; chronic glomerulonephritis develops over decades and can progress to ESKD.
  • Risk cues include recent skin or upper-respiratory infection, bacterial/viral/fungal/parasitic exposure, systemic disease, recent surgery, or illness.
  • Expected findings include anorexia, nausea, dysuria, oliguria, fatigue, hypertension, difficulty breathing, crackles, S3 heart sound, weight gain, and reddish-brown or cola-colored urine.
  • Older adults can show circulatory-overload findings that resemble heart failure.

Monitoring and care

  • Labs can show RBCs and protein in urine, decreased GFR, elevated BUN/creatinine, elevated antistreptolysin O after streptococcal infection, decreased C3 complement, cryoglobulins, ANA presence, and electrolyte changes including hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia.
  • Kidney biopsy can confirm the diagnosis, determine prognosis, and guide treatment.
  • Coordinate care to conserve energy, determine fluid restrictions with the provider, administer antibiotics and antihypertensives as prescribed, monitor blood pressure, respiratory status, fluids, and electrolytes.
  • Collaborate on potassium/protein restriction when indicated and prepare for dialysis or plasmapheresis if needed.
  • Teach full antibiotic-course completion, daily weights with reporting of increases, adherence to diet/fluid restrictions, and infection-control practices such as hand hygiene.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Chronic Pyelonephritis Teaching

ATI-supported ALS

Alteration and complications

  • Chronic pyelonephritis is repeated infection and inflammation of the kidney pelvis, calyces, and medulla, usually from bacteria ascending from a lower UTI.
  • Septic shock can occur when microorganisms from the infected kidney enter the bloodstream.
  • CKD can develop from inflammation, fibrosis, scarring, and damage to the kidney filtration structures.
  • Hypertension can signal CKD from fluid/sodium retention after filtration-system destruction.

Teaching points

  • Drink at least 2 L of fluid daily unless restricted.
  • Take all medications as prescribed.
  • Notify the provider of acute, rapid onset of pain.
  • Discuss fears and anxiety, and balance rest with activity.

Application Exercises

1

Which actions should the nurse include for a client who has chronic pyelonephritis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Refer the client for nutrition counseling.
  • B. Encourage fluid intake of only 1 L/day.
  • C. Gently palpate the costovertebral angle.
  • D. Monitor urinary output.
  • E. Administer prescribed antibiotics.
A, C, D, E Nutrition supports healing, CVA tenderness can indicate kidney inflammation/infection, output shows renal response, and antibiotics treat bacteriuria and reduce progressive kidney damage.
B When not contraindicated, teaching supports about 2 L/day to maintain dilute urine.
2

A client has a UTI. Which intervention has priority?

  • A. Offer a warm sitz bath.
  • B. Recommend cranberry juice for prevention.
  • C. Encourage increased fluids when allowed.
  • D. Administer the prescribed antibiotic.
D Antibiotics are the priority because the greatest risk is renal injury and sepsis from untreated infection.
A, B, C These can support comfort or prevention, but they do not treat the active infection first.
3

Which teaching should the nurse include for a female client who has frequent UTIs? Select all that apply.

  • A. Avoid sitting in a wet bathing suit.
  • B. Wipe from back to front after elimination.
  • C. Empty the bladder when there is an urge to void.
  • D. Wear synthetic-fabric underwear.
  • E. Take a shower daily.
A, C, E Avoiding wet bathing suits, voiding with urgency, and showering daily reduce bacterial growth and urinary stasis.
B, D Wipe front to back, and choose cotton underwear that absorbs moisture.
4

Which clients are at risk for developing pyelonephritis? Select all that apply.

  • A. A client who is 32 weeks pregnant.
  • B. A client who has kidney calculi.
  • C. A client who has urine pH 4.2.
  • D. A client who has neurogenic bladder.
  • E. A client who has diabetes mellitus.
A, B, D, E Pregnancy can promote reflux/retention, stones harbor bacteria, neurogenic bladder causes retention, and diabetes can promote bacterial growth when glucose is present in urine.
C Alkaline urine promotes bacterial growth; pH 4.2 is acidic.
5

Which urinalysis result supports a urinary tract infection?

  • A. Positive hyaline casts.
  • B. Positive leukocyte esterase.
  • C. Positive ketones.
  • D. Positive crystals.
B Positive leukocyte esterase supports UTI.
A, C, D Hyaline casts can occur with proteinuria or after exercise, ketones suggest starvation or poor diabetes control, and crystals suggest stone risk.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 61

Renal Calculi

Renal calculi questions usually hinge on pain pattern, obstruction, infection, urine straining, procedure teaching, medication safety, and stone-specific recurrence prevention.

TL;DR · Pain, Passage, and Obstruction

Renal colic is severe and wave-like as a stone moves. Strain all urine, save the stone, promote fluids/ambulation if not contraindicated, treat pain and spasms safely, and report anuria or obstruction immediately because kidney damage can become permanent.

Assessment cues

  • Most stones are calcium phosphate or calcium oxalate; other types include uric acid, struvite, and cystine.
  • Flank pain suggests kidney or ureter location; flank pain radiating to the abdomen, scrotum, testes, or vulva suggests ureter or bladder involvement.
  • Frequency or dysuria can occur with bladder stones; fever, diaphoresis, pallor, nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, tachypnea, blood pressure changes, oliguria/anuria, and hematuria can occur.

Priority cues

  • Obstruction with diminished or absent urine output is a medical emergency; notify the provider and prepare for calculus removal.
  • ESWL breaks calculi into fragments; teach moderate sedation, expected bruising/hematuria, and urine straining after the procedure.
  • Prevention is stone-specific: calcium oxalate means avoid oxalate sources such as black tea and spinach; calcium phosphate means limit animal protein and sodium.

Core Concepts

Assessment and Diagnostics

ATI source-authored

Risk and location

  • Urolithiasis means stones are present in the urinary tract; many stones pass without invasive procedures depending on composition, size, and location.
  • Recurrence risk rises with family history or first stone before age 25.
  • Risk factors include male sex, damaged urinary tract lining, concentrated or particle-containing urine, metabolic defects, high urine alkalinity or acidity, urinary stasis/retention, immobilization, dehydration, decreased fluid intake, and older-adult dehydration risk.
  • Nephrolithiasis forms in the kidney and commonly causes acute costovertebral pain; ureterolithiasis forms in the ureter and often causes wave-like excruciating pain.

Findings and tests

  • Assess severe renal colic, flank pain, radiating pain, urinary frequency, dysuria, fever, diaphoresis, pallor, nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, tachypnea, pain-related hypertension, shock-related hypotension, oliguria/anuria, and rusty/smoky hematuria.
  • Urinalysis evaluates pH, specific gravity, osmolarity, odor/turbidity, RBCs, WBCs, bacteria, crystals, calcium, phosphate, and uric acid.
  • Decreased urine pH supports uric acid or cystine stones; increased pH supports calcium or struvite stones.
  • KUB or IVP can locate calculi, but IVP is contraindicated if urinary obstruction is present.
  • Noncontrast helical CT or MRI can identify cystine or uric acid stones that standard x-rays can miss; renal ultrasound or cystoscopy can confirm the diagnosis.

Nursing Care and Medication Safety

Pain and passage

Core nursing care

  • Report lab and diagnostic findings, provide pre/postprocedure care, administer prescribed medications, and strain all urine to check for stone passage.
  • Save passed stones for laboratory analysis.
  • Encourage oral intake up to 3 L/day unless contraindicated, administer IV fluids as prescribed, and encourage ambulation to promote passage.
  • Hot baths and moist heat can promote comfort.
  • Closely monitor clients attempting spontaneous passage, especially when stones are small enough to pass without intervention.
  • Assess pain, intake/output, and urinary pH.

Medication cautions

  • Morphine can be used early for moderate to severe acute stone pain; monitor sedation, hypotension, and respiratory depression, especially in older adults or clients with asthma/emphysema.
  • Ketorolac can treat mild to moderate pain, fever, and inflammation, but monitor bleeding and renal function/perfusion risk.
  • Oxybutynin decreases bladder spasms; check glaucoma history and monitor dizziness, tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation, nausea, and voiding problems.
  • Gentamicin and cephalexin can treat UTIs; give with food if directed, and monitor gentamicin for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
  • Thiazides and allopurinol can support prevention depending on stone type and provider plan.

Procedures and Complications

Obstruction watch

Procedures

  • Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy uses sound, laser, or shock-wave energy to break stones into fragments; moderate sedation and ECG monitoring are used.
  • After ESWL, strain all urine, monitor the site, and teach that bruising at the wave site and hematuria can be expected.
  • Nonsurgical chemolysis uses chemical agents to dissolve the calculus.
  • Stenting can dilate the ureter and help stone passage during ureteroscopy; retrograde ureteroscopy uses a basket, forceps, or loop to remove the stone.
  • Percutaneous ureterolithotomy/nephrolithotomy uses an ultrasonic or laser lithotripter with basket/forceps extraction; open surgery is reserved for large, impacted, or refractory stones.

Complications

  • Urosepsis can occur with struvite stones when UTI spreads to the bloodstream; monitor infection cues, culture/sensitivity results, WBC elevation, shock, urine turbidity/odor, fever, tachycardia, and dysuria.
  • Obstruction can block urine flow into the kidney, ureter, or bladder; diminished or absent urine output requires immediate provider notification and preparation for removal.
  • Hydroureter can occur when urine flow is blocked and the ureter enlarges.
  • Hydronephrosis occurs when backed-up urine distends the kidney and can cause permanent kidney damage.
  • Antibiotics can be used prophylactically before invasive treatment or to treat existing infection.

Stone-Specific Prevention

Diet and recurrence

Calcium and struvite patterns

  • For calcium phosphate stones, limit animal protein and sodium; calcium restriction is individualized.
  • Thiazide diuretics can increase calcium reabsorption, orthophosphates can decrease urine calcium oxalate saturation, and sodium cellulose phosphate can reduce intestinal calcium absorption.
  • For calcium oxalate stones, avoid oxalate sources such as spinach, black tea, rhubarb, cocoa, beets, pecans, strawberries, peanuts, okra, chocolate, wheat germ, lime peel, and Swiss chard; also limit sodium.
  • For struvite stones, avoid high-phosphate foods such as dairy products, red/organ meats, and whole grains.

Uric acid and cystine patterns

  • For uric acid stones, decrease purine sources such as organ meats, poultry, fish, gravies, red wine, and sardines.
  • Lemon or orange juice can help alkalinize urine when recommended.
  • Allopurinol can help prevent uric acid stone formation; potassium citrate, sodium citrate, or sodium bicarbonate can alkalinize urine.
  • For cystine stones, limit animal protein; alpha mercaptopropionylglycine and captopril can lower urine cystine.
  • Teach adherence to prescribed diet and medications to prevent recurrence.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Morphine and Oxybutynin for Renal Calculi

ATI-supported ALS

Therapeutic uses and complications

  • Morphine treats moderate to severe pain during the early acute renal calculi period.
  • Oxybutynin reduces bladder spasms that can occur with renal calculi.
  • Morphine complications include respiratory depression, euphoria, sedation, and decreased GI motility.
  • Oxybutynin complications include dizziness, tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation, and nausea.

Nursing interventions

  • Use morphine cautiously with asthma or emphysema and monitor respirations, sedation, blood pressure, and constipation prevention.
  • If respirations are 12/min or less after morphine, stop the medication and notify the provider immediately.
  • Before oxybutynin, check for glaucoma history because intraocular pressure can increase.
  • With oxybutynin, monitor dizziness, tachycardia, and urinary retention; teach clients to report palpitations, voiding problems, or constipation.
  • Teach dry-mouth measures such as hard candy, oral hygiene, and increased dietary fiber/bulk as appropriate.

Application Exercises

1

Which finding should the nurse expect during admission assessment of a client who has renal calculi?

  • A. Bradycardia.
  • B. Diaphoresis.
  • C. Nocturia.
  • D. Bradypnea.
B Diaphoresis can occur with renal calculi and severe pain.
A, C, D Tachycardia, oliguria, and tachypnea are more consistent expected findings than bradycardia, nocturia, or bradypnea.
2

Which discharge instructions fit spontaneous passage of a calcium phosphate renal calculus? Select all that apply.

  • A. Limit foods high in animal protein.
  • B. Reduce sodium intake.
  • C. Continue straining urine for 48 hr after the calculus has passed.
  • D. Report burning with urination.
  • E. Increase fluid intake to 2 to 3 L/day unless restricted.
A, B, D, E Calcium phosphate recurrence prevention includes limiting animal protein and sodium, reporting UTI cues, and maintaining adequate fluid intake if not restricted.
C Once the calculus has passed, continued urine straining is not needed for that passed stone.
3

Which statement shows understanding of ESWL teaching?

  • A. "I will be fully awake during the procedure."
  • B. "Lithotripsy will prevent future stones."
  • C. "I should report any bruising at the wave site."
  • D. "I need to strain my urine after the procedure."
D Urine is strained after lithotripsy to verify passage of stone fragments.
A, B, C Moderate sedation is used, lithotripsy breaks stones but does not prevent recurrence, and bruising can be expected.
4

A client has a left renal calculus and an indwelling urinary catheter. Which finding is the priority to report?

  • A. Flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen.
  • B. Nausea.
  • C. Absent urine output for 1 hr.
  • D. WBC count 15,000/mm3.
C Anuria can indicate obstruction of urine flow and places kidney function at greatest risk.
A, B, D These are relevant findings, but obstruction with absent urine output is the priority escalation.
5

Which foods should a client who passed a calcium oxalate calculus avoid to reduce recurrence risk? Select all that apply.

  • A. Red meat.
  • B. Black tea.
  • C. Cheese.
  • D. Whole grains.
  • E. Spinach.
B, E Black tea and spinach are oxalate sources and should be avoided with calcium oxalate stones.
A, C, D Animal protein is limited for calcium phosphate, struvite, uric acid, or cystine patterns; dairy and whole grains are more relevant to other stone-type restrictions.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 62

Diagnostic and Therapeutic Procedures for Female Reproductive Disorders

Female reproductive procedure questions often test preparation details, specimen handling, expected discomfort or spotting, restrictions after biopsy, STI test interpretation, mammography teaching, and hysterectomy complication surveillance.

TL;DR · Prep, Pads, and Reportable Bleeding

Empty the bladder before pelvic procedures, support the client during specimen collection, expect mild discomfort or small spotting after many tests, and escalate heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain, foul drainage, low urine output, or hysterectomy shock/thrombosis cues.

Screening and biopsy logic

  • Pap testing identifies precancerous or cancerous cervical cells; HPV testing identifies HPV infections that can lead to cervical cancer.
  • Colposcopy and cervical biopsy follow atypical or abnormal Pap results and can cause temporary discomfort, cramping, and some bleeding.
  • After cervical biopsy, rest briefly, avoid intercourse, douching, vaginal creams, tampons, and heavy lifting until healing/discharge resolves as instructed.

Procedure safety logic

  • For mammography, avoid deodorant, lotion, or powder on the breasts/axilla because residue can alter imaging.
  • Hysterosalpingography uses contrast to view the cervix, uterus, and fallopian tubes; confirm last menstrual period and assess iodine allergy.
  • After hysterectomy, monitor bleeding, vital signs, breath/bowel sounds, urine output, incision, Hgb/Hct, thrombosis cues, infection, and psychological response.

Core Concepts

Pelvic Exam, Pap/HPV, Colposcopy, and Biopsy

ATI source-authored

Pelvic exam with Pap/HPV

  • Prepare by having the client empty the bladder, placing the client in lithotomy position, draping appropriately, explaining the procedure, and having specimen equipment ready.
  • Schedule Pap testing when the client is not menstruating; vaginal medications, douching, or intercourse within 24 hr can alter results.
  • During the procedure, remain with the client, provide support, transfer specimens to slides, and apply fixative when needed.
  • Afterward, provide perineal pads/tissues, teach that minimal cervical bleeding can occur, and reinforce follow-up for abnormal results.

Colposcopy and cervical biopsy

  • Colposcopy examines vaginal and cervical tissue with magnification; biopsy can follow abnormal Pap findings.
  • Endocervical curettage, cone biopsy, cryosurgery, laser, or LEEP can be used depending on the lesion and treatment goal.
  • Provide psychological support, prepare similarly to Pap testing, and have a sterile biopsy container ready.
  • Teach that tissue collection can cause temporary discomfort and cramping.
  • After cervical biopsy, provide pads/tissues, teach rest for the first 24 hr, avoid intercourse/douching/vaginal creams/tampons until discharge stops, avoid heavy lifting for about 2 weeks, avoid aspirin if bleeding risk is a concern, and report excessive bleeding, fever, or foul-smelling drainage.

Endometrial Biopsy, STI Testing, and Imaging

Diagnostics and teaching

Endometrial biopsy and STI tests

  • Endometrial biopsy samples endometrial tissue to evaluate uterine cancer, menstrual irregularities, infertility causes, and abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding.
  • Before endometrial biopsy, obtain menstrual history, give analgesic as prescribed, prepare as for pelvic exam, witness consent, teach that the client is awake, and encourage bladder emptying and relaxation.
  • After endometrial biopsy, allow rest until cramping decreases; spotting can occur for 1 to 2 days, results can be available in about 72 hr, and intercourse/douching/vaginal creams/tampons are avoided until discharge stops.
  • Syphilis screening can use VDRL or RPR; reactive screening is confirmed with treponemal testing such as FTA-ABS or microhemagglutination assay.
  • HIV screening uses EIA, which can become positive weeks to months after infection; a positive EIA is confirmed with Western blot assay.
  • Genital herpes confirmation can use viral culture, PCR testing, or antibody testing.

Mammography, ultrasound, and HSG

  • Screening mammography detects breast lesions before symptoms; diagnostic mammography follows abnormal screening findings or breast cancer manifestations.
  • Before mammography, avoid deodorant, lotion, or powder on the breast/axillary area and avoid mammography if pregnant unless directed by the provider.
  • Teach that breast compression can cause brief discomfort, and reinforce regular breast inspection and provider-directed follow-up timing.
  • Ultrasound can assess masses, cysts, fibroids, treatment effects, or mammography lesions; transvaginal ultrasound requires an empty bladder, while abdominal ultrasound can require a full bladder.
  • Hysterosalpingography visualizes the cervix, uterus, and fallopian tubes with contrast and is performed shortly after menstruation to avoid harm to an existing pregnancy.
  • Before hysterosalpingography, confirm last menstrual cycle date, assess iodine allergy, witness consent, and prepare as for pelvic exam; after, teach minimal bleeding, prescribed analgesics for cramping, possible shoulder referred pain, and reporting prolonged bleeding or infection signs.

Hysterectomy

Therapeutic procedure

Types and indications

  • Total hysterectomy removes uterus and cervix; subtotal removes uterus only; bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy removes ovaries and fallopian tubes.
  • Panhysterectomy removes uterus, cervix, ovaries, and fallopian tubes; radical hysterectomy removes uterus, cervix, upper vagina, and adjacent tissue including lymph nodes.
  • Approaches include abdominal, vaginal, and laparoscopy-assisted vaginal hysterectomy.
  • Indications include uterine cancer and noncancerous conditions such as fibroids, endometriosis, and genital prolapse that cause pain, bleeding, or emotional stress.
  • Presenting cues can include painful intercourse, heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, urinary urgency/frequency, and constipation.

Preprocedure priorities

  • Ensure anticoagulants, aspirin, NSAIDs, or vitamin E have been discontinued as prescribed.
  • Rule out pregnancy, administer preoperative antibiotics, place anti-embolism stockings, maintain NPO status, and verify informed consent.
  • Complete psychological assessment and teach turning, coughing, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and medication expectations.
  • After surgery, an indwelling urinary catheter is usually placed intraoperatively and remains initially postoperatively.

Postprocedure monitoring

  • Monitor vaginal bleeding; excessive bleeding is more than one saturated perineal pad in 4 hr.
  • Priority assessments include vital signs, breath sounds, bowel sounds, urine output, incision integrity/infection/dehiscence, Hgb/Hct, and signs of thrombophlebitis.
  • Report urine output below 30 mL/hr.
  • Use thromboembolism precautions, including sequential compression devices and ambulation as prescribed.
  • Provide IV fluid/electrolyte replacement until bowel sounds return.

Teaching and complications

  • Teach high-protein/high-vitamin C intake for wound healing and iron-rich intake if anemic.
  • If ovaries are removed, menopausal manifestations can develop and hormone therapy considerations might be discussed with the provider.
  • Restrict heavy lifting, strenuous activity, driving, stairs, and sexual activity as prescribed; avoid tampons.
  • Report fever, foul-smelling drainage, incision pain/redness, calf swelling, or burning with urination.
  • Monitor for hypovolemic shock, infection, and psychological responses; support groups can help with coping after surgery.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Total Abdominal Hysterectomy

ATI-supported ALS

Preprocedure nursing actions

  • Maintain NPO status and ensure informed consent is complete.
  • Rule out pregnancy.
  • Confirm prescribed discontinuation of anticoagulants, aspirin, NSAIDs, or vitamin E.
  • Administer preoperative antibiotics and place anti-embolism stockings as prescribed.
  • Teach turning, coughing, deep breathing, incentive spirometer use, early ambulation, and medication expectations.
  • Complete psychological assessment.

Postprocedure nursing actions

  • Monitor vaginal bleeding; more than one saturated pad in 4 hr is excessive.
  • Maintain the indwelling urinary catheter and monitor urine output; expected output is at least 30 mL/hr.
  • Monitor vital signs, breath sounds, bowel sounds, Hgb/Hct, incision status, and thrombosis cues.
  • Assist with ambulation and use thromboembolism precautions.
  • Provide IV fluid and electrolyte replacement until bowel sounds return.
  • Teach wound-healing diet, activity restrictions, tampon avoidance, reportable infection/bleeding/thrombosis/urinary cues, and hormone-therapy considerations if ovaries were removed.

Application Exercises

1

Which information should the nurse include when teaching a new employee about HIV testing?

  • A. EIA is typically reactive within 72 hr after infection.
  • B. Western blot assay is used to confirm HIV diagnosis after a positive screening result.
  • C. PCR testing confirms HIV diagnosis.
  • D. CD4+ counts are elevated in HIV infection.
B HIV confirmation is a two-step process in this source pattern: positive EIA screening is confirmed with Western blot assay.
A, C, D EIA reactivity can take weeks to months, PCR is listed for herpes confirmation, and CD4+ counts decrease rather than elevate with HIV progression.
2

Which instruction should the nurse give before an initial mammogram?

  • A. Avoid aspirin products before the mammogram.
  • B. Do not apply deodorant the day of the exam.
  • C. Avoid sexual intercourse the day before the mammogram.
  • D. Avoid exercise before the exam.
B Deodorant, powders, or lotions can create shadows or interfere with mammography accuracy.
A, C, D These actions do not alter mammogram accuracy in the source teaching.

Which statement should the nurse include before an initial Pap test?

  • A. "You should urinate immediately after the procedure."
  • B. "You will not feel any discomfort."
  • C. "You may have some bleeding after the procedure."
  • D. "You will need to hold your breath during the procedure."
C A small amount of bleeding can occur after cervical scraping.
A, B, D The client empties the bladder before the procedure, can feel discomfort, and should use relaxation/deep breathing rather than breath-holding.
4

A client's RPR is positive. Which test confirms syphilis diagnosis?

  • A. Venereal Disease Research Laboratory.
  • B. D-dimer.
  • C. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed.
  • D. Sickledex.
C FTA-ABS is used to confirm syphilis after a reactive screening test.
A, B, D VDRL is another screening test, D-dimer evaluates fibrin/clotting activity, and sickledex screens for sickle cell disease.
5

Which teaching should the nurse include before cervical biopsy? Select all that apply.

  • A. "The procedure is painless."
  • B. "Avoid heavy lifting for about 2 weeks after the procedure."
  • C. "Heavy bleeding is common during the first 12 hr."
  • D. "Plan to rest for the first 72 hr after the procedure."
  • E. "Avoid tampons until the cervix has healed."
B, E Avoid heavy lifting and tampons until healing; the source timeframe for cervical healing/discharge restrictions is about 2 weeks.
A, C, D Temporary discomfort/cramping can occur, heavy bleeding is a complication, and rest is focused on the first 24 hr rather than 72 hr.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 63

Female Physiologic Processes

Female physiologic-process questions often test normal menstrual timing, when bleeding becomes abnormal, PMS/PMDD treatment patterns, endometriosis infertility risk, menopause lab/assessment cues, and hormone therapy safety.

TL;DR · Cycles, Symptoms, and Estrogen Shift

Know the cycle anchors: menarche averages 12.4 years, typical cycles range 23 to 35 days, day 1 is the first day of bleeding, ovulation is around day 14, and menstruation can last up to 9 days. Escalate excessive bleeding, infertility risk from endometriosis, and hormone therapy thrombotic or cancer warning cues.

Menstrual-process logic

  • Assessment is indicated if menstruation has not begun by 16.5 years.
  • Menorrhagia means excessive amount/duration of menstrual bleeding; metrorrhagia means bleeding between periods.
  • Amenorrhea can indicate pregnancy, thyroid or structural disorders, strenuous activity with low body fat, or anorexia nervosa.

Menopause logic

  • Perimenopause can last about 4 years before menopause and can still involve pregnancy risk.
  • Menopause is complete after 12 months without menses and can be natural or surgically induced.
  • Expected findings include hot flashes, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, mood/sleep changes, decreased bone density, decreased HDL, increased LDL, and increased FSH.

Core Concepts

Menstrual Disorders and Endometriosis

ATI source-authored

Normal timing and abnormal bleeding

  • Average menarche is 12.4 years, with a possible range from 9 to 17 years.
  • Typical menstrual cycles are 28 days, with a normal range of 23 to 35 days; day 1 is the first day of menstruation.
  • Ovulation typically occurs around day 14, and menstruation begins about 14 days after ovulation.
  • Menstruation typically lasts 4 to 6 days but can continue up to 9 days.
  • Dysmenorrhea is painful menstruation and is common in adolescents and young clients.
  • DUB can include menorrhagia and metrorrhagia and is associated with hormonal imbalance.

PMS/PMDD and endometriosis

  • PMS is associated with estrogen/progesterone imbalance; manifestations can vary between clients and cycles.
  • Expected PMS findings include irritability, impaired memory, depression, poor concentration, mood swings, binge eating, breast tenderness, bloating, weight gain, headache, and back pain.
  • PMDD is a severe form of PMS that interferes with daily activities.
  • Endometriosis occurs when endometrial tissue grows outside the uterus into the fallopian tubes, ovaries, or pelvis.
  • Endometrial tissue can block fallopian tubes and cause infertility.

Assessment and diagnostics

  • Assess menstrual history, sexual history, nutritional history, flow characteristics, pain location/characteristics, pelvic tenderness, and metabolic disorders such as thyroid disease.
  • Hgb/Hct can be low from excessive blood loss.
  • CA-125 can be elevated in ovarian cancer, endometriosis, and other conditions.
  • Endometrial biopsy can evaluate the relationship between menstrual flow and hormone cycle and identify pathologic bleeding causes such as uterine cancer.
  • Transvaginal ultrasound can identify fibroids, endometrial abnormalities, or leiomyomas.

Treatments

  • Hormonal contraceptives can decrease PMS, PMDD, dysmenorrhea, DUB, and can be an initial endometriosis treatment.
  • Spironolactone can reduce bloating and weight gain with PMS/PMDD.
  • Leuprolide lowers FSH/LH, suppresses estrogen/testosterone, can treat DUB and endometriosis, and requires reliable contraception due to birth-defect risk.
  • NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can relieve pain/discomfort and inhibit prostaglandins.
  • Iron treats anemia associated with DUB; SSRIs such as fluoxetine and sertraline treat emotional and physical PMS/PMDD manifestations.
  • D&C, endometrial ablation, hysterectomy, or laparoscopic removal of ectopic tissue/adhesions can be used when indicated.

Perimenopause and Menopause

Estrogen decline and risk prevention

Perimenopause

  • Perimenopause is approximately the 4 years before menopause, when ovarian function declines and cycles can become anovulatory.
  • Irregular bleeding can include spotting for 2 to 3 days followed by 1 to 2 days of heavy bleeding.
  • Genitourinary findings can include vaginal/urethral atrophy, dryness, vaginitis, dyspareunia, and postcoital bleeding.
  • Vasomotor findings include hot flashes/flushes, irregular menses, night sweats, dizziness, numbness/tingling, and headaches.
  • Sleep loss, fatigue, depression, and reduced emotional control can occur.
  • Pregnancy can still occur during perimenopause, so contraception is needed if pregnancy is not desired.

Menopause findings

  • Menopause is cessation of menses and is complete when no menses occur for 12 months.
  • Expected findings include hot flashes, irregular menses, atrophic vaginitis, decreased vaginal secretions, dyspareunia, incontinence, mood swings, sleep changes, decreased REM sleep, decreased bone density, decreased skin elasticity, hair loss, and breast tissue changes.
  • Cardiovascular changes include decreased HDL and increased LDL.
  • FSH increases during menopause; hormone levels can also be evaluated in blood, urine, or saliva.
  • Diagnostics can include pelvic exam/Pap for abnormal bleeding, breast exam/mammogram for breast changes, uterine lining biopsy for unexplained bleeding after age 40 or postmenopausal bleeding, and DXA to assess osteoporosis risk.

Hormone Therapy and Complication Prevention

Risk-benefit teaching

HT teaching

  • HT can reduce hot flashes, prevent vaginal tissue atrophy, and reduce fracture risk from osteoporosis.
  • Clients with a uterus receive estrogen plus progestin; clients without a uterus can receive estrogen alone.
  • HT can be oral, transdermal, intravaginal, or intramuscular and can be continuous combined or cyclic.
  • Use the shortest appropriate duration when HT is needed, based on provider risk-benefit discussion.
  • Risks include coronary heart disease, MI, DVT, stroke, breast cancer, and possible ovarian/endometrial cancer patterns with some long-term regimens.
  • Stop smoking, learn self-administration, and report unilateral leg pain, edema, warmth, or redness.

Risk reduction

  • Avoid restrictive knee-high stockings, tight socks/clothing, and prolonged sitting; walk, do ankle pumps, and move/stretch legs to promote circulation.
  • Female MI manifestations can include dyspnea, jaw discomfort, indigestion, and pain between the shoulders; seek help immediately.
  • For oral HT nausea, taking medication with food can help.
  • For vaginal estrogen creams/suppositories, avoid insertion before intercourse to reduce partner exposure.
  • Ask about complementary therapies such as black cohosh, ginseng, red clover, phytoestrogens, vitamin E, or vitamin B6 because evidence varies and interactions are possible.
  • Reduce osteoporosis risk with weight-bearing exercise, high-protein/high-calcium intake, alcohol/caffeine/tobacco avoidance, and calcium with vitamin D supplements as recommended.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - PMS Manifestation Journal

ATI-supported ALS

Why journal symptoms

  • PMS/PMDD manifestations begin a few days before menstruation and end a few days after menstruation begins.
  • Journaling helps connect symptoms to the menstrual cycle and supports diagnosis.
  • Patterns can vary from one cycle to the next, so repeated tracking matters.

Expected findings to track

  • Irritability, impaired memory, depression, poor concentration, and mood swings.
  • Binge eating, breast tenderness, bloating, and weight gain.
  • Headache and back pain.

Application Exercises

1

Which menstruation teaching should the school nurse include? Select all that apply.

  • A. Average onset of menstruation is age 10.
  • B. A typical cycle range is 23 to 35 days.
  • C. The first day of the cycle is the last day of the period.
  • D. Ovulation typically occurs around day 14.
  • E. A menstrual period can last as long as 9 days.
B, D, E A normal cycle can range from 23 to 35 days, ovulation is often around day 14, and menses can continue up to 9 days.
A, C Average menarche is 12.4 years, and day 1 is the first day of bleeding.
2

Which medications can be used to treat PMS? Select all that apply.

  • A. Fluoxetine.
  • B. Spironolactone.
  • C. Ethinyl estradiol/drospirenone.
  • D. Ferrous sulfate.
  • E. Methylergonovine.
A, B, C SSRIs, spironolactone, and oral contraceptives can reduce emotional and physical PMS manifestations.
D, E Iron treats anemia related to DUB, and methylergonovine is used for postpartum hemorrhage.
3

Which statements show understanding of dysfunctional uterine bleeding? Select all that apply.

  • A. "My heavy bleeding can be due to a hormonal imbalance."
  • B. "If I have menstrual pain, I should take aspirin."
  • C. "Oral contraceptives are contraindicated for heavy uterine bleeding."
  • D. "A D&C can help identify what is causing abnormal bleeding."
  • E. "This condition is more common in clients in their 30s."
A, D DUB is linked with hormonal imbalance, and D&C can collect endometrial tissue for evaluation.
B, C, E Avoid aspirin because it can increase bleeding, contraceptives can be prescribed for DUB, and DUB is more common near menopause or in adolescence.
4

Which complication can occur with endometriosis?

  • A. Insulin resistance.
  • B. Infertility.
  • C. Vaginitis.
  • D. Pelvic inflammatory disease.
B Endometrial tissue can block the fallopian tubes, causing infertility.
A, C, D Insulin resistance is associated with PCOS, vaginitis is usually infectious, and PID is infection of pelvic organs.
5

Which findings should the nurse expect in a menopausal client? Select all that apply.

  • A. Increased vaginal secretions.
  • B. Decreased bone density.
  • C. Increased HDL.
  • D. Decreased skin elasticity.
  • E. Increased pubic hair growth.
  • F. Decreased FSH.
B, D Menopause is associated with decreased bone density and decreased skin elasticity.
A, C, E, F Vaginal secretions decrease, HDL decreases while LDL increases, pubic/head hair can decrease, and FSH increases.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 64

Disorders of Female Reproductive Tissue

Female reproductive tissue questions often test which structure is protruding, whether the client needs pessary/Kegel or surgical teaching, what to report after repair, and how fibrocystic breast condition differs from cancer warning cues.

TL;DR · Prolapse, Pessary, and Benign Breast Lumps

Separate cystocele from rectocele by the symptoms: cystocele points to urinary stasis, urgency, stress incontinence, and frequent UTIs; rectocele points to constipation, rectal pressure, fecal incontinence, and needing vaginal pressure to evacuate stool. Teach pessary care, Kegel technique, postoperative restrictions, infection reporting, and that fibrocystic breast condition is benign and does not increase breast cancer risk.

Prolapse logic

  • Cystocele is bladder protrusion through the anterior vaginal wall; rectocele is rectal wall protrusion through the posterior vaginal wall.
  • Risk patterns include aging, postmenopausal estrogen loss, obesity, family history, multiparity, pregnancy pressure, childbirth strain, pelvic-structure defects, and constipation.
  • Pelvic exam with bearing down helps confirm anterior or posterior wall bulging.

Care priorities

  • Pessary clients need fit checks, cleaning teaching, latex-allergy screening if rubber is used, and reporting of pain, discomfort, or discharge.
  • Kegels require pelvic contraction, 10-second hold and 10-second relaxation, multiple positions, and relaxed abdominal muscles.
  • Fibrocystic breast condition causes painful rubberlike upper-outer quadrant lumps and can be treated with analgesics, hormonal therapy, or diuretics.

Core Concepts

Pelvic Organ Prolapse: Cystocele and Rectocele

ATI source-authored

Definitions and prevention

  • Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when pelvic floor muscles and ligaments weaken or become damaged.
  • Cystocele involves bladder protrusion through the anterior vaginal wall.
  • Rectocele involves rectal protrusion through the posterior vaginal wall.
  • Uterine prolapse is another form of pelvic organ prolapse.
  • Health promotion includes weight loss when obesity is present, high-fiber intake, and adequate fluids to prevent constipation and chronic bearing down.

Risk factors

  • Cystocele and rectocele are more likely in older adult female clients, especially after menopause.
  • Cystocele risk factors include obesity, advanced age with estrogen loss, family history, multiparity, pregnancy-related abdominal pressure, and vaginal-birth strain or injury.
  • Rectocele risk factors include pelvic-structure defects, obesity, aging, constipation, family history, and difficult vaginal childbirth that required tear repair.
  • Chronic constipation can worsen displacement because repeated bearing down stresses weakened pelvic structures.

Cystocele cues

  • Urinary frequency, urgency, stress incontinence, and frequent urinary tract infections can occur from urinary stasis.
  • Clients can report vaginal fullness, dyspareunia, fatigue, back pain, or pelvic pain.
  • Pelvic examination can show anterior vaginal wall bulging when the client bears down.
  • Bladder ultrasound can measure residual urine; urine culture and sensitivity can evaluate UTI; cystography or x-ray can help define the degree of protrusion.

Rectocele cues

  • Constipation and the need to press inside the vagina to complete stool evacuation point toward rectocele.
  • Expected findings include a vaginal mass sensation, pelvic or rectal pressure/pain, dyspareunia, fecal incontinence, uncontrollable flatus, and hemorrhoids.
  • Pelvic examination can show posterior vaginal wall bulging with bearing down.
  • Rectal examination can confirm the presence of a rectocele.

Prolapse Treatment and Postoperative Safety

Pessary, Kegels, and repair

Nonoperative care

  • Intravaginal estrogen can be used after menopause to reduce pelvic muscle atrophy.
  • Bladder training supports continence when urinary symptoms are present.
  • A vaginal pessary is a removable rubber, plastic, or silicone device that supports pelvic structures and blocks organ protrusion.
  • Teach pessary insertion, removal, and cleaning; verify latex allergy status if a rubber pessary is prescribed.
  • Clients need routine provider checks for fit and complications and should report pain, discomfort, or vaginal discharge.

Kegel technique

  • Contract circumvaginal and perirectal muscles as though stopping urine flow or flatus.
  • Gradually increase contraction time to 10 seconds, followed by a 10-second relaxation period.
  • Perform exercises while lying down, sitting, and standing.
  • Complete 30 to 80 contractions daily.
  • Keep abdominal and thigh muscles relaxed during contractions.

Surgical options

  • Transvaginal repair can support pelvic organs using mesh or tape as a sling.
  • Anterior-posterior repair addresses both cystocele and rectocele.
  • Hysterectomy can be performed at the same time as prolapse repair when indicated.
  • Anterior colporrhaphy tightens pelvic muscles to improve bladder support for cystocele.
  • Posterior colporrhaphy tightens pelvic muscles to reduce rectal protrusion into the vaginal canal.

Postoperative teaching

  • Administer prescribed analgesics, antimicrobials, and stool softeners or laxatives.
  • Warm abdominal compresses, frequent sitz baths, and a low-residue diet until bowel function returns can reduce discomfort and strain.
  • Report fever, increased pulse or respirations, foul-smelling or purulent vaginal discharge, or persistent pain.
  • Avoid straining, sneezing/coughing without pelvic support, prolonged sitting/walking/standing, strenuous activity, lifting more than 5 lb, and intercourse for about 6 weeks or as prescribed.
  • Absorbable sutures do not require removal; dyspareunia and mesh/tape-related erosion or serious infection are possible complications.

Fibrocystic Breast Condition

Benign breast tissue changes

Assessment and diagnostics

  • Fibrocystic breast condition is a noncancerous breast condition associated with cyclic hormonal changes.
  • It is more common in younger or premenopausal clients and less common after menopause.
  • Postmenopausal hormone therapy is a risk factor.
  • Expected findings include breast pain and tender, rubberlike palpable lumps, often in the upper outer quadrant.
  • Breast ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration can help confirm the diagnosis; aspiration can also decrease pain from fluid buildup.

Care and medication teaching

  • Teach that fibrocystic breast condition does not increase breast cancer risk.
  • Supportive measures include reducing salt intake before menses, wearing a supportive bra, and applying local heat or cold for temporary pain relief.
  • Encourage the client to follow the provider's plan and journal the effectiveness of interventions.
  • Analgesics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can reduce pain.
  • Oral contraceptives or other hormonal therapy can suppress estrogen/progesterone secretion for severe manifestations, but clients need risk teaching such as liver disease and stroke.
  • Diuretics can reduce breast engorgement.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Fibrocystic Breast Condition

ATI-supported ALS

Therapeutic uses

  • Analgesics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen are used to relieve breast pain.
  • Oral contraceptives or hormonal medication therapy can suppress estrogen/progesterone secretion when manifestations are severe.
  • Diuretics can decrease breast engorgement.

Teaching focus

  • Ask the client to track pain, lump tenderness, and response to medications across cycles.
  • Discuss medication risks before hormonal therapy is started.
  • Keep follow-up appointments for breast evaluation and imaging as prescribed.

Application Exercises

1

Which instructions should the nurse include when teaching Kegel exercises? Select all that apply.

  • A. Perform the exercises about 50 times each day.
  • B. Contract the circumvaginal and perirectal muscles.
  • C. Gradually increase contraction time to 10 seconds.
  • D. Relax for at least 10 seconds after each contraction.
  • E. Practice while lying, sitting, and standing.
  • F. Tighten the abdominal muscles during each contraction.
A, B, C, D, E Kegels are performed 30 to 80 times daily by contracting pelvic muscles, building to a 10-second hold, relaxing 10 seconds, and practicing in multiple positions.
F Abdominal and thigh muscles should remain relaxed during pelvic-floor contractions.
2

Which client statement best supports the indication for an anterior colporrhaphy?

  • A. "I have to press inside my vagina to pass stool."
  • B. "I have pain and bleeding with bowel movements."
  • C. "I keep getting urinary tract infections."
  • D. "I have uncontrollable flatus."
C Anterior colporrhaphy treats cystocele; urinary stasis from cystocele can cause frequent UTIs.
A, B, D Stool pouching, bowel-movement pain/bleeding, and uncontrollable flatus are rectocele cues and align with posterior repair.
3

Which finding is a risk factor for cystocele?

  • A. BMI of 18.
  • B. Nulliparity.
  • C. Chronic constipation.
  • D. Postmenopausal status.
D Postmenopausal status is associated with aging and estrogen loss, which increase cystocele risk.
A, B, C Obesity and multiparity are cystocele risks; constipation is emphasized as a rectocele risk.
4

Which discharge instruction should the nurse give after anterior and posterior colporrhaphy?

  • A. "Avoid bending over for at least 6 weeks."
  • B. "You may lift objects that weigh up to 10 lb."
  • C. "Avoid sexual intercourse for about 6 weeks or as prescribed."
  • D. "Foul-smelling drainage is expected during the first week."
C Intercourse is restricted while the repair heals, commonly about 6 weeks or according to provider instructions.
A, B, D Bending is not the specific restriction, lifting should stay below 5 lb, and foul-smelling drainage can indicate infection.
5

Which assessment finding should the nurse expect with fibrocystic breast condition?

  • A. Palpable rubberlike lump in the upper outer breast quadrant.
  • B. BRCA1 gene mutation.
  • C. Elevated CA-125.
  • D. Peau d'orange dimpling of the breast.
A Fibrocystic breast condition commonly causes painful, rubberlike lumps in the upper outer quadrant.
B, C, D These findings point to other cancer-related concerns rather than benign fibrocystic breast condition.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 65

Diagnostic Procedures for Male Reproductive Disorders

Male reproductive diagnostic questions often test prostate screening order, what an abnormal PSA or DRE means, TRUS latex/enema teaching, and which tests evaluate infection, anemia, erectile dysfunction, or prostate-cancer risk.

TL;DR · PSA First, Then DRE

Draw PSA before the DRE because prostate palpation can raise PSA. A PSA above 4 ng/mL needs follow-up, EPCA-2 at 30 ng/mL or greater strongly suggests prostate cancer, and abnormal DRE findings include a large, hard, irregular, or nodular prostate. TRUS uses sound waves through a rectal probe, can guide biopsy, and is contraindicated with latex allergy.

Screening sequence

  • PSA is a blood test for a protein produced by the prostate gland.
  • Perform PSA before DRE because palpation can irritate the gland and raise PSA.
  • DRE palpates the posterior prostate through the rectal wall to assess size, shape, consistency, and lumps.

Follow-up cues

  • Weak urine stream, urinary retention, or hematuria can indicate BPH or prostate cancer.
  • TRUS is used after elevated PSA or abnormal DRE and can guide needle biopsy.
  • Penile Doppler ultrasonography evaluates penile anatomy and blood flow; avoid erectile-dysfunction medications for 2 days before the test.

Core Concepts

PSA, EPCA-2, and Digital Rectal Exam

ATI source-authored

Purpose and order

  • Diagnostic procedures for male reproductive disorders include PSA, EPCA-2, DRE, Doppler ultrasonography, urinalysis/urine culture, CBC, and TRUS.
  • PSA measures a prostate-produced protein in the bloodstream using a blood sample.
  • PSA is collected before DRE because prostate irritation during palpation can raise PSA.
  • EPCA-2 measures a protein produced only by abnormal prostate cells.
  • DRE is performed in an office or clinic with the client leaning over the table, side-lying, or in lithotomy position.

Risk and screening discussion

  • Prostate changes are common with aging; enlargement can be benign, and prostate cancer is common in male clients.
  • Clients should have an informed provider discussion about screening benefits, risks, and uncertainty.
  • Screening discussion timing is age 50 for average risk, age 45 for high risk, and age 40 for higher risk.
  • Risk discussion includes age greater than 50 years, African American descent, and family history of prostate cancer.
  • Some providers use EPCA-2 instead of biopsy because of its sensitivity, and it can also monitor treatment response.

Interpretation

  • PSA can increase with prostate cancer, prostatitis, BPH, or recent urinary tract infection.
  • For a client younger than 50 years, 2.5 ng/mL is within expected range.
  • A PSA value greater than 4 ng/mL requires additional evaluation.
  • A urinary tract infection can elevate PSA for up to 6 weeks.
  • EPCA-2 at 30 ng/mL or greater is highly suggestive of prostate cancer.

DRE and client presentation

  • DRE evaluates the posterior prostate through the rectal wall for abnormalities in size, shape, consistency, or lumps.
  • Abnormal DRE findings include an abnormally large, hard, irregularly shaped, or nodular prostate.
  • If DRE reveals an abnormality, ultrasonography can localize the lesion and biopsy can confirm findings.
  • As prostate enlargement encroaches on the urethra, clients can have diminished urine flow and urinary retention.
  • Hematuria can also be present and can indicate BPH or prostate cancer.

TRUS, Penile Doppler, and Infection Labs

Diagnostic teaching

Transrectal ultrasound

  • TRUS uses a rectal probe and sound waves to create an image of the prostate gland.
  • The client is placed in a left side-lying position for the procedure.
  • The provider can prescribe an enema before TRUS to improve visualization.
  • TRUS is contraindicated with latex allergy because the rectal probe is covered by a latex sac.
  • TRUS is done for elevated PSA or abnormal DRE; if an irregularity is found, imaging can guide needle biopsy.

Penile Doppler ultrasonography

  • Penile Doppler ultrasonography determines normal penile anatomy and blood flow.
  • It can identify conditions of the penis, including erectile dysfunction.
  • An injection increases penile blood flow and causes an erection so arterial flow can be measured.
  • Position the client supine with the penis in correct anatomical position against the abdomen.
  • Teach the client not to take erectile-dysfunction medications for 2 days before the test.

Infection and anemia evaluation

  • If prostatitis or infection is suspected, expressed prostatic fluid can be sent for culture and sensitivity.
  • Culture and sensitivity identifies the causative bacteria and guides antibiotic selection.
  • CBC can evaluate systemic infection.
  • CBC can also evaluate anemia related to hematuria.

High-yield distinctions

  • TRUS creates an image; biopsy or EPCA-2 is used to diagnose prostate cancer.
  • An enlarged and nodular prostate needs follow-up because it can indicate prostate cancer.
  • Weak urine stream needs follow-up because it can be a BPH manifestation.
  • Nocturia once can be expected in an older adult male; smegma can normally collect beneath the glans.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - PSA and DRE Teaching

ATI-supported ALS

Description of procedure

  • PSA is a blood test for a protein produced by the prostate gland and is collected first.
  • DRE follows PSA because the exam can irritate the prostate and increase PSA.
  • During DRE, the provider palpates the prostate through the rectal wall with a gloved, lubricated finger.

Indications and risk teaching

  • Discuss screening with older adult clients using shared decision-making language about benefits, risks, and uncertainty.
  • Risk factors to include are age greater than 50 years, African American descent, and family history of prostate cancer.
  • Teach that elevated PSA or abnormal DRE findings require follow-up rather than automatic cancer diagnosis.

Application Exercises

1

Which annual physical findings require additional prostate follow-up? Select all that apply.

  • A. PSA is 7.1 ng/mL.
  • B. DRE reveals an enlarged, nodular prostate.
  • C. The client reports a weak urine stream.
  • D. The client reports urinating once at night.
  • E. Smegma is present below the glans penis.
A, B, C PSA greater than 4 ng/mL, an enlarged/nodular prostate, and weak stream require follow-up.
D, E Urinating once at night can be expected in older adult male clients, and smegma can normally accumulate beneath the glans.
2

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client scheduled for TRUS?

  • A. "This procedure will determine whether you have prostate cancer."
  • B. "The procedure is contraindicated if you have an egg allergy."
  • C. "Sound waves will be used to create a picture of your prostate."
  • D. "Avoid having a bowel movement for 1 hour before the procedure."
C TRUS uses sound waves through a rectal probe to image the prostate.
A, B, D Biopsy or EPCA-2 is used for diagnosis, latex allergy is the contraindication, and an enema can be prescribed to reduce stool interference.
