Unit 11 · Integumentary Disorders · Chapter 73

Integumentary Diagnostic Procedures

Integumentary diagnostic testing helps identify skin infection type, lesion behavior, and abnormal tissue characteristics. Nursing priorities center on standard precautions, correct specimen collection, prompt transport, biopsy consent and bleeding control, and targeted client teaching after culture, KOH testing, Tzanck smear, or biopsy.

TL;DR · Collect Clean, Match the Test, Protect the Site

For skin diagnostics, think: use bright light or Wood's light for color changes, diascopy checks blanching, cultures identify the organism and medication sensitivity, Tzanck smear supports viral lesions, KOH supports fungal lesions, and biopsy rules in or out abnormal tissue such as malignancy. Always use standard precautions with nonintact skin, collect before antimicrobials when possible, label and transport specimens promptly, and teach biopsy-site infection/bleeding reporting.

Test matching

  • Wood's light uses ultraviolet light in a darkened room to highlight pigment changes and some skin infections.
  • Diascopy presses a slide or lens on a lesion to see whether it blanches.
  • Skin culture and sensitivity identify the microbe and which antimicrobials are likely effective.

Specimen safety

  • Collect bacterial, viral, or fungal specimens with the correct technique for the suspected organism.
  • Place viral specimens on ice and send them promptly.
  • After biopsy, monitor bleeding, keep the site clean, and report infection cues.

Integumentary Diagnostic Priorities

Visual and Blanching Tests

Wood's light and diascopy

Wood's light

  • Use bright lighting to assess clients who have dark skin tones for changes in underlying red tones or bluish-gray undertones.
  • Use Wood's light for light skin tones or hypopigmented areas when color changes need clearer identification.
  • Darken the room; ultraviolet light helps reveal selected skin infections, pigment changes, and dermal-versus-epidermal patterns.
  • Explain that the test is noninvasive and depends on the room being dark enough for the light pattern to show.

Diascopy

  • Press a glass slide or lens against the lesion to assess blanchability.
  • Inflammatory/vascular lesions blanch; hemorrhagic or nonvascular lesions generally do not.
  • Use the blanching response to help separate erythema from petechiae, purpura, nevus-type lesions, or vascular inflammation.
  • Tell the client the pressure can feel firm but the procedure should not be painful.

Culture, Sensitivity, and Specimen Collection

Collect before antimicrobials

Culture and sensitivity

  • Culture isolates the suspected pathogen; sensitivity testing shows which antimicrobial agents affect it.
  • When possible, collect specimens before starting antimicrobial therapy.
  • Drainage from a purulent skin lesion can be collected for testing when infection is suspected.
  • Preliminary results can become available before the final report; final sensitivity results take longer.

Collection priorities

  • Use standard precautions when collecting or handling all specimens from nonintact skin.
  • For bacterial or viral lesions, lift or puncture the crusted/scabbed area and swab the moist lesion bed with sterile technique.
  • For suspected herpes lesions, collect vesicle fluid from an intact lesion using a cotton-tipped applicator.
  • Place viral specimens on ice immediately and transport them to the laboratory promptly.
  • For fungal specimens, collect enough scales by scraping the skin and placing the specimen in a clean container.

Postcollection Teaching by Infection Type

Prevent spread and treat correctly

Bacterial and viral lesions

  • For bacterial lesions, bathe daily with antibacterial soap and do not squeeze lesions.
  • Remove crusted exudate so topical antibacterial medication can reach the lesion bed.
  • Warm compresses can promote comfort for furuncles or cellulitis when prescribed.
  • Use hand hygiene consistently and avoid sharing personal items.
  • For viral lesions, use prescribed Burow's solution compresses, avoid tight clothing, let the lesion dry between treatments, and avoid lying on the lesion.

Medication anchors

  • Superficial bacterial infections can use topical antibacterial therapy; more extensive cellulitis/lymphatic involvement can require systemic antibiotics.
  • MRSA culture results can require targeted therapy such as vancomycin, linezolid, or clindamycin as prescribed.
  • Topical antivirals can reduce active virus and discomfort from herpetic lesions, but recurrent infections can respond less strongly.
  • Yeast or dermatophyte infections can be treated with topical antifungal cream or powder.
  • Clean and dry the skin before applying topical antifungal medication; clotrimazole is continued for the prescribed period after visible lesions resolve.

Tzanck Smear, KOH Test, and Biopsy

Viral, fungal, tissue diagnosis

Microscopy tests

  • Tzanck smear examines cells from the base of a lesion and supports a viral lesion when multinucleated giant cells are present.
  • Potassium hydroxide testing helps confirm a fungal lesion by showing fungal hyphae in scraped scales.
  • Use test choice to match the suspected source: Tzanck for viral, KOH for fungal, culture/sensitivity for organism and medication guidance.
  • If a deeper fungal infection is suspected or results are inconclusive, a biopsy can be needed.

Biopsy types

  • Biopsy removes tissue for cytology or histology to establish an exact diagnosis or rule out cancer.
  • Punch biopsy removes a small plug of tissue and can require sutures.
  • Shave biopsy removes only the raised portion of a lesion and usually does not require sutures.
  • Excisional biopsy removes a larger, deeper sample and requires suturing.

Biopsy Nursing Care and Discharge Teaching

Consent, bleeding, infection report

Before and during

  • Verify informed consent before biopsy and explain that scarring can occur.
  • Assist with local anesthetic setup and sterile-field preparation.
  • Place the tissue specimen in the appropriate solution, label it accurately, and send it to the laboratory.
  • Apply pressure to control bleeding and cover the biopsy site with a sterile dressing as needed.

Aftercare

  • Monitor the biopsy site for bleeding; mild discomfort is usually managed with mild analgesics.
  • Teach the client to check the site daily and report excessive bleeding, redness, warmth, drainage, or fever.
  • Clean dried blood or crusting as instructed after the initial dressing period.
  • Apply antibacterial topical medication only if prescribed.
  • If sutures are used, return for removal in 7 to 10 days; biopsy results can take several days.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Skin Biopsy Preparation and Safety

ATI-supported ALS

Underlying principles

  • Punch biopsy removes a small plug of tissue and can be closed with or without sutures.
  • Shave biopsy removes the raised portion of a lesion using a blade and usually does not require suturing.
  • Excisional biopsy removes a larger, deeper tissue sample and requires suturing.

Nursing interventions

  • Assist with local anesthetic materials and sterile setup.
  • Prepare the biopsy skin area as directed.
  • Apply pressure to control bleeding after the specimen is obtained.
  • Label the specimen and send it in the correct container or solution.
  • Apply a sterile dressing if needed and teach bleeding/infection reporting.

Application Exercises

1

Which finding best supports that a skin lesion is viral in origin?

  • A. Positive KOH test
  • B. Blanching with diascopy
  • C. Tzanck smear report
  • D. Biopsy report confirming malignancy
C Tzanck smear evaluates cells from the lesion base and supports viral origin when the expected cytology is present.
A, B, D KOH supports fungal lesions, diascopy assesses blanching/vascular behavior, and biopsy evaluates tissue diagnosis such as malignancy.
2

Which actions should the nurse take when collecting a specimen from a suspected herpes lesion? Select all that apply.

  • A. Scrape scales with a wooden tongue depressor.
  • B. Swab vesicle fluid with a cotton-tipped applicator.
  • C. Obtain fluid from an intact lesion when possible.
  • D. Place the viral specimen on ice promptly.
  • E. Place the sample in a KOH solution tube.
B, C, D Herpes testing uses vesicle fluid collected with a cotton-tipped applicator, and the viral specimen is placed on ice and sent promptly.
A, E Scraping scales and KOH preparation are used for suspected fungal lesions, not herpes culture collection.
3

Which home-care instruction is appropriate after culture collection for a bacterial skin infection with cellulitis?

  • A. Use moisturizing soap daily.
  • B. Apply topical medication over crusted exudate.
  • C. Apply warm compresses to the affected area.
  • D. Cover the area with snug clothing.
C Warm compresses can promote comfort for cellulitis or furuncle areas when prescribed.
A, B, D ATI teaching emphasizes antibacterial soap, removing crust so medication can reach the lesion bed, and avoiding tight or occlusive garments.
4

Which statement indicates the client understands discharge teaching after a skin biopsy with sutures?

  • A. "I should report redness, warmth, drainage, or fever."
  • B. "A fever is expected for the first few days."
  • C. "My sutures should be removed in 3 days."
  • D. "Bleeding from the site is expected until the result returns."
A Redness, warmth, drainage, fever, and excessive bleeding should be reported after biopsy.
B, C, D Fever is not expected, sutures are commonly removed in 7 to 10 days, and ongoing bleeding is not an expected finding.
5

Which teaching should the nurse include for clotrimazole topical cream?

  • A. "Use this medication for a herpetic lesion."
  • B. "Apply it to clean, dry skin."
  • C. "Stop applying it as soon as the lesion disappears."
  • D. "Apply it while the skin is moist."
B Topical antifungals are applied to clean, dry skin; clotrimazole is continued for the prescribed period after visible fungal lesions resolve.
A, C, D Clotrimazole is antifungal, not antiviral; it should not be stopped early unless prescribed, and skin should be clean and dry before use.

Unit 11 · Integumentary Disorders · Chapter 74

Skin Disorders

Skin-disorder care in this chapter centers on psoriasis and dermatitis. Priority nursing work includes recognizing lesion patterns, reducing itching and skin breakdown, preventing secondary infection, teaching safe topical/systemic medication use, and protecting clients receiving immunosuppressive or light-based therapies.

TL;DR · Soften Scales, Stop Scratching, Watch the Meds

For psoriasis, think autoimmune-like overproduction of keratin with exacerbations/remissions, silvery scales, possible nail changes, and therapies that slow cell turnover. For dermatitis, think allergen/irritant exposure, itching, poorly defined or exposure-pattern rashes, and infection risk from scratching. Teach no picking/scratching, fragrance-free products, cool moist compresses for dermatitis, emollient/oatmeal comfort measures, steroid safety, no live vaccines with biologics, eye protection with PUVA, and sun/tanning avoidance with pimecrolimus.

Psoriasis anchors

  • Common sites include scalp, elbows, knees, trunk, sacrum, and lateral extremities.
  • Severity can be mild, moderate, or severe based on body surface area involvement.
  • Topical corticosteroids, tar, vitamin D analogs, vitamin A derivatives, cytotoxic medications, biologics, immunosuppressants, and light therapy all carry specific teaching needs.

Dermatitis anchors

  • Nonspecific eczematous, contact, and atopic dermatitis differ by cause and distribution.
  • Avoid identified irritants/allergens, fragrance-containing products, and fabric softener dryer sheets.
  • Use cool damp compresses and colloidal oatmeal baths to reduce inflammation and itching.

Skin Disorder Priorities

Psoriasis Recognition and Severity

Scales, nails, BSA

Pattern

  • Psoriasis is a chronic disorder with rapid keratin production and periods of exacerbation and remission.
  • Risk factors include infection, skin trauma, genetics, stress, seasonal changes, hormone shifts, selected medications, and obesity.
  • Psoriasis vulgaris usually presents with reddened, thickened skin and silvery-white scales in a bilateral distribution.
  • Common findings include scaly patches, pruritic lesions, bleeding when scales are removed, and pitting or crumbling nails.

Severity and variants

  • Mild psoriasis involves less than 5% body surface area; moderate involves 5% to 10%; severe involves more than 10%.
  • Exfoliative psoriasis can cause widespread erythema/scaling and fluid or temperature instability.
  • Palmoplantar pustulosis affects palms and soles with reddened hyperkeratotic plaques and pustules that crust and peel.
  • Some clients develop joint pain or arthritis-type changes with psoriasis.

Psoriasis Topical Medication Safety

Steroids, tar, vitamins D/A

Corticosteroids and tar

  • Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation and cellular proliferation; monitor for thinning, striae, and hypopigmentation with high-potency products.
  • Apply high-potency corticosteroids only as prescribed and use medication vacations when directed.
  • Avoid high-potency corticosteroids on the face or in skin folds because adverse effects are more likely.
  • Occlusive dressings can enhance exposed-lesion steroid effect when recommended, but prolonged or inappropriate occlusion raises risk.
  • Coal tar and other tar preparations can sting, burn, stain skin/hair, and smell strongly; many clients apply them at night with old clothing or coverings.

Vitamin D and vitamin A products

  • Calcipotriene and calcitriol regulate skin-cell division; monitor for itching, irritation, erythema, and hypercalcemia cues.
  • Teach clients using vitamin D analogs to limit sun exposure, avoid face application, and monitor for concerning lesions.
  • Tazarotene slows cellular division and causes sloughing; monitor for burning, inflammation, and desquamation.
  • Tazarotene is teratogenic and contraindicated during pregnancy; teach reliable contraception and provider notification if pregnancy occurs.
  • Avoid sun or artificial ultraviolet exposure with tazarotene unless the provider gives specific direction.

Systemic and Light-Based Psoriasis Therapy

Immunosuppression and eye protection

Systemic medications

  • Methotrexate or acitretin can be used for severe, intractable psoriasis; monitor liver and renal function for toxicity.
  • Methotrexate can suppress bone marrow, causing leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or anemia.
  • Cytotoxic medications are contraindicated during pregnancy and can harm the fetus; teach alcohol avoidance when prescribed.
  • Biologic agents suppress immune function; screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before therapy.
  • Teach infection reporting, injection-site rotation, medication light protection, lifelong-treatment expectations, cancer-risk discussion, and no live vaccines while taking biologics.
  • Cyclosporine and azathioprine are short-term immunosuppressive options when lesions do not respond; monitor for infection, nephrotoxicity, and hypertension.

Phototherapy and comfort

  • PUVA uses a psoralen photosensitizer followed by UVA to decrease epidermal-cell proliferation.
  • Methoxsalen is taken before UV treatment; treatments are done 2 to 3 times per week and not on consecutive days.
  • Ensure eye protection during PUVA and for 24 hr afterward indoors and outside; encourage regular eye exams.
  • Teach clients to report extreme redness, swelling, or discomfort and to use sunscreen as directed.
  • Long-term PUVA risks include premature skin aging, cataracts, and skin cancer.
  • Comfort measures include emollient/oatmeal baths and creams to soften scales; teach clients not to scratch or pick lesions.

Dermatitis Recognition and Avoidance

Allergens, irritants, pruritus

Types and findings

  • Dermatitis is skin inflammation from allergen or irritant exposure that can cause skin-structure changes and tissue breakdown.
  • Nonspecific eczematous dermatitis can cause thickened skin that appears dry or moist/crusted, with pruritus and symmetric involvement.
  • Contact dermatitis follows direct exposure to an allergen, chemical, or mechanical irritant and is usually well-demarcated/localized.
  • Atopic dermatitis can be chronic, intensely pruritic, scaly, thickened, and common on the face, neck, upper torso, and skin folds.
  • Scratching breaks skin integrity and increases risk for secondary bacterial infection.

Avoidance and comfort

  • Avoid harsh chemicals and known allergens/irritants when identified.
  • Use soaps, laundry detergents, and cosmetics without fragrance.
  • Avoid fabric softener dryer sheets; wash skin thoroughly after irritant exposure.
  • Apply cool, damp compresses to reduce inflammation.
  • Use colloidal oatmeal baths to relieve itching.
  • Consider mittens or hand covering at night for children who scratch unconsciously.

Dermatitis Medication Teaching

Steroids, antihistamines, pimecrolimus

Steroids and antihistamines

  • Steroids can be topical, intralesional, or systemic and reduce inflammatory response.
  • Monitor for adrenal suppression with steroid therapy; taper long-term steroids when discontinuing as prescribed.
  • Avoid topical steroids on infected lesions and avoid occlusive dressings over dermatitis after topical steroid application unless specifically directed.
  • Antihistamines can relieve redness, pruritus, and edema.
  • Monitor for urinary retention with systemic antihistamines; teach photosensitivity risk, drowsiness, bedtime dosing, and avoiding driving or machinery.

Topical immunosuppressants

  • Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus can be used for eczematous dermatitis resistant to glucocorticoid treatment.
  • Monitor for erythema and burning sensation.
  • Avoid occlusive dressings with topical immunosuppressants.
  • Avoid use if infection is present.
  • Discontinue when the rash clears as directed.
  • Avoid direct sunlight and tanning beds during therapy.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Pimecrolimus for Severe Eczematous Dermatitis

ATI-supported ALS

Therapeutic use and monitoring

  • Therapeutic use: relieve itching and inflammation associated with atopic/eczematous dermatitis when glucocorticoid treatment has not been effective.
  • Teach the client how and where to apply the medication.
  • Monitor for erythema and burning sensation.
  • Avoid occlusive dressings over the treated area.

Client education

  • Avoid use when a skin infection is present unless the provider gives specific direction.
  • Discontinue use when the rash clears as prescribed.
  • Avoid direct sunlight and tanning beds.
  • Report worsening rash, infection cues, or intolerable burning.

Application Exercises

1

Which instructions should the nurse include for a client using a high-potency corticosteroid cream for mild psoriasis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Use an occlusive dressing over exposed lesions if prescribed.
  • B. Apply the cream three to four times daily for several months.
  • C. Wear gloves after applying the medication to hand lesions if directed.
  • D. Avoid applying the medication in skin folds.
  • E. Take medication vacations when prescribed.
A, C, D, E Occlusion/gloves can enhance effect on exposed lesions when prescribed, skin folds should be avoided, and medication vacations reduce adverse effects.
B Frequent long-term continuous application increases local and systemic corticosteroid adverse effects.
2

Which teaching should the nurse provide for a client receiving PUVA therapy for psoriasis?

  • A. Apply vitamin A cream before each treatment.
  • B. Take a psoralen medication before ultraviolet treatment.
  • C. Schedule treatments every evening.
  • D. Gently remove scales after each treatment.
B PUVA uses a psoralen photosensitizer before long-wave UVA therapy.
A, C, D PUVA is not vitamin A cream, treatments are typically 2 to 3 times weekly and not consecutive, and scale removal can cause bleeding.
3

Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor for a client using calcipotriene for psoriasis?

  • A. Potassium
  • B. Calcium
  • C. Sodium
  • D. Chloride
B Vitamin D analogs such as calcipotriene can cause hypercalcemia.
A, C, D Potassium, sodium, and chloride are not the key ATI-supported monitoring focus for calcipotriene.
4

Which teaching should the nurse include for a child who has contact dermatitis?

  • A. Use fabric softener dryer sheets with clothing.
  • B. Apply warm, dry compresses to the rash.
  • C. Use a colloidal oatmeal bath for itching.
  • D. Leave the hands uncovered during sleep.
C Colloidal oatmeal baths can relieve itching from dermatitis.
A, B, D Avoid dryer sheets, use cool moist compresses, and consider hand covering at night to reduce scratching.
5

A client with contact dermatitis starts diphenhydramine. Which adverse effect should the nurse monitor for?

  • A. Elevated blood glucose
  • B. Anorexia
  • C. Increased salivation
  • D. Insomnia
B ATI lists anorexia as a possible adverse effect to monitor with diphenhydramine.
A, C, D Elevated glucose is associated with glucocorticoids, dry mouth is more expected than salivation, and diphenhydramine commonly causes drowsiness rather than insomnia.

Unit 11 · Integumentary Disorders · Chapter 75

Burns

Burn care begins with stopping the burning process and protecting airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, and pain control. Major burns can affect every body system, so nursing priorities include inhalation-injury recognition, fluid resuscitation, infection prevention, nutrition, wound care, graft protection, mobility, and long-term psychosocial support.

TL;DR · Airway First, Fluids Fast, Infection Always

For burns, think: stop the burn, cool water not ice, remove heat-conducting jewelry/clothing, cover to prevent contamination and hypothermia, and assess ABCDE. Hoarseness, brassy cough, drooling, stridor, or wheezing can mean inhalation injury and impending airway loss. During resuscitation, use IV opioids, large-bore IV fluids, urine output goals, warm the client, and watch for shock. In later phases, prevent infection, support high-calorie/high-protein nutrition, maintain ROM/splints, protect grafts, and monitor for sepsis, contractures, compartment syndrome, ileus, and PTSD.

Early priorities

  • Classify by type, depth, location, TBSA, age, cause, respiratory involvement, other injuries, and overall health.
  • Major burns include electrical/inhalation injury, burns to key areas, major TBSA/depth, older age, or significant comorbidity.
  • Initial labs reflect fluid shift, hemoconcentration, stress response, electrolyte changes, and possible inhalation/toxin exposure.

Ongoing priorities

  • Use protective infection precautions, client-dedicated equipment, strict asepsis, and tetanus/antibiotics as prescribed.
  • Nutrition needs can be very high; protein and calories support wound healing and limit catabolism.
  • Autografts need immobilization, elevation, donor-site care, analgesia, and infection surveillance.

Burn Care Priorities

Burn Types, Depth, and Severity

TBSA, depth, location

Causes and classifications

  • Dry heat, moist heat, hot surfaces, chemicals, electricity, and radiation can destroy skin layers and deeper tissue.
  • Scald injuries are more common in young children and older adults.
  • Electrical injuries can cause severe internal damage, organ dysfunction, tissue destruction, amputation need, or cardiac/respiratory arrest.
  • Radiation burns can follow cancer treatment or sun exposure.
  • Depth ranges from superficial to deep full thickness, with deeper burns causing less sensation, more scarring, and possible grafting needs.

Severity cues

  • Use TBSA tools to estimate extent and guide fluids, medications, and nutrition needs.
  • Rule of Nines gives a quick adult estimate; Lund and Browder is more precise; palmar method estimates scattered burns using the client's palm as about 1% TBSA.
  • Burns to the face, hands, feet, eyes, ears, or perineum are higher risk because of function, thinner skin, or complication potential.
  • Major-burn criteria include large full- or partial-thickness TBSA, older age, chronic cardiac/pulmonary/endocrine disease, electrical injury, inhalation injury, other complicated injury, or key body-location involvement.

Airway Injury, Fluid Shift, and Diagnostics

Hoarseness and urine output

Inhalation and toxin cues

  • Assess for singed nasal hair, eyebrows, or eyelashes; sooty sputum; hoarseness; wheezing; nasal-septum edema; and smoky breath.
  • Hoarseness, brassy cough, drooling, swallowing difficulty, audible wheezing/crowing, or stridor can indicate impending airway loss.
  • Suspect carbon monoxide poisoning after enclosed-space burns; findings can include headache, weakness, dizziness, confusion, pink/cherry-red skin, and upper airway edema.
  • Carboxyhemoglobin greater than 10% strongly supports smoke inhalation exposure.
  • Elevated plasma lactate can suggest cyanide toxicity.

Resuscitation labs and shifts

  • In the first 12 hr and through the first 24 to 36 hr, fluid shifts into interstitial space can cause hypovolemia and shock.
  • Expected resuscitation-phase labs include elevated glucose, BUN, hematocrit, and hemoglobin; decreased sodium; increased potassium; possible metabolic acidosis; and low protein/albumin.
  • Fluid remobilization starts around 24 hr and diuresis begins around 48 to 72 hr after injury.
  • During remobilization, hematocrit/hemoglobin can decrease from hemodilution and potassium can fall from renal loss and movement back into cells.
  • Diagnostic studies can include bronchoscopy, imaging, renal studies, indirect calorimetry, and burn-depth evaluation by video angiography or laser Doppler imaging.

Emergent and Resuscitation-Phase Care

ABCDE, fluids, pain

Stop the burn

  • Extinguish flames or remove the heat source, then remove clothing or jewelry that can conduct heat.
  • Use cool water soaks or running cool water; do not apply ice.
  • Flush chemical burns with a large volume of water.
  • Cover the burn with a clean cloth to reduce contamination and hypothermia.
  • Provide warmth and perform an ABCDE primary survey.
  • For minor burns, cleanse gently with mild soap/tepid water, apply antimicrobial ointment, use nonadherent or hydrocolloid dressing if needed, avoid greasy lotions/butter, check tetanus need, and teach infection observation.

Airway, fluids, and pain

  • Provide humidified oxygen, support ventilation, and prepare for intubation if airway edema or respiratory failure cues develop.
  • Insert large-bore IV access; central venous or intraosseous access can be needed for extensive burns.
  • Fluid resuscitation is guided by TBSA, depth, inhalation injury, associated injuries, age, urine output, cardiac output, blood pressure, and electrolytes.
  • Give half of the prescribed first-24-hr IV fluid volume in the first 8 hr from the time of burn, then the rest over the next 16 hr.
  • Use isotonic crystalloids initially; colloids can be used after the first 24 hr as prescribed.
  • Monitor hourly urine output, aiming for at least 30 mL/hr in adults; if output is low, request increased fluids rather than giving diuretics.
  • Use IV opioid analgesics during resuscitation because other routes absorb poorly; monitor for respiratory depression and premedicate before dressing changes.

Temperature, Infection, Nutrition, and Mobility

Protect and rebuild

Protection and nutrition

  • Burned skin loses heat; use warm inspired air, warm room temperature, warming blankets, and warmed fluids as needed.
  • Maintain a protective environment, restrict plants/flowers, limit visitors, exclude sick visitors and small children when indicated, and use dedicated equipment.
  • Use strict asepsis with wound care and administer tetanus toxoid and prescribed antibiotics.
  • Large burns create a hypermetabolic and hypercatabolic state; calorie needs can be very high and can double or triple 4 to 12 days after burn.
  • Increase protein and provide high carbohydrates to support healing and reduce protein catabolism.
  • Enteral therapy or parenteral nutrition can be needed when motility is decreased and calorie needs are high.

Mobility and psychosocial support

  • Maintain correct body alignment, splint extremities, turn/reposition, and use active/passive ROM to prevent contractures.
  • Ambulate as soon as the client is stable and apply pressure dressings/garments as prescribed to reduce scarring and contractures.
  • Monitor high-risk pressure areas such as heels, sacrum, and back of head.
  • Provide emotional support, body-image support, grief support, and antianxiety medication as prescribed.
  • Peer support can help when the client agrees.
  • Rehabilitation can last for years and focuses on highest possible functioning and return to work, family, and social roles.

Wound Medications, Debridement, and Grafts

Topicals and autografts

Topical medication anchors

  • Silver nitrate reduces fluid evaporation and is bacteriostatic, but does not penetrate eschar, stains fabric, and can deplete sodium/potassium.
  • Silver sulfadiazine is usually pain-free and broad, but is contraindicated with sulfa allergy and can cause transient neutropenia and discoloration.
  • Mafenide acetate penetrates eschar and underlying tissue but can be painful and can cause metabolic acidosis.
  • Polymyxin B-bacitracin is painless/easy and keeps burns moist, but hypersensitivity can develop.
  • Gentamicin topical is bactericidal but requires kidney-function and hearing monitoring.
  • Mannitol can be used after selected electrical burns when myoglobin obstructs renal tubules and urine output is impaired.

Procedures and graft care

  • Premedicate before wound care, remove old dressings, assess drainage/odor/eschar/bleeding/regeneration, cleanse thoroughly, and assist with debridement.
  • Mechanical, hydrotherapy, chemical, or surgical debridement can remove nonviable tissue.
  • Escharotomy relieves constriction from circumferential eschar; fasciotomy extends through fascia when pressure remains.
  • Biologic, synthetic, and biosynthetic coverings can protect wounds, reduce pain, and support healing.
  • Autografts use the client's own skin and can permanently cover large burn areas.
  • After grafting, immobilize graft sites, elevate extremities, provide donor-site care, administer analgesics, and monitor infection before and after skin coverings/grafts.

Complications and Discharge Priorities

Sepsis, mobility, long recovery

Complications to catch

  • Airway injury can progress for 24 to 48 hr; continue airway support, oxygen, deep breathing/coughing, and head-of-bed elevation as prescribed.
  • Inadequate fluids can cause hypovolemic shock; excessive fluids can contribute to heart failure.
  • Sepsis is the most common cause of death after burn injury; assess wound color, edema, odor, drainage, temperature/heart-rate changes, and culture needs.
  • Contractures and scarring can limit joints; perform ROM at least three times daily, use neutral positioning/splints, encourage ambulation, and use compression dressings as prescribed.
  • Compartment syndrome can occur as edema increases; monitor peripheral circulation and report adverse findings.
  • Paralytic ileus requires bowel-sound/distention monitoring and NG decompression until motility returns; it can signal systemic infection.

Teaching and interprofessional care

  • Teach that infection-control precautions are extremely important.
  • Normalize anxiety, fear, confusion, appearance changes, and the need for peer/support resources.
  • Wear compression garments as prescribed, often for most of the day, to reduce scarring and mobility difficulty.
  • Massage scars with moisturizer daily, avoid tight clothing over burned areas, and choose loose dye-free fabrics.
  • Use splints and assistive devices as instructed and keep follow-up appointments, which can continue for years.
  • Coordinate dietitian, social work, mental health, physical therapy, respiratory therapy, case management, home health, occupational therapy, and specialty referrals as needed.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Autograft Skin Covering

ATI-supported ALS

Description

  • An autograft uses donor skin from another area of the client's own body.
  • It is a permanent skin covering and can be used for larger burn areas.
  • Sheet grafts cover wounds directly; mesh grafts are slit so the graft can stretch over larger areas.

Nursing interventions

  • Maintain immobilization of the graft site.
  • Elevate the affected extremity.
  • Provide wound care to the donor site.
  • Administer analgesics and assess donor-site pain.
  • Monitor for infection before and after graft/skin covering application, including discoloration around the wound, green subcutaneous fat, degeneration of granulation tissue, subeschar hemorrhage, hyperventilation, or unstable temperature.

Application Exercises

1

Which classification should the nurse document for a severe sunburn?

  • A. Superficial thickness
  • B. Superficial partial thickness
  • C. Deep partial thickness
  • D. Full thickness
A Sunburn is a superficial-thickness burn involving the top skin layer.
B, C, D Deeper classifications involve more tissue damage, blisters/eschar, scarring risk, and possible grafting.
2

A burned client develops hoarseness, a brassy cough, and drooling. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

  • A. Pulmonary edema
  • B. Bacterial pneumonia
  • C. Inhalation injury
  • D. Carbon monoxide poisoning
C Hoarseness, brassy cough, drooling, wheezing/stridor, or swallowing difficulty suggest inhalation injury and possible impending airway loss.
A, B, D Pulmonary edema is more consistent with pink frothy sputum; pneumonia often has productive cough/fever; carbon monoxide often causes headache, confusion, dizziness, or cherry-red/pink skin.
3

Which findings are common during the initial phase after deep partial- and full-thickness burns over 40% TBSA? Select all that apply.

  • A. Temperature 36.1 C (97 F)
  • B. Bradycardia
  • C. Hyperkalemia
  • D. Hyponatremia
  • E. Decreased hematocrit
A, C, D Early burns impair temperature regulation, shift sodium into interstitial space, and release potassium from cellular destruction.
B, E Tachycardia is expected from sympathetic response, and hematocrit usually rises early from hemoconcentration.
4

Which route should the nurse use for fentanyl during the resuscitation phase after extensive burns?

  • A. Subcutaneous
  • B. Oral
  • C. Intravenous
  • D. Transdermal
C IV analgesia is preferred during resuscitation because tissue and gastrointestinal absorption are unreliable.
A, B, D Subcutaneous, oral, and transdermal routes can have delayed or unreliable absorption during burn resuscitation.
5

Which interventions should the nurse include for an adult client with severe burns? Select all that apply.

  • A. Limit visitors in the room.
  • B. Encourage unrestricted fresh vegetables.
  • C. Increase protein intake.
  • D. Limit intake to 2,000 calories/day.
  • E. Restrict fresh flowers in the room.
A, C, E Visitor limits and flower restrictions reduce infection risk; higher protein supports healing and prevents tissue breakdown.
B, D Some facilities restrict fresh produce because of bacteria, and severe burns can require far more than 2,000 calories/day.

Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 76

Endocrine Diagnostic Procedures

Endocrine diagnostic questions ask you to match the gland, the hormone pattern, and the test-risk cue. Priority nursing work includes fasting and medication instructions, dehydration or hypotension monitoring during suppression/stimulation tests, and recognizing which results point toward DI, SIADH, adrenal disease, pheochromocytoma, diabetes mellitus, or thyroid dysfunction.

TL;DR · Match the Hormone, Protect the Client

For endocrine diagnostics, start with the axis. Posterior pituitary testing separates DI, SIADH, and excess water intake by urine concentration and ADH response. Adrenal cortex testing uses cortisol, ACTH, dexamethasone, or cosyntropin patterns. Adrenal medulla testing looks for catecholamine excess and pheochromocytoma. Glucose testing evaluates carbohydrate metabolism, while TSH/T3/T4 and thyroid scan data localize thyroid problems.

Fast sorting

  • DI produces large amounts of dilute urine; SIADH produces water retention, concentrated urine, and low serum sodium/chloride.
  • Cortisol that does not suppress or stimulate as expected points toward adrenal or pituitary-axis pathology.
  • HbA1c reflects average glucose control across the prior 120 days, not just one morning's glucose.

Safety cues

  • Water deprivation testing requires close observation for dehydration, dizziness, tachycardia, and orthostatic hypotension.
  • Clonidine suppression testing can cause hypotension, so blood pressure monitoring continues after administration.
  • Thyroid scan is contraindicated in pregnancy and after recent iodine-containing dye exposure.

Endocrine Diagnostic Priorities

Posterior Pituitary and ADH Testing

ATI source-authored

ADH pattern

  • ADH increases water reabsorption in the renal distal tubules.
  • ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus, with large-volume dilute urine.
  • Excess ADH causes SIADH, with water retention, decreased urine output, concentrated urine, and increased extracellular fluid volume.
  • Diagnostic tests include water deprivation testing, ADH level, blood and urine electrolytes/osmolality, urine specific gravity, and urine sodium.

Interpretation cues

  • In SIADH, expect low sodium/chloride, increased urine osmolality, increased urine specific gravity, and increased urine sodium.
  • In diabetes insipidus, expect dilute urine with decreased urine osmolality and decreased urine specific gravity.
  • High ADH can occur with SIADH or nephrogenic DI; low ADH supports central/neurogenic DI.
  • Urine osmolality reflects concentration more directly than urine specific gravity.

Water Deprivation Test Safety

DI vs SIADH sorting

Purpose and preparation

  • The water deprivation test evaluates whether the kidneys can concentrate urine when plasma osmolality rises and ADH is low.
  • The client withholds fluids before or during testing, and total fluid deprivation can last many hours in a controlled setting.
  • Use the test to help differentiate central DI, nephrogenic DI, and psychogenic polydipsia.
  • For ADH testing, fasting and stress avoidance are expected before the blood draw; selected medications can interfere and should be reviewed with the provider.

During and after

  • Measure weight hourly and check urine osmolality repeatedly until the ordered endpoint is reached.
  • When blood osmolality is high enough, vasopressin/ADH can be administered and urine osmolality is rechecked.
  • After testing, assist with rehydration and monitor for orthostatic hypotension.
  • Stop and escalate if dehydration cues appear, especially postural hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, or excessive weight loss.

Adrenal Cortex Tests

Cortisol and ACTH response

Cushing and Addison logic

  • Excess cortisol characterizes Cushing disease/syndrome; inadequate cortisol characterizes Addison disease.
  • Adrenal cortex tests include dexamethasone suppression, blood cortisol, salivary cortisol, 24-hr urine cortisol, ACTH, and ACTH stimulation.
  • Stress, exercise, pregnancy, and some medications can alter adrenal test results, so preparation instructions matter.
  • Cortisol varies by time of day; blood testing is usually timed to the sleep-wake pattern.

Suppression and stimulation

  • Dexamethasone should suppress ACTH and lower cortisol when the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is functioning normally.
  • Failure to suppress after low or high dosing helps separate Cushing disease, adrenal tumors, and ACTH-producing tumors.
  • ACTH stimulation uses cosyntropin after a baseline cortisol level and checks whether cortisol rises appropriately.
  • A weak cortisol response after cosyntropin supports primary adrenal insufficiency; an exaggerated response can point toward adrenal hyperplasia or secondary adrenal insufficiency patterns.

Adrenal Medulla Tests

Pheochromocytoma screen

When to suspect

  • Adrenal medulla tumors can release excess catecholamines and create sympathetic findings such as hypertension, tachycardia, and diaphoresis.
  • Plasma-free metanephrine testing measures metanephrine and normetanephrine to evaluate for pheochromocytoma.
  • Clonidine suppression testing measures catecholamines before and after clonidine.
  • Hypovolemia is a contraindication to clonidine suppression testing because severe hypotension can occur.

Interpretation and monitoring

  • Elevation of both plasma-free metanephrine markers strongly supports pheochromocytoma; elevation of one marker makes it probable.
  • If pheochromocytoma is absent, clonidine suppresses catecholamine release and lowers catecholamine level and blood pressure.
  • If pheochromocytoma is present, clonidine does not reduce the blood pressure response.
  • Before clonidine testing, the client rests; after the procedure, continue blood pressure monitoring for hypotension.

Carbohydrate Metabolism Tests

Glucose and HbA1c

Blood glucose testing

  • Fasting blood glucose requires no calories other than water for about 8 hr; antidiabetes medication is generally held until after the specimen as prescribed.
  • A fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL supports prediabetes; more than 126 mg/dL on two different occasions can indicate diabetes mellitus.
  • Casual/random glucose can be drawn without regard to meals; less than 200 mg/dL is expected.
  • A single elevated glucose result should be confirmed with repeat testing on another day.

Glucose tolerance and HbA1c

  • Glucose tolerance testing requires balanced intake for several days before the test and fasting for 10 to 12 hr before the first sample.
  • After a prescribed glucose load, blood samples are collected at timed intervals; observe for dizziness, weakness, sweating, or giddiness.
  • HbA1c uses a random blood sample and is the best indicator of average blood glucose over the past 120 days.
  • HbA1c helps evaluate treatment effectiveness and adherence to diet, medication, and exercise plans; anemia, blood loss, and kidney disease can lower results.

Thyroid and Anterior Pituitary Tests

TSH, T3, T4, and scan

Blood tests

  • TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid to release T3 and T4.
  • TSH, T3, and T4 results help monitor thyroid replacement therapy and differentiate thyroid disorders.
  • High T3/T4 levels support hyperthyroidism; low T3/T4 levels support hypothyroidism.
  • Increased TSH suggests primary hypothyroidism; decreased TSH suggests hyperthyroidism or secondary hypothyroidism.

Thyroid scan

  • Thyroid scan evaluates thyroid size, shape, position, and function after an oral radioactive isotope dose.
  • Hot or warm areas show isotope uptake; cold areas show decreased uptake and can suggest nonfunctioning tissue.
  • Pregnancy and recent iodine-containing dye exposure are contraindications.
  • Thyroid or iodine-containing medications might need to be withheld before testing as prescribed; routine radiation precautions are not usually required for standard low-dose testing.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Clonidine Suppression Test

ATI-supported ALS

Indication and interpretation

  • Use the test to help confirm or rule out pheochromocytoma when catecholamine excess is suspected.
  • Plasma catecholamine levels are measured before and after clonidine administration.
  • Without pheochromocytoma, clonidine suppresses catecholamine release and lowers blood pressure.
  • With pheochromocytoma, catecholamine-driven hypertension does not suppress as expected.

Nursing actions

  • Screen for hypovolemia because clonidine can cause severe hypotension.
  • Have the client rest before specimen collection to reduce false elevation from stress or activity.
  • Monitor blood pressure during testing and for at least 1 hr after the procedure.
  • Report symptomatic hypotension, dizziness, or an unsafe blood pressure drop promptly.

Application Exercises

1

A client asks why the provider is using HbA1c instead of only the morning glucose log. Which response should the nurse make?

  • A. "HbA1c shows the average blood glucose pattern over about 120 days."
  • B. "HbA1c is the first screening test used to diagnose diabetes."
  • C. "HbA1c shows whether insulin worked between yesterday's meals."
  • D. "HbA1c determines whether you need a thyroid scan."
A HbA1c reflects average glucose control over the prior 120 days and helps evaluate treatment effectiveness.
B, C, D Fasting glucose is commonly used for diagnosis, finger-stick logs show shorter-term patterns, and thyroid scan evaluates thyroid uptake/function.
2

Which findings should the nurse expect for SIADH? Select all that apply.

  • A. Low serum sodium.
  • B. Decreased urine osmolality.
  • C. Increased urine specific gravity.
  • D. Increased urine sodium.
  • E. Large amounts of dilute urine.
A, C, D SIADH causes water retention with low sodium and concentrated urine, including increased urine specific gravity and urine sodium.
B, E Decreased urine osmolality and large dilute urine output fit diabetes insipidus more than SIADH.
3

A client with suspected primary adrenal insufficiency is receiving cosyntropin for ACTH stimulation testing. Which result should the nurse anticipate if the disorder is present?

  • A. Little or no rise in cortisol after the medication.
  • B. A sharp drop in blood glucose.
  • C. A large increase in urine osmolality.
  • D. Suppression of catecholamine release.
A In primary adrenal insufficiency, the adrenal cortex cannot produce an adequate cortisol rise after ACTH/cosyntropin stimulation.
B, C, D These do not best describe ACTH stimulation results; urine osmolality fits ADH testing, and catecholamine suppression fits clonidine testing.
4

Which nursing action is the priority during a water deprivation test?

  • A. Encourage oral fluids after each hourly urine sample.
  • B. Monitor for dizziness, tachycardia, and orthostatic hypotension.
  • C. Give clonidine before the first blood sample.
  • D. Place the client on radiation precautions.
B Water deprivation testing can cause dehydration, so the nurse monitors for early hypovolemia cues and escalates unsafe changes.
A, C, D Fluids are restricted during the test, clonidine belongs to pheochromocytoma testing, and radiation precautions relate to high-dose radioactive procedures rather than water deprivation.
5

Which statement indicates the client needs more teaching before a thyroid scan?

  • A. "I should tell the provider if I might be pregnant."
  • B. "I should report recent iodine contrast exposure."
  • C. "The scan shows areas of increased or decreased thyroid uptake."
  • D. "I can keep taking iodine-containing medication unless the provider tells me otherwise."
D Thyroid or iodine-containing medications might need to be withheld before a thyroid scan as prescribed, so the client should not assume they continue without review.
A, B, C Pregnancy and recent iodine-containing contrast are contraindication concerns, and uptake patterns are part of the scan interpretation.

Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 77

Pituitary Disorders

Pituitary disorders split cleanly into anterior-pituitary growth hormone problems and posterior-pituitary water-balance problems. High-yield nursing work centers on acromegaly findings and hypophysectomy precautions, then contrasting diabetes insipidus with SIADH by urine concentration, sodium/osmolality patterns, fluid strategy, and neurologic safety.

TL;DR · Big Gland, Water Rules

The pituitary regulates other endocrine glands. Acromegaly is excess growth hormone in adults; watch progressive body-part enlargement and pressure effects, then protect the client after hypophysectomy from increased ICP and CSF leak. DI means not enough effective ADH: massive dilute urine, thirst, dehydration, and concentrated blood. SIADH means too much ADH: water retention, concentrated urine, low sodium/osmolality, neurologic decline, and fluid restriction.

Compare fast

  • DI: polyuria, polydipsia, dilute urine, increased blood osmolality/sodium, dehydration risk, and ADH replacement for neurogenic DI.
  • SIADH: reduced urine output, concentrated urine, dilutional hyponatremia, low blood osmolality, fluid overload, seizure risk, and fluid restriction first.
  • Acromegaly: excess GH in adults causes enlarged hands/feet/facial structures, headaches, visual changes, hyperglycemia, sleep apnea, and possible increased ICP.

Safety cues

  • After transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, no toothbrushing, nose blowing, bending at the waist, or forceful coughing.
  • Report glucose in nasal drainage or postnasal drip/increased swallowing because it can indicate a CSF leak.
  • During SIADH treatment, sodium must rise carefully; rapid correction can cause central pontine myelinolysis.

Pituitary Disorder Priorities

Pituitary Hormone Map

ATI source-authored

Anterior pituitary

  • The anterior pituitary secretes TSH, ACTH, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, prolactin, and growth hormone.
  • ACTH stimulates adrenal glucocorticoid secretion; excess ACTH can produce Cushing disease.
  • Excess growth hormone causes gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults.
  • Broad anterior pituitary hypofunction can impair the thyroid, adrenal cortex, and gonadal target organs.

Posterior pituitary

  • Posterior pituitary hormones are made in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary, and released as needed.
  • ADH increases kidney water reabsorption; deficiency causes DI and excess secretion causes SIADH.
  • Oxytocin supports uterine contraction after birth and breast milk ejection during lactation.
  • Posterior pituitary disorders are high-yield because they disrupt fluid balance, sodium, osmolality, and neurologic safety.

Acromegaly

Growth hormone excess

Pattern recognition

  • Acromegaly is excess growth hormone in adults; body parts enlarge but adult height does not increase.
  • Expected findings include severe headaches, visual disturbances, coarse facial features, thick lips, protruding lower jaw, enlarged hands/feet, joint pain, voice change, menstrual-pattern change, sleep apnea, hyperglycemia, and barrel-shaped chest.
  • Pressure from tumor growth can increase intracranial pressure, causing decreased level of consciousness, pupillary changes, severe hypertension, widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, or seizures.
  • Untreated acromegaly can contribute to hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cardiac problems.

Diagnostics and medications

  • Growth hormone suppression testing checks baseline growth hormone and glucose, gives prescribed glucose, then repeats levels; acromegaly shows little or no growth hormone suppression.
  • Skull x-ray can show sella turcica changes; CT/MRI can locate soft-tissue lesions; cerebral angiography can evaluate vascular malformation or aneurysm.
  • Dopamine agonists, somatostatin analogs, and growth hormone receptor blockers can reduce growth hormone effects through different mechanisms.
  • Teach clients taking bromocriptine to report chest pain, dizziness, or watery nasal drainage promptly.

Hypophysectomy Care

CSF leak and ICP precautions

Procedure and position

  • Hypophysectomy removes the pituitary gland, most often through an endoscopic transnasal or transsphenoidal approach; craniotomy is used if those approaches do not reach the tumor.
  • Maintain high-Fowler's position after surgery unless contraindicated.
  • Monitor neurologic status and observe the mustache dressing/drip pad for drainage.
  • Glucose in drainage suggests cerebrospinal fluid leak and should be reported promptly.

Teaching and complications

  • Teach no toothbrushing, nose blowing, or bending at the waist after surgery because these actions can increase intracranial pressure.
  • Encourage deep breathing but limit coughing because forceful coughing can increase ICP and worsen CSF leak risk.
  • Assess for meningitis, monitor fluid balance for postoperative DI, and administer replacement hormones as prescribed.
  • Teach lifelong hormone replacement, frequent mouth rinses/flossing instead of toothbrushing at first, high-fiber intake to reduce straining, and reporting postnasal drip or increased swallowing.

Diabetes Insipidus

Dilute urine, concentrated blood

Types and findings

  • DI results from ADH deficiency or poor renal response to ADH, reducing distal tubule water collection and urine concentration.
  • Neurogenic DI involves inadequate ADH production or release; nephrogenic DI involves renal tubules that do not respond to ADH and can follow kidney damage or medications such as lithium or demeclocycline.
  • Expected findings include abrupt polyuria, intense thirst, tachycardia, hypotension, poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, weak pulses, decreased cognition, and ataxia.
  • Older adults have higher dehydration risk because of lower body water, reduced thirst response, reduced kidney concentration ability, diuretic use, swallowing difficulty, or poor intake.

Labs and care

  • Think dilute urine: decreased urine specific gravity, osmolality, pH, sodium, and potassium.
  • Think concentrated blood: increased blood osmolality, sodium, and potassium as fluid volume drops.
  • Monitor vital signs, urine output, intake/output, central venous pressure when used, urine specific gravity, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, daily weight, skin, mucous membranes, and fall risk.
  • Hydrate and replace electrolytes as prescribed; match intake and output to prevent dehydration.
  • Neurogenic DI can require lifelong desmopressin or vasopressin; monitor for headache, confusion, or other water-intoxication cues.

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone

Concentrated urine, diluted blood

Pattern recognition

  • SIADH is excess ADH release, leading to kidney water reabsorption, decreased urine output, sodium excretion, water intoxication, cellular edema, and dilutional hyponatremia.
  • Risk factors include malignant tumors, positive-pressure ventilation, head injury, meningitis, stroke, tuberculosis, and medications such as chemotherapy agents, TCAs, SSRIs, opioids, and fluoroquinolone antibiotics.
  • Early findings include headache, weakness, anorexia, muscle cramps, and weight gain without edema.
  • Progression can cause personality changes, hostility, sluggish deep tendon reflexes, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, oliguria with dark concentrated urine, confusion, lethargy, Cheyne-Stokes respirations, seizures, coma, and death.

Labs and nursing care

  • Think concentrated urine: increased urine sodium and osmolality as urine volume decreases.
  • Think diluted blood: decreased sodium and decreased blood osmolality.
  • Fluid restriction is first priority; use mouth care, ice chips, lozenges, and staggered water intake for thirst comfort as prescribed.
  • Monitor intake/output, decreased urine output, vital signs, lung sounds for pulmonary edema, daily weight, serum sodium/osmolality, urine sodium/osmolality, mental status, and seizure risk.
  • Use a safe, low-stimulation environment when level of consciousness changes and maintain seizure precautions when indicated.

SIADH Medications and Complications

Correct sodium carefully

Medication map

  • Demeclocycline can be used off-label for mild SIADH to promote urine flow and correct fluid/electrolyte imbalance; avoid use with impaired kidney function.
  • Monitor effectiveness by looking for increased blood sodium/osmolality and decreased urine sodium/osmolality.
  • Tolvaptan and conivaptan promote water excretion without sodium loss in acute inpatient settings and can raise sodium quickly.
  • Furosemide can increase water excretion but must be used cautiously because sodium loss can worsen hyponatremia.

Escalation cues

  • Hypertonic sodium chloride can be used for severe hyponatremia/water intoxication to improve neurologic compromise; monitor for fluid overload and heart failure.
  • Report difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, neurologic changes, tremors, disorientation, nausea, poor appetite, vomiting, or worsening fluid overload cues.
  • Water intoxication, cerebral edema, pulmonary edema, and severe hyponatremia can progress to coma and death without prompt treatment.
  • During treatment with vasopressin antagonists, hypertonic saline, or loop diuretics, sodium/osmolality must be monitored closely because rapid sodium correction can cause central pontine myelinolysis.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Demeclocycline for SIADH

ATI-supported ALS

Therapeutic use and monitoring

  • Demeclocycline is a tetracycline derivative used off-label for mild SIADH to increase urine flow and improve fluid/electrolyte balance.
  • Monitor for effective treatment: rising blood sodium/osmolality and decreasing urine sodium/osmolality.
  • Screen kidney function because demeclocycline is contraindicated with impaired kidney function.
  • Track intake/output, sodium trends, neurologic status, and ongoing SIADH manifestations.

Client education

  • Avoid taking demeclocycline at the same time as calcium, iron, magnesium, aluminum-containing antacids, or milk products.
  • Report a white, cheese-like film in the mouth because it can indicate yeast infection.
  • Avoid prolonged sun exposure; use sunscreen and protective clothing.
  • Notify the provider if diarrhea develops.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings should the nurse expect for SIADH? Select all that apply.

  • A. Decreased blood sodium.
  • B. Urine specific gravity 1.001.
  • C. Blood osmolality 230 mOsm/L.
  • D. Large-volume dilute urine output.
  • E. Weight gain without edema.
A, C, E SIADH causes water retention with dilutional hyponatremia, low blood osmolality, and weight gain from retained water.
B, D Very low urine specific gravity and large amounts of dilute urine fit DI, not SIADH.
2

Which urinalysis finding should the nurse expect for diabetes insipidus?

  • A. Presence of glucose.
  • B. Decreased specific gravity.
  • C. Increased urine sodium.
  • D. Presence of red blood cells.
B DI produces dilute urine, so urine specific gravity is low.
A, C, D Glucose and red blood cells point to other disorders, while increased urine sodium is more consistent with SIADH patterns.
3

Which statement by a client with new diabetes insipidus indicates teaching was effective?

  • A. "I should limit fluids to 2 quarts each day."
  • B. "I might have confusion or balance problems if this worsens."
  • C. "I should expect my urine to become very concentrated before treatment."
  • D. "I will need insulin to control this disorder."
B DI can cause dehydration and hyperosmolarity, leading to neurologic findings such as confusion and ataxia.
A, C, D Fluid intake is not restricted by default in DI, urine is dilute, and insulin treats diabetes mellitus rather than diabetes insipidus.
4

Which intervention should the nurse include after a transsphenoidal hypophysectomy?

  • A. Maintain the client in low-Fowler's position.
  • B. Encourage forceful coughing every hour.
  • C. Encourage toothbrushing as soon as the client is awake.
  • D. Check mustache dressing drainage for glucose.
D Glucose in nasal drainage can indicate CSF leak and should be reported.
A, B, C High-Fowler's positioning is used; coughing, toothbrushing, nose blowing, and bending can increase ICP or trauma risk after this approach.
5

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client taking demeclocycline for SIADH?

  • A. Take the medication with milk to protect the stomach.
  • B. Use sunscreen and protective clothing outdoors.
  • C. Expect diarrhea as a desired effect.
  • D. Stop fluid restriction once the first dose is taken.
B Demeclocycline can increase sun sensitivity, so prolonged sun exposure should be avoided and protection used.
A, C, D Milk products can interfere with tetracycline derivatives, diarrhea should be reported, and fluid restriction continues as prescribed.

Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 78

Hyperthyroidism

Hyperthyroidism is a hypermetabolic thyroid state, most often from Graves disease. Nursing priorities are to recognize heat and cardiac overdrive, protect nutrition and eye comfort, give antithyroid and symptom-control medications safely, teach radioactive iodine precautions, and catch post-thyroidectomy airway, bleeding, calcium, nerve, and thyroid storm complications fast.

TL;DR · Too Hot, Too Fast, Too Much Thyroid

Hyperthyroidism speeds up metabolism: heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, diarrhea, insomnia, tremor, emotional lability, tachycardia, palpitations, dysrhythmias, and widened pulse pressure. Graves adds autoimmune markers, goiter, eye changes, and sometimes pretibial myxedema. Treatment may include thionamides, beta blockers, short-term iodine, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy. After surgery, airway and hemorrhage come first, then hypocalcemia and voice changes.

Recognition

  • Labs usually show low TSH with high T3/T4 in Graves disease; Graves-specific antibodies can be elevated.
  • Exophthalmos needs eye protection, lubricant, and support because pressure can blur or double vision.
  • Older adults can show subtle cues such as weight loss, fatigue, bowel change, atrial fibrillation, angina, or heart failure.

Rescue cues

  • A 1 F temperature increase can warn of thyroid crisis; fever, restlessness, palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, or confusion need escalation.
  • After thyroidectomy, sudden stridor, restlessness, bleeding behind the neck, or voice change can signal airway compromise or bleeding.
  • Perioral tingling, extremity tingling, muscle twitching, Chvostek sign, or Trousseau sign can indicate hypocalcemia after parathyroid injury.

Hyperthyroidism Priorities

Thyroid Hormone Pattern

ATI source-authored

Feedback loop

  • The thyroid produces T4, T3, and calcitonin; T3 and T4 are regulated through anterior pituitary TSH feedback.
  • T3 and T4 regulate overall metabolism, energy production, and how tissues use fats, proteins, and carbohydrates.
  • Hyperthyroidism creates excessive circulating thyroid hormone and exaggerates normal body functions into a hypermetabolic state.
  • Protein and iodine intake are needed for thyroid hormone production, so iodine exposure matters in testing and treatment.

Causes

  • Graves disease is the most common cause and is autoimmune.
  • Toxic nodular goiter and toxic adenoma can overproduce thyroid hormone.
  • Thyroiditis can create hyperthyroid manifestations.
  • Exogenous hyperthyroidism can occur when thyroid hormone dosage is excessive.

Assessment and Laboratory Cues

Hypermetabolic pattern

Expected findings

  • Expected findings include nervousness, irritability, hyperactivity, emotional lability, decreased attention, weakness, easy fatigue, exercise intolerance, heat intolerance, weight loss with increased appetite, insomnia, frequent stools, and diarrhea.
  • Skin can be warm, sweaty, flushed, and smooth; hair can become thin, fine, soft, and silky.
  • Neuromuscular findings include tremor, hyperkinesia, and hyperreflexia.
  • Cardiac findings can include elevated systolic pressure, widened pulse pressure, tachycardia, palpitations, dysrhythmias, and dyspnea.
  • Reproductive findings can include menstrual irregularity, decreased fertility, and libido changes as the disorder progresses.

Graves and labs

  • Graves-specific findings can include exophthalmos, photophobia, excessive tearing, bloodshot eyes, eyelid lag, globe lag, goiter, thyroid bruit, and pretibial myxedema.
  • In Graves disease, TSH is usually decreased, while free T4 index, total T4, and T3 are elevated.
  • Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins and thyrotropin receptor antibodies can be elevated with Graves disease.
  • Older adults can have vague or single-system presentations, including atrial fibrillation, angina, or heart failure.

Diagnostics and Daily Nursing Care

Calm, cool, nourished

Diagnostics

  • Ultrasound can image the thyroid gland and surrounding tissue.
  • ECG evaluates cardiac effects of excess thyroid hormone, including tachycardia, dysrhythmias, atrial fibrillation, and P/T wave changes.
  • Thyroid scan evaluates gland size and function after oral radioactive isotope; increased uptake supports hyperthyroidism.
  • Before thyroid scan, confirm the client is not pregnant and review iodine contrast, iodides, vitamins, oral contraceptives, foods, and medications that can affect results.

Nursing care

  • Reduce energy expenditure by assisting with activities and alternating activity with rest.
  • Promote a calm environment and assess mental status, judgment, and safety.
  • Monitor nutritional status, intake/output, weight, vital signs, hemodynamic status, and ECG rhythm.
  • Provide increased calories, protein, and nutrition support as needed.
  • Reduce room temperature, provide cool bathing measures, change linens as needed, protect eyes for exophthalmos, and avoid excessive palpation of the thyroid gland.

Medication Map

Thionamides, beta blockers, iodine

Thionamides and beta blockers

  • Methimazole and propylthiouracil inhibit thyroid hormone production and can be used for Graves disease, thyrotoxicosis, preparation for surgery, or as adjuncts to radioactive iodine.
  • Monitor for hypothyroidism, CBC changes such as leukopenia or thrombocytopenia, and hepatotoxicity.
  • Teach taking thionamides with meals in divided regular doses and reporting fever, sore throat, jaundice, or bruising.
  • Propranolol, atenolol, and metoprolol reduce sympathetic effects such as tachycardia and palpitations but do not lower thyroid hormone levels.
  • With beta blockers, monitor blood pressure, heart rate, ECG, and hypoglycemia risk in clients who have diabetes mellitus.

Iodine solution

  • Lugol solution is short-term nonradioactive iodine that inhibits thyroid hormone release and is usually taken briefly before surgery.
  • Take iodine solution after an antithyroid medication as prescribed.
  • Mix the solution with juice or another liquid, use a straw to avoid tooth staining, and take with food.
  • Iodine solutions should not be used during pregnancy and can pass into breast milk.
  • Report fever, sore throat, metallic taste, or mouth ulcers.

Radioactive Iodine and Thyroidectomy

Cell destruction and surgical care

Radioactive iodine

  • Radioactive iodine is absorbed by thyroid tissue and destroys some hormone-producing cells.
  • It is contraindicated during pregnancy.
  • The effect might take several weeks, and more than one dose can be needed.
  • Because thyroid destruction varies, lifelong thyroid replacement can be required; monitor for hypothyroidism.
  • Teach radiation precautions to reduce exposure to others after treatment.

Thyroidectomy

  • Subtotal thyroidectomy can treat hyperthyroidism when medications fail or radioactive iodine is contraindicated; total thyroidectomy requires lifelong replacement therapy.
  • Before surgery, antithyroid medication and iodine can be prescribed to lower hormone activity, reduce gland size, and reduce bleeding risk.
  • Teach neck support with deep breathing, coughing, and position changes after surgery.
  • Expect a neck incision with dressing and possible drain; hoarseness and sore throat can follow intubation.
  • Report mouth/extremity tingling or muscle twitching because these can indicate hypocalcemia.

Postoperative Complications

Airway, bleeding, calcium, voice

Immediate care

  • After thyroidectomy, keep the client semi-Fowler's, support the head and neck, and avoid neck extension.
  • Check the dressing and the back of the neck for bleeding; monitor drainage and vocal changes.
  • Respiratory distress can occur from hemorrhage, edema, tracheal collapse, mucus accumulation, laryngeal edema, or vocal cord paralysis.
  • Keep tracheostomy supplies and suction equipment immediately available, provide humidified air and suction as needed, and alert the provider/Rapid Response for respiratory manifestations.

Calcium and nerve checks

  • Parathyroid injury can cause hypocalcemia and tetany.
  • Monitor for tingling of fingers, toes, or mouth, carpopedal spasm, convulsions, muscle twitching, Chvostek sign, and Trousseau sign.
  • Keep IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride available as prescribed and maintain seizure precautions when indicated.
  • Assess the client's ability to speak and compare voice tone/quality with baseline because swelling or nerve injury can cause vocal cord paralysis and voice changes.

Thyroid Storm/Crisis

Medical emergency
  • Thyroid storm is a sudden surge of large amounts of thyroid hormone into the bloodstream, creating an extreme metabolic state with high mortality risk.
  • Triggers can include uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, Graves disease, infection, trauma, emotional stress, diabetic ketoacidosis, digitalis toxicity, surgery, thyroidectomy, or thyroid manipulation.
  • Findings can include hyperthermia, hypertension, delirium, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachydysrhythmias, chest pain, dyspnea, and palpitations.
  • Maintain a patent airway, provide continuous cardiac monitoring, give oxygen and IV fluids as prescribed, and monitor hourly intake/output.
  • Use acetaminophen and cooling measures for fever; avoid aspirin because it can increase free thyroxine.
  • Administer thionamides, then prescribed sodium iodide after thionamide timing, beta blockers, glucocorticoids if indicated, and fluid support as prescribed.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Radioactive Iodine Therapy

ATI-supported ALS

Description

  • Radioactive iodine therapy gives a larger radioactive iodine dose than diagnostic testing.
  • The thyroid absorbs the radiation, which destroys thyroid hormone-producing cells.
  • The therapeutic effect might not be evident for 6 to 8 weeks.
  • Continue prescribed antithyroid medication or thyroid-related medication exactly as directed.

Radiation precautions

  • Avoid close contact with infants, young children, and pregnant individuals for the first week after treatment.
  • Use a separate toilet if directed, sit to urinate, and flush the toilet three times after use.
  • Take a laxative 2 to 3 days after treatment if prescribed to clear contaminated stool.
  • Wash contaminated clothing separately and run a full machine cycle after laundering.
  • Do not share a toothbrush and use disposable food-service items if instructed.

Application Exercises

1

Which laboratory findings should the nurse expect for Graves disease?

  • A. Decreased thyrotropin receptor antibodies.
  • B. Decreased thyroid-stimulating hormone.
  • C. Decreased free thyroxine index.
  • D. Decreased triiodothyronine.
B In Graves disease, thyroid hormone is elevated and the pituitary decreases TSH release through negative feedback.
A, C, D Graves disease is associated with elevated thyrotropin receptor antibodies and elevated thyroid hormones such as T3 and free T4 index.
2

Which manifestations should the nurse include when teaching about hyperthyroidism? Select all that apply.

  • A. Heat intolerance.
  • B. Palpitations.
  • C. Weight loss.
  • D. Constipation.
  • E. Bradycardia.
A, B, C Hyperthyroidism raises metabolic and sympathetic activity, causing heat intolerance, palpitations, and weight loss.
D, E Diarrhea and tachycardia are more consistent with hyperthyroidism than constipation and bradycardia.
3

Which instruction should the nurse include for a client taking propranolol for Graves disease?

  • A. "Take your pulse before each dose."
  • B. "This medication stops thyroid hormone production."
  • C. "Stop the medication if you have a sore throat."
  • D. "Yellow skin is an expected effect."
A Propranolol can cause bradycardia, so the client should check pulse and follow provider parameters.
B, C, D Propranolol controls sympathetic effects; thionamides reduce hormone production, sore throat is a thionamide warning, and jaundice should be reported.
4

Which equipment should be available for a client returning from thyroidectomy? Select all that apply.

  • A. Suction equipment.
  • B. Humidified oxygen.
  • C. Tracheostomy tray.
  • D. Chest tube tray.
  • E. Flashlight for pupil checks.
A, B, C Airway obstruction is a priority risk after thyroidectomy, so suction, humidified oxygen, and tracheostomy supplies should be available.
D, E Chest tube setup and routine pupil checks are not the expected immediate thyroidectomy equipment priorities.
5

Which findings 12 hr after thyroidectomy should make the nurse suspect thyroid storm? Select all that apply.

  • A. Dyspnea.
  • B. Abdominal pain.
  • C. Mental confusion.
  • D. Hypothermia.
  • E. Bradycardia.
A, B, C Thyroid storm can cause dyspnea, abdominal pain or vomiting, and delirium/confusion from extreme metabolic activation.
D, E Hyperthermia and tachycardia are expected in thyroid crisis rather than hypothermia or bradycardia.
