Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 79

Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism is too little circulating thyroid hormone, so metabolism slows across body systems. Nursing priorities are to recognize the slow, cold, constipated, bradycardic pattern; protect cardiac and respiratory safety; teach levothyroxine timing and interaction rules; and treat myxedema coma as an airway, temperature, glucose, sodium, and cardiac emergency.

TL;DR · Too Slow, Too Cold, Too Little Thyroid

Hypothyroidism lowers metabolic rate. Expect fatigue, lethargy, cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain without extra calories, dry thick skin, brittle nails, hair loss, hoarse speech, slow thinking/speech, bradycardia, hypotension, dysrhythmias, hypoventilation, edema, menstrual changes, and low libido. Primary disease usually has low T3/T4 with high TSH; secondary disease can have low or normal TSH. Levothyroxine is lifelong for many clients and must be taken consistently on an empty stomach. Myxedema coma is the rescue priority.

Recognize it

  • Findings can mimic aging, especially in older adults, so vague fatigue, slowing, cold intolerance, constipation, and weight change still matter.
  • Primary hypothyroidism starts in the thyroid gland; central hypothyroidism starts from pituitary or hypothalamic failure.
  • Thyroid scan can show low uptake, and ECG can show sinus bradycardia or dysrhythmias.

Rescue it

  • Use caution with sedatives, opioids, anesthetics, and other medications because slowed metabolism can intensify effects.
  • Teach levothyroxine consistency: same dose timing, same brand unless directed, empty stomach, and separation from calcium, iron, antacids, and fiber products.
  • Myxedema coma needs airway/ventilation support, ECG monitoring, warming with blankets, IV thyroid hormone, 0.9% sodium chloride, glucose if hypoglycemic, corticosteroids, and trigger treatment.

Hypothyroidism Priorities

Classification and Risk Pattern

ATI source-authored

What failed?

  • Hypothyroidism means circulating T3 and T4 are inadequate, so metabolic rate drops and multiple body systems slow down.
  • Primary hypothyroidism is the most common type and comes from thyroid gland dysfunction.
  • Primary causes include autoimmune thyroiditis, medications that reduce thyroid hormone synthesis, iodine deficiency, radioactive iodine or radiation treatment, and surgical thyroid removal.
  • Secondary hypothyroidism comes from inadequate anterior pituitary stimulation or poor tissue response; tertiary hypothyroidism comes from hypothalamic failure to produce thyroid-releasing hormone.

Who is higher risk?

  • Risk is higher in female clients between ages 30 and 60.
  • Lithium and amiodarone can contribute to hypothyroidism.
  • Low iodine intake and head/neck radiation therapy are risk factors.
  • Older adults can be underdiagnosed because findings overlap with aging and can increase sensitivity to sedatives, opioids, and anesthetics.

Assessment Pattern

Slow metabolism

Body-wide slowing

  • Expected findings can be vague and slowly progressive: fatigue, lethargy, irritability, cold intolerance, constipation, and weight gain without increased intake.
  • Skin and hair findings include pallor, thick or dry skin, dry/flaky skin, brittle nails, hair loss, and thinning of the eyebrows.
  • Neurologic and mood findings can include depression, apathy, slow thinking, and slow speech.
  • Musculoskeletal and sensory findings can include joint/muscle pain and decreased taste or smell.

Cardiac, respiratory, reproductive

  • Cardiovascular findings can include bradycardia, hypotension, dysrhythmias, peripheral edema, and increased cardiovascular disease risk over time.
  • Respiratory findings can include hypoventilation and pleural effusion.
  • Myxedema can create nonpitting facial, tongue, hand, and foot swelling; laryngeal myxedema can cause hoarse, raspy speech.
  • Reproductive findings can include menorrhagia, amenorrhea, decreased libido, and impotence.

Labs and Diagnostics

T3/T4 low; TSH depends on cause

Laboratory pattern

  • T3 and T4 are decreased in hypothyroidism.
  • TSH increases with primary hypothyroidism because the pituitary is trying to stimulate the thyroid gland.
  • TSH can be decreased or within the expected range in secondary hypothyroidism.
  • Cholesterol can increase, and antithyroid antibodies can be present in some cases.

Diagnostic cues

  • A thyroid scan can show low radioactive uptake when thyroid activity is low.
  • ECG can show sinus bradycardia or dysrhythmias.
  • In adults older than 80, treatment for low thyroid hormone levels is not automatically started unless the client has manifestations.
  • Follow-up TSH monitoring helps guide levothyroxine titration and confirms whether the dose is moving the client toward a euthyroid state.

Daily Nursing Care

Protect heart, lungs, skin, warmth

Monitoring and activity

  • Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, rhythm, chest pain, peripheral edema, and weight.
  • If mental status is altered, reorient the client and implement safety measures.
  • Increase activity gradually and provide rest periods to reduce fatigue and myocardial oxygen demand.
  • Use anti-embolism stockings and leg elevation as prescribed to support venous return.
  • Monitor respiratory rate, depth, pattern, oxygen saturation, and ABGs; encourage coughing and deep breathing to prevent pulmonary complications.

Comfort and prevention

  • Request nutrition support for low-calorie, high-bulk food choices with fluids and activity to address constipation and weight gain.
  • Use stool softeners or cathartics as prescribed, but avoid fiber laxatives because they reduce levothyroxine absorption.
  • Provide careful skin care, repositioning when on bed rest, alcohol-free products, and emollient lotion.
  • Support warmth with layers, blankets, room-temperature adjustment, and warm fluids when allowed.
  • Avoid electric blankets and heating devices because vasodilation, reduced sensation, and decreased alertness can lead to burns.

Levothyroxine Teaching

Replacement therapy

Start low, titrate carefully

  • Levothyroxine is synthetic thyroid hormone replacement and is the common medication used for hypothyroidism.
  • Older adults and clients who have coronary artery disease need cautious low-dose starts and gradual increases because thyroid replacement raises cardiac oxygen demand.
  • Monitor for chest pain, palpitations, tachycardia, shortness of breath, and other cardiovascular compromise.
  • Blood TSH is checked on a schedule while the provider adjusts the dose, often over several weeks, until the desired response is reached.

Timing and interactions

  • Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed without stopping or changing dose, timing, or brand unless the provider directs it.
  • Take the medication on an empty stomach, usually 30 to 60 min before breakfast.
  • Fiber supplements/laxatives, calcium, iron, and antacids can reduce absorption; consult the provider before adding over-the-counter products.
  • Levothyroxine can increase the effects of warfarin and can change insulin and digoxin needs.
  • Report hyperthyroid manifestations such as irritability, tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, heat intolerance, or rapid weight loss because the dose might be too high.

Medication Safety in Hypothyroidism

Slowed metabolism changes response
  • Hypothyroidism slows metabolism and excretion of many medications, so usual doses can have stronger or longer effects.
  • Use caution with CNS depressants such as sedatives and barbiturates because respiratory depression risk increases.
  • Clients with chronic hypothyroidism can have cardiovascular disease risk, so new chest pain or discomfort should be reported immediately.
  • Home health follow-up can be useful during the first weeks of replacement therapy to assess response and adverse effects.
  • Body image concerns can improve slowly; reassure the client that many physical findings improve as euthyroid function returns.

Myxedema Coma

Medical emergency

Triggers and findings

  • Myxedema coma is life-threatening and can occur when hypothyroidism is untreated, poorly managed, or worsened by a stressor.
  • Stressors can include acute illness, surgery, chemotherapy, stopping thyroid replacement, and use of sedatives or opioids.
  • Expected findings include respiratory failure, hypotension, hypothermia, bradycardia, dysrhythmias, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, and coma.
  • Assess for infection sources such as blood, sputum, or urine because infection can precipitate the crisis.

Emergency care

  • Maintain airway patency and provide ventilatory support if needed.
  • Use continuous ECG monitoring and monitor ABGs for hypoxia, hypercapnia, and respiratory acidosis.
  • Monitor mental status, temperature, blood pressure, intake/output, and daily weight.
  • Warm with blankets, not electric heating devices, and replace fluid with 0.9% sodium chloride IV as prescribed.
  • Give IV levothyroxine bolus as prescribed until GI absorption is reliable; T3 IV, glucose, and corticosteroids can also be prescribed.
  • Initiate aspiration precautions and treat the underlying illness that triggered the coma.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Hypothyroidism

ATI-supported ALS

Alteration and risks

  • Hypothyroidism is inadequate circulating T3 and T4, causing a decreased metabolic rate that affects all body systems.
  • High-yield risk factors include female clients age 30 to 60 and use of lithium or amiodarone.
  • Other supports include iodine deficiency, head/neck radiation, thyroid removal, radioactive iodine therapy, autoimmune thyroiditis, and central pituitary/hypothalamic problems.

Diagnostics to capture

  • Blood T3 and T4 are key thyroid hormone labs.
  • TSH distinguishes primary from secondary patterns.
  • Free T4 index, thyroid antibodies, and blood cholesterol can support the diagnosis.
  • Thyroid scan and ECG add functional and cardiac information.

Application Exercises

1

Which laboratory finding should the nurse expect for a client being evaluated for secondary hypothyroidism?

  • A. Elevated T4.
  • B. Decreased T3.
  • C. Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone.
  • D. Decreased cholesterol.
B Hypothyroidism lowers circulating thyroid hormone, so decreased T3 is expected.
A, C, D T4 is decreased, cholesterol is elevated, and secondary hypothyroidism has decreased or expected-range TSH rather than elevated TSH.
2

Which findings should the nurse expect when collecting a history for hypothyroidism? Select all that apply.

  • A. Diarrhea.
  • B. Menorrhagia.
  • C. Dry skin.
  • D. Increased libido.
  • E. Hoarseness.
B, C, E Hypothyroidism can cause abnormal menstrual bleeding, dry skin, and hoarse/raspy speech from laryngeal myxedema.
A, D Constipation and decreased libido are more consistent with hypothyroidism than diarrhea or increased libido.
3

Which instructions should the nurse include for a client starting levothyroxine? Select all that apply.

  • A. "Weight gain is expected while taking this medication."
  • B. "Do not stop the medication unless your provider tells you to."
  • C. "Keep follow-up appointments for blood TSH monitoring."
  • D. "Take this medication on an empty stomach."
  • E. "Use fiber laxatives first for constipation."
B, C, D Levothyroxine dosing is provider-titrated, monitored with TSH, and absorbed best when taken on an empty stomach.
A, E Replacement therapy increases metabolic activity, so weight gain is not the intended effect; fiber products can reduce levothyroxine absorption.
4

Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care for myxedema coma? Select all that apply.

  • A. Observe the cardiac monitor for dysrhythmias.
  • B. Assess for urinary tract infection.
  • C. Initiate IV fluids using 0.9% sodium chloride.
  • D. Administer levothyroxine IV bolus as prescribed.
  • E. Apply an electric heating pad for warming.
A, B, C, D Myxedema coma requires cardiac monitoring, trigger assessment such as infection, sodium chloride replacement as prescribed, and IV thyroid hormone because GI absorption is unreliable.
E Warm with blankets; avoid heating pads because decreased sensation and alertness increase burn risk.
5

A client recently started levothyroxine. Which finding should the nurse report because the dose might need to be decreased?

  • A. Hand tremors.
  • B. Bradycardia.
  • C. Pallor.
  • D. Slow speech.
A Tremor suggests over-replacement and a hyperthyroid response, so the provider might need to lower the levothyroxine dose.
B, C, D Bradycardia, pallor, and slow speech are hypothyroid findings and can indicate continued need for replacement therapy.

Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 80

Cushing's Disease/Syndrome

Cushing's disease/syndrome is the high-cortisol side of adrenal disorders. Nursing priorities are to recognize the cortisol-overload pattern, protect fragile skin and bones, prevent infection, watch sodium/water/glucose/potassium shifts, prepare for pituitary or adrenal procedures, and prevent adrenal crisis when cortisol drops too fast.

TL;DR · Too Much Cortisol

Cushing disease/syndrome means excess adrenal cortex hormone effect, especially cortisol. Expect infection without strong inflammatory cues, fragile skin, bruising, hypertension, tachycardia, edema, weight gain, moon face, truncal obesity, buffalo hump, purple striae, osteoporosis/fractures, muscle wasting, impaired glucose tolerance, hyperglycemia, mood changes, hirsutism, and poor wound healing. Labs trend high cortisol, high urine free cortisol, high sodium/glucose, low potassium/calcium/lymphocytes. Rescue priorities are fluid overload, infection, fracture/skin injury, GI bleeding, and adrenal crisis.

Sort the cause

  • Cushing disease can come from pituitary ACTH excess or adrenal cortex hyperplasia.
  • Cushing syndrome can come from long-term therapeutic glucocorticoid use.
  • ACTH helps separate pituitary-driven cortisol excess from adrenal or medication-related patterns.

Protect the client

  • Daily weight and intake/output catch fluid retention before pulmonary edema, hypertension, or heart failure.
  • Use infection, skin, and fall precautions because cortisol suppresses immunity, weakens tissue, and contributes to osteoporosis.
  • After tumor removal or steroid withdrawal, watch for adrenal crisis: hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, abdominal pain, weakness, and weight loss.

Cushing Priorities

Hormone and Cause Map

ATI source-authored

Adrenal cortex hormones

  • Mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone increase sodium absorption and potassium excretion in the kidney.
  • Glucocorticoids such as cortisol affect glucose, protein, and fat metabolism, the stress response, and immune function.
  • The adrenal cortex also produces sex hormones, including androgens and estrogens.
  • Excess cortisol drives many of the metabolic, immune, skin, bone, and cardiovascular findings in Cushing disease/syndrome.

Disease vs syndrome

  • Cushing disease can result from a pituitary tumor releasing ACTH, which stimulates adrenal cortisol secretion.
  • Adrenal cortex hyperplasia can also cause Cushing disease.
  • Cushing syndrome can result from long-term therapeutic glucocorticoid use for conditions such as asthma, autoimmune disease, allergies, chemotherapy support, organ transplant, or chronic fibrosis.
  • Other endogenous causes include adrenal tumors and ACTH-producing tumors in the lung, gastrointestinal tract, or pancreas.

Assessment Pattern

Cortisol overload

General and skin cues

  • Expected findings include weakness, fatigue, sleep disturbance, back/joint pain, irritability, depression, emotional lability, and decreased libido.
  • Immune suppression can hide infection signs, so infection might occur without expected fever, swelling, drainage, or redness.
  • Skin and tissue findings include thin fragile skin, bruising, petechiae, poor wound healing, acne, red cheeks, hirsutism, thinning hair, and reddish-purple striae.
  • Female reproductive changes can include irregular scant menses and clitoral hypertrophy.

Cardiometabolic and bone cues

  • Sodium and water retention can cause hypertension, tachycardia, dependent edema, and hypervolemia risk.
  • Weight gain and increased appetite are common, with moon face, truncal obesity, and a fat pad on the back of the neck.
  • Impaired glucose tolerance and hyperglycemia occur because cortisol changes glucose metabolism.
  • Osteoporosis, bone pain, fractures, increased fall risk, and extremity muscle wasting are high-yield safety concerns.

Labs and Diagnostics

Cortisol, ACTH, electrolytes

Laboratory pattern

  • Elevated blood cortisol without acute illness or stress supports Cushing disease/syndrome.
  • Twenty-four-hour urine collection can show elevated free cortisol, and elevated salivary cortisol can confirm the diagnosis.
  • ACTH is elevated when the anterior pituitary hypersecretes ACTH; ACTH is decreased when adrenal cortex disease or medication therapy is the driver.
  • Potassium, calcium, and lymphocytes decrease; glucose and sodium increase.

Suppression and imaging

  • Dexamethasone suppression testing evaluates whether cortisol excretion suppresses after oral dexamethasone.
  • Lack of cortisol suppression supports Cushing disease/syndrome.
  • Acute illness and alcohol use disorder can create false-positive dexamethasone suppression results.
  • X-ray, MRI, arteriography, and CT can help identify lesions in the pituitary, adrenal gland, lung, gastrointestinal tract, or pancreas.

Daily Nursing Care

Fluid, skin, infection, fracture

Fluid and safety monitoring

  • Monitor intake/output and daily weight.
  • Assess for hypervolemia: edema, distended neck veins, shortness of breath, adventitious breath sounds, hypertension, and tachycardia.
  • Keep the environment safe to reduce pathologic fracture risk and skin trauma.
  • Encourage physical activity within the client's limits and arrange home follow-up when weakness or fall risk requires support.

Skin and infection prevention

  • Use frequent hand hygiene and surgical asepsis for dressing changes and invasive procedures.
  • Provide meticulous skin care and reposition at least every 2 hr when indicated.
  • Monitor skin breakdown, infection sources, and WBC count with differential.
  • Teach daily weight reporting for weight gain greater than 2 lb in 24 hr or 3 lb in a week.
  • Request a dietitian consult for decreased sodium and increased potassium, protein, calcium, and vitamin D intake.

Medication Map

Inhibit, destroy, replace

Ketoconazole and mitotane

  • Treatment depends on cause; exogenous Cushing syndrome can require tapering glucocorticoids while managing findings.
  • High-dose ketoconazole inhibits adrenal corticosteroid synthesis and can supplement radiation or surgery.
  • With ketoconazole, monitor liver enzymes, yellow sclera, dark urine, fluids, electrolytes, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, skin changes, and dizziness; taking with food can reduce gastric effects.
  • Mitotane selectively destroys adrenocortical cells and can treat inoperable adrenal carcinoma.
  • With mitotane, monitor shock, renal damage, hepatotoxicity, and orthostatic hypotension; teach reporting visual changes or hematuria and using caution with driving.

Hydrocortisone replacement

  • Hydrocortisone can replace glucocorticoid after treatment causes adrenocortical insufficiency.
  • It can be used with ketoconazole to avoid adrenal insufficiency.
  • Monitor potassium, glucose, blood pressure, pulse, daily weight, and infection manifestations.
  • Notify the provider for weight gain greater than 5 lb in a week.
  • Teach emergency corticosteroid identification, no skipped doses, infection avoidance, and provider consultation before over-the-counter medications or supplements.

Procedures and Surgical Care

Pituitary or adrenal source

Hypophysectomy

  • Hypophysectomy removes the pituitary gland when indicated by the cause of Cushing disease.
  • Monitor and correct sodium, potassium, chloride, glucose, and ECG changes.
  • Prevent infection and fractures, monitor bleeding, and assess nasal drainage for glucose or halo sign indicating possible CSF leak.
  • Assess neurologic status hourly for the first 24 hr and then every 4 hr.
  • Give glucocorticoids before, during, and after surgery to prevent abrupt cortisol drop.

Adrenalectomy

  • Adrenalectomy removes one or both adrenal glands and requires close postoperative monitoring, often in ICU.
  • Provide glucocorticoid and hormone replacement as prescribed.
  • Monitor for adrenal crisis after abrupt cortisol drop: hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, nausea, and headache.
  • Monitor vital signs and hemodynamics initially every 15 min, plus fluids, electrolytes, incision bleeding, bowel sounds, pain, abdominal distention, and incision infection cues.
  • Teach postoperative pain control, deep breathing, anti-embolism care, and replacement medication adherence.

Transsphenoidal Teaching

Prevent increased ICP and CSF leak
  • Transsphenoidal hypophysectomy reaches the pituitary through the sphenoid sinus via the nasal cavity or under the upper lip.
  • Expect nasal packing and a drip pad; the client will breathe through the mouth.
  • Avoid coughing, sneezing, blowing the nose, bending at the waist, straining, and constipation because these increase intracranial pressure.
  • If bending is necessary, bend at the knees; eat high-fiber foods and take docusate as prescribed.
  • Avoid tooth brushing for 2 weeks; floss and rinse the mouth with warm water instead.
  • Report increased swallowing, halo drainage, clear nasal drainage, headache, excessive bleeding, or confusion.
  • Numbness at the surgical site and diminished smell can occur for several months.

Complications

GI, bone, infection, adrenal crisis

Cortisol excess complications

  • Perforated viscera or ulceration can occur because high cortisol decreases protective gastric mucus and increases gastric acid.
  • Monitor for GI bleeding, including tarry black stool and coffee-ground emesis; administer antacids or H2 blockers as prescribed.
  • Teach avoiding alcohol, caffeine, smoking, aspirin, and NSAIDs when GI bleeding risk is a concern.
  • Bone fracture risk increases with hypocalcemia and osteoporosis; use careful movement, ambulation assistance, fall prevention, calcium/vitamin D intake, and avoidance of dangerous activities.
  • Infection risk increases from immunosuppression and reduced inflammatory response; monitor subtle cues, WBCs, urine, and skin sources.

Adrenal crisis

  • Adrenal crisis is acute adrenal insufficiency from sudden tumor removal, stress, dehydration, or abrupt steroid withdrawal.
  • Findings include hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, abdominal pain, weakness, and weight loss.
  • Administer glucocorticoids as prescribed to treat acute adrenal insufficiency.
  • Treat hyperkalemia as prescribed with insulin plus dextrose, potassium-binding/excreting resin, or loop/thiazide diuretics.
  • Treat hypoglycemia with glucagon or IV glucose bolus, and monitor vital signs, glucose, and ECG.
  • Teach steroid tapering and the need for additional glucocorticoids during stress.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Hydrocortisone After Adrenal Treatment

ATI-supported ALS

Therapeutic use

  • Hydrocortisone is a glucocorticoid replacement medication.
  • It treats adrenal insufficiency that can occur after adrenalectomy or other Cushing disease treatment.
  • Replacement prevents an abrupt cortisol deficit and helps reduce adrenal crisis risk.

Client teaching

  • Carry emergency identification about corticosteroid use.
  • Take doses as prescribed without skipping.
  • Report abdominal pain or black, tarry stools.
  • Report manifestations of infection.
  • Eat foods high in calcium and vitamin D, and consult the provider before taking over-the-counter medications or supplements.

Application Exercises

1

Which risks should the nurse anticipate for a client who has Cushing's disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Infection.
  • B. Gastric ulcer.
  • C. Renal calculi.
  • D. Bone fractures.
  • E. Dysphagia.
A, B, D Cortisol suppresses immune function, increases gastric ulcer risk, and contributes to osteoporosis with fracture risk.
C, E Renal calculi and dysphagia are not the expected high-yield Cushing risks in this ATI source set.
2

At the beginning of shift, which finding is the priority for a client who has Cushing's disease?

  • A. Weight gain.
  • B. Fatigue.
  • C. Fragile skin.
  • D. Joint pain.
A Weight gain signals fluid retention, which can progress to pulmonary edema, hypertension, and heart failure.
B, C, D Fatigue, fragile skin, and joint pain matter, but fluid overload creates the more immediate physiologic risk.
3

Which laboratory findings should the nurse expect with Cushing's disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Sodium 150 mEq/L.
  • B. Potassium 3.3 mEq/L.
  • C. Calcium 8.0 mg/dL.
  • D. Lymphocyte count 35%.
  • E. Fasting glucose 145 mg/dL.
A, B, C, E Cushing disease can cause hypernatremia, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperglycemia.
D Lymphocytes are expected to decrease; 35% is not the decreased pattern tested here.
4

Six hours after transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, the nurse should test nasal drainage for which finding?

  • A. RBCs.
  • B. Ketones.
  • C. Glucose.
  • D. Streptococci.
C Cerebrospinal fluid contains glucose, so glucose in nasal drainage can support concern for a CSF leak.
A, B, D RBCs, ketones, and bacteria are not the expected bedside test target for post-hypophysectomy CSF leak screening.
5

Which discharge instructions should the nurse include after transsphenoidal hypophysectomy? Select all that apply.

  • A. Brush teeth after every meal or snack.
  • B. Avoid bending at the knees.
  • C. Eat a high-fiber diet.
  • D. Notify the provider of increased swallowing.
  • E. Notify the provider of a diminished sense of smell.
C, D High-fiber intake helps prevent straining and increased intracranial pressure; increased swallowing can indicate CSF leak.
A, B, E Avoid tooth brushing for 2 weeks, bend at the knees rather than the waist, and diminished smell can be expected temporarily.

Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 81

Addison's Disease and Acute Adrenal Insufficiency (Addisonian Crisis)

Addison's disease is adrenocortical insufficiency: too little aldosterone and cortisol. Nursing priorities are to recognize the salt-losing, volume-depleted, low-glucose, high-potassium pattern; prevent circulatory shock; replace glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids safely; and treat Addisonian crisis as a rapid-onset emergency.

TL;DR · Too Little Cortisol and Aldosterone

Addison's disease decreases mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids, so the body loses sodium and water, retains potassium, and cannot meet stress needs. Expect weight loss, salt craving, hyperpigmentation, weakness, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, bowel changes, dizziness with orthostatic hypotension, dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and hypercalcemia. Addisonian crisis is fast and dangerous: establish IV access, give 0.9% sodium chloride, hydrocortisone, hyperkalemia treatment, glucose support, and vasopressors if needed.

Think low hormones

  • Aldosterone loss causes sodium/water loss and potassium retention.
  • Cortisol loss impairs stress response and contributes to hypoglycemia.
  • Older adults tolerate complications poorly and need closer monitoring.

Rescue pattern

  • The primary goal in acute adrenal insufficiency is preventing circulatory shock.
  • Hyperkalemia cues include bradycardia, heart block, peaked T waves, muscle weakness, tingling, and irregular heartbeat.
  • Teach no abrupt steroid stopping, stress-dose planning, emergency hydrocortisone, and immediate care for illness, trauma, or major stress.

Addison and Addisonian Crisis Priorities

Hormone Pattern

ATI source-authored

Adrenal cortex output

  • Addison's disease is adrenocortical insufficiency caused by adrenal cortex damage or dysfunction.
  • Mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone normally increase sodium absorption and potassium excretion in the kidney.
  • Glucocorticoids such as cortisol affect glucose, protein, and fat metabolism, the stress response, and immune function.
  • When aldosterone and cortisol fall, sodium and water losses, potassium retention, and poor stress response become the core safety problems.

Crisis definition

  • Acute adrenal insufficiency, or Addisonian crisis, has rapid onset and is a medical emergency.
  • The crisis occurs when the body's need for cortisol is greater than the available supply.
  • If Addisonian crisis is not diagnosed and treated quickly, the prognosis is poor.
  • Older adult clients need more frequent monitoring because complications are harder to tolerate.

Causes and Crisis Triggers

Primary, secondary, acute

Primary and secondary causes

  • The most common primary cause is idiopathic autoimmune dysfunction.
  • Other primary causes include tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, adrenalectomy, metastatic cancer, and abdominal radiation therapy.
  • Secondary Addison's disease can result from steroid withdrawal, hypophysectomy, pituitary neoplasm, or high-dose radiation to the pituitary gland or entire brain.
  • ACTH testing helps separate primary from secondary patterns when the client is not in acute crisis.

Acute triggers

  • Sepsis and trauma can precipitate acute adrenal insufficiency.
  • Stressors include myocardial infarction, surgery, anesthesia, hypothermia, volume loss, and hypoglycemia.
  • Adrenal hemorrhage and steroid withdrawal can also trigger crisis.
  • Clients should notify the provider about infection, trauma, or stress because glucocorticoid needs can increase.

Expected Findings

Slow chronic, fast acute

Chronic Addison pattern

  • Chronic findings develop slowly and can include weight loss, salt craving, hyperpigmentation of skin and mucous membranes, weakness, and fatigue.
  • GI findings can include nausea, anorexia, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, or diarrhea.
  • Orthostatic hypotension can cause dizziness when standing or moving from lying to sitting.
  • Dehydration can develop from sodium and water losses.

Acute danger pattern

  • Acute adrenal insufficiency develops rapidly and can cause severe hypotension.
  • Expected electrolyte and metabolic findings include hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and hypercalcemia.
  • Hyperkalemia can produce muscle weakness, tingling, irregular heartbeat, bradycardia, heart block, and peaked T waves.
  • Hypoglycemia cues can include diaphoresis, shaking, tachycardia, and headache.

Labs and Diagnostics

Electrolytes, cortisol, ACTH

Expected labs

  • Blood electrolytes can show increased potassium, increased calcium, decreased sodium, and increased WBC.
  • BUN and creatinine can increase due to dehydration.
  • Blood glucose is normal to decreased.
  • Blood or salivary cortisol is decreased.

ACTH and imaging

  • In the ACTH stimulation test, ACTH is infused and cortisol response is measured 30 min and 1 hr after injection.
  • With primary adrenal insufficiency, plasma cortisol does not rise after ACTH.
  • With secondary adrenal insufficiency, plasma cortisol levels are increased in response to ACTH.
  • Do not perform the ACTH test during acute crisis.
  • ECG monitors electrolyte-related dysrhythmias; x-ray, CT, or MRI can help identify tumor, adrenal atrophy, or another source.

Addisonian Crisis Care

Prevent shock

First priorities

  • The primary goal is preventing circulatory shock.
  • Establish IV access and begin rapid 0.9% sodium chloride infusion as prescribed.
  • Position the client recumbent with legs elevated.
  • Monitor vital signs, orthostatic vital signs, daily weight, dehydration, fluid balance, electrolytes, glucose, and ECG.
  • Administer hydrocortisone sodium as an IV bolus initially, then as continuous infusion or intermittent IV bolus; IM administration can also be used.

Correct potassium and glucose

  • For hyperkalemia, measure potassium, obtain ECG, monitor dysrhythmias, and give prescribed potassium-shifting or potassium-removing therapies.
  • Insulin plus dextrose moves potassium into cells; sodium polystyrene sulfonate absorbs potassium.
  • Calcium helps counter hyperkalemia effects and protect the heart.
  • Sodium bicarbonate can be prescribed when acidosis is present to promote alkalinity and potassium shift into cells.
  • Loop or thiazide diuretics can help manage hyperkalemia.
  • Treat hypoglycemia with glucose support or glucagon as prescribed.

Replacement Medication Map

Glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid

Hydrocortisone, prednisone, cortisone

  • Glucocorticoids are used as adrenocorticoid replacement for adrenal insufficiency and can also be anti-inflammatory.
  • Monitor weight, blood pressure, and electrolytes.
  • Increase dosage during periods of stress or illness if prescribed.
  • Taper the dose if discontinuing to avoid acute adrenal insufficiency.
  • Give with food to reduce GI effects.

Fludrocortisone and support meds

  • Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid replacement for adrenal insufficiency.
  • Hypertension is a potential adverse effect, and the dosage can need adjustment during stress or illness.
  • Monitor weight, blood pressure, and electrolytes.
  • Mild peripheral edema can be expected, but weight gain should be reported.
  • Vasopressors can be used for persistent hypotension, and antibiotics treat infection when present.

Client Education

Prevent crisis
  • Do not stop glucocorticoids abruptly; medication therapy can be lifelong.
  • Take hydrocortisone with food, report acute illness, and report adrenal insufficiency cues such as fever, fatigue, muscle weakness, dizziness, or anorexia.
  • Report Cushing-type overreplacement cues such as round face, edema, or weight gain.
  • Avoid alcohol and caffeine, and monitor for GI bleeding such as coffee-ground emesis or tarry black stool.
  • Monitor for hypoglycemia and keep a 15 g carbohydrate snack readily available.
  • Keep an emergency kit with hydrocortisone for Addisonian crisis; inject it and seek immediate medical care as directed.
  • Avoid stress and strenuous activity in hot weather, and replace sodium lost during nausea/vomiting episodes as directed.

Complication Focus

Hypoglycemia and electrolytes

Hypoglycemia

  • Insufficient glucocorticoid increases insulin sensitivity and decreases glycogen, leading to hypoglycemia.
  • Monitor glucose levels.
  • Administer glucagon as needed.
  • Teach hypoglycemia cues: diaphoresis, shaking, tachycardia, and headache.

Hyperkalemia/hyponatremia

  • Low aldosterone increases sodium excretion and decreases potassium excretion.
  • Monitor electrolytes and ECG.
  • Administer prescribed IV insulin, sodium polystyrene sulfonate, or loop diuretics.
  • Teach reporting muscle weakness, tingling, or irregular heartbeat.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Addison's Disease

ATI-supported ALS

Risk factors

  • Most common cause: autoimmune dysfunction.
  • Additional primary causes include tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, adrenalectomy, and cancer.
  • Radiation therapy of the abdomen can also damage adrenal function.

Expected findings

  • Hyperpigmentation.
  • Weight loss and craving for salt.
  • Weakness and fatigue.
  • Nausea and vomiting.
  • Dizziness when standing or moving from lying to sitting.

Application Exercises

1

Which instructions should the nurse include for a client who has Addison's disease and takes hydrocortisone? Select all that apply.

  • A. Take the medication on an empty stomach.
  • B. Notify the provider of any illness or stress.
  • C. Report manifestations of weakness or dizziness.
  • D. Do not discontinue the medication suddenly.
  • E. Eat a low-sodium diet.
B, C, D Stress can increase glucocorticoid need, weakness/dizziness can indicate adrenal insufficiency, and abrupt stopping can trigger crisis.
A, E Hydrocortisone should be taken with food, and Addison's disease can require sodium replacement rather than sodium restriction.
2

Which laboratory results should the nurse expect for Addison's disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Sodium 130 mEq/L.
  • B. Potassium 6.1 mEq/L.
  • C. Calcium 11.6 mg/dL.
  • D. BUN 28 mg/dL.
  • E. Fasting blood glucose 148 mg/dL.
A, B, C, D Addison's disease can cause hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia, and dehydration-related BUN elevation.
E Blood glucose is expected to be normal to low, not elevated fasting hyperglycemia.
3

Which prescriptions should the nurse expect for acute adrenal insufficiency? Select all that apply.

  • A. IV therapy with 0.45% sodium chloride.
  • B. Regular insulin.
  • C. Hydrocortisone sodium succinate.
  • D. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate.
  • E. Furosemide.
B, C, D, E Insulin shifts potassium into cells, hydrocortisone replaces deficient corticosteroid, sodium polystyrene sulfonate removes potassium, and loop diuretics promote potassium excretion.
A Acute adrenal insufficiency requires volume and sodium replacement with 0.9% sodium chloride, not hypotonic 0.45% sodium chloride.
4

Which teaching point should the nurse include about the ACTH stimulation test?

  • A. The test measures the kidney response to ACTH.
  • B. Primary adrenal insufficiency causes cortisol to rise after ACTH.
  • C. ACTH is a hormone produced by the pituitary gland.
  • D. The client takes ACTH by mouth the evening before the test.
C ACTH is secreted by the pituitary after hypothalamic stimulation and is used to test adrenal cortisol response.
A, B, D The test measures adrenal response, primary adrenal insufficiency does not produce a cortisol rise, and ACTH is infused during testing with cortisol measured afterward.
